passages.title: Arrays & hashing — Intuition
passages.text: A hash map trades memory for time: instead of searching for something, you compute where it lives. Most "find a pair / group things / count things" array problems drop from O(n²) to O(n) the moment you ask "what would I like to look up instantly?" and store exactly that.

passages.title: Arrays & hashing — Core idea / math
passages.text: - A hash function maps a key to an integer; `index = hash(key) % num_buckets`. - **Collisions** (two keys, same bucket) are unavoidable. Separate chaining keeps a small list per bucket; open addressing probes for the next free slot. - **Load factor** α = items / buckets. Expected chain length is α, so keeping α below a constant (0.75 here) keeps operations O(1) on average. Doubling on resize makes the resize cost O(1) *amortized* per insert (total copy work 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n < 2n).

passages.title: Arrays & hashing — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Average | Worst | |---|---|---| | HashMap get / put / delete | O(1) | O(n) (all keys in one bucket) | | two_sum, longest_consecutive, product_except_self, top_k (bucket sort) | O(n) time, O(n) space | | | group_anagrams | O(total characters) | |

passages.title: Arrays & hashing — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using a mutable object (list) as a key: keys must be hashable and must not change. - `longest_consecutive`: forgetting the "only start at the beginning of a run" check makes it O(n²). - `product_except_self`: division breaks when the array contains a zero. - `two_sum`: insert *after* checking, otherwise an element pairs with itself. - Iterating over a dict while modifying it.

passages.title: Arrays & hashing — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Hash map: need fast exact-match lookup, order does not matter. - Sorting + two pointers: O(1) extra space matters, or you need ordered output. - Balanced tree / sorted list: you need range queries or the min/max (hash maps cannot do these). - Array indexed by value (counting): keys are small integers.

passages.title: Backtracking — Intuition
passages.text: Backtracking is organised trial and error. Picture a tree of decisions: at each level you make one choice (take this number or not, put the queen in this column, write this digit). You walk down the tree; if you reach a dead end you step back one level, undo the last choice, and try the next option. The power comes from **pruning**: detecting a dead end early cuts off the whole subtree below it.

passages.title: Backtracking — Core idea — the template
passages.text: ``` def explore(state): if state is a complete answer: record a COPY; return for choice in choices(state): if not valid(choice): continue # prune apply(choice) # choose explore(state) # explore undo(choice) # un-choose ``` - Subsets: binary take/skip decisions → 2ⁿ leaves. - Permutations: pick any unused element → n! leaves. - Combinations: pick in increasing order (a `start` index) so each set is generated once. - Duplicates: sort, then skip a value equal to the previous one *at the same depth*. - N-Queens: one queen per row; columns and both diagonals tracked in sets (`r - c`, `r + c`). - Sudoku: choose the most constrained cell first (fewest candidates).

passages.title: Backtracking — Complexity
passages.text: | Problem | Time | Space (besides output) | |---|---|---| | subsets | O(n · 2ⁿ) | O(n) | | permutations | O(n · n!) | O(n) | | combinations | O(k · C(n, k)) | O(k) | | N-Queens | O(n!) worst case | O(n) | | Sudoku | exponential worst case; fast in practice with pruning | O(81) |

passages.title: Backtracking — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Appending `current` instead of `current.copy()` → every answer ends up identical (and empty). - Forgetting to undo a choice (state leaks into sibling branches). - Generating duplicates: missing the `start` index (combinations) or the same-depth skip rule. - Checking validity only at the leaves instead of pruning as early as possible.

passages.title: Backtracking — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Need to **enumerate all** solutions, or constraints are irregular → backtracking. - Only need a count/optimum and subproblems overlap → dynamic programming (often bitmask DP). - Greedy works if a local choice is provably safe. - Very hard constraint problems → constraint propagation / SAT solvers (same idea, more pruning).

passages.title: Binary search — Intuition
passages.text: Binary search is not really about sorted arrays. It is about a **yes/no question whose answer flips exactly once** as you move along a range: `No No No Yes Yes Yes`. Ask the question in the middle; whichever answer you get, half the range is ruled out. "Is `nums[mid] >= target`?" is one such question; "can we finish in time at speed `mid`?" is another (search on the *answer space*).

passages.title: Binary search — Core idea
passages.text: Maintain the invariant "the boundary is inside `[lo, hi]`". Template used here: ``` while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 if pred(mid): hi = mid # mid could be the first True else: lo = mid + 1 # mid is False, boundary is to the right return lo ``` The range shrinks every iteration because `mid < hi` whenever `lo < hi`.

passages.title: Binary search — Complexity
passages.text: O(log n) probes. For answer-space search: O(log(range) × cost of one feasibility check), e.g. `min_eating_speed` is O(n log max(piles)). Space O(1).

passages.title: Binary search — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Infinite loop from `lo = mid` with `mid = (lo + hi) // 2` (rounds down, never advances). If you need `lo = mid`, round up: `mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2`. - Mixing the two styles: `while lo <= hi` goes with `hi = mid - 1`; `while lo < hi` goes with `hi = mid`. - Overflow of `lo + hi` in fixed-width languages (use `lo + (hi - lo) // 2`); not an issue in Python. - Answer-space search with a predicate that is **not monotonic**. - Rotated arrays with duplicates: `nums[lo] == nums[mid]` is ambiguous; worst case degrades to O(n).

passages.title: Binary search — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Static sorted data, lookups → binary search (O(log n), O(1) space). - Frequent inserts/deletes → balanced BST / hash map. - "Minimise the maximum" / "maximise the minimum" with a cheap greedy check → search the answer. - Unimodal function (single peak) → ternary search or binary search on the slope.

passages.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D grid — Intuition
passages.text: Dynamic programming (DP) is "recursion without repeated work". If a problem can be answered by combining answers to smaller versions of itself, and those smaller versions *repeat*, solve each one once and remember it. Two ingredients must be present: - **Optimal substructure:** the best answer is built from best answers to subproblems. - **Overlapping subproblems:** the same subproblem is needed many times (otherwise plain divide-and-conquer suffices).

passages.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D grid — Core idea — the five steps
passages.text: 1. **State:** what does `dp[i]` (or `dp[r][c]`) mean, in one sentence? 2. **Recurrence:** how does it depend on smaller states? (Think about the *last* decision.) 3. **Base cases.** 4. **Order:** fill so that dependencies are computed first (or memoize top-down). 5. **Space:** keep only what the recurrence looks back at. | Problem | State | Recurrence | |---|---|---| | house robber | best using first i houses | `max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + v[i])` | | max subarray (Kadane) | best sum ending at i | `max(x, dp[i-1] + x)` | | coin change | fewest coins for amount a | `1 + min(dp[a-c])` | | word break | can s[:i] be segmented | `any(dp[j] and s[j:i] in words)` | | unique paths | #paths to (r, c) | `dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1]` | | maximal square | side of square ending at (r, c) | `1 + min(up, left, diag)` |

passages.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D grid — Complexity
passages.text: Time = (number of states) × (work per state). Space = number of states you keep. Most 1D problems here: O(n) time, O(1) space. Coin change: O(amount × coins). Word break: O(n × L) set lookups. Grids: O(rows × cols) time, O(cols) space possible.

passages.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D grid — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Vague state definition ("best so far" vs "best *ending here*" are different problems). - Greedy coin change (largest coin first) fails for coins like {1, 3, 4} and amount 6. - Off-by-one base cases; using padding (an extra row/column of zeros) removes them. - Top-down recursion depth in Python for large n. - Initialising "impossible" with a value that can be mistaken for a real answer.

passages.title: Dynamic programming: 1D and 2D grid — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Counting ways / min / max / feasibility over sequential decisions → DP. - Local choice provably optimal → greedy (faster, simpler). - Need to list all solutions → backtracking. - Grid shortest path with moves in all four directions → BFS/Dijkstra (DP needs an acyclic order).

passages.title: Interval DP and bitmask DP — Intuition
passages.text: **Interval DP.** The state is a contiguous range `[i, j]` of the input. The answer for a range is found by trying every way to split it into two smaller ranges (or every choice of the *last* action inside it). Solve ranges in order of increasing length so the pieces are ready. **Bitmask DP.** Sometimes the state must remember *which items have been used*, not just how many. For small n, a set of items fits in the bits of one integer: bit `i` is 1 iff item `i` is used. The DP table is indexed by that integer. This turns n! orderings into 2ⁿ subsets.

passages.title: Interval DP and bitmask DP — Core math
passages.text: - Matrix chain: `cost[i][j] = min_k cost[i][k] + cost[k+1][j] + d[i]·d[k+1]·d[j+1]`. - Burst balloons: choose the **last** balloon `k` in the open interval `(i, j)`: `best[i][j] = max_k best[i][k] + best[k][j] + v[i]·v[k]·v[j]`. - Palindromes: `pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and pal[i+1][j-1]`. - Held-Karp TSP: `best[mask][last] = min over prev in mask: best[mask − {last}][prev] + d[prev][last]`. - Bit tricks: test `mask & (1 << i)`, set `mask | (1 << i)`, clear `mask & ~(1 << i)`, full set `(1 << n) − 1`, count `bin(mask).count("1")`, iterate submasks `sub = (sub − 1) & mask`.

passages.title: Interval DP and bitmask DP — Complexity
passages.text: | Problem | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Matrix chain, burst balloons | O(n³) | O(n²) | | Palindrome partitioning | O(n²) | O(n²) | | Longest palindromic substring (expand) | O(n²) | O(1) | | TSP (Held-Karp) | O(n² · 2ⁿ) | O(n · 2ⁿ) | | Assignment | O(n · 2ⁿ) | O(2ⁿ) | | Partition into k equal subsets | O(n · 2ⁿ) | O(2ⁿ) |

passages.title: Interval DP and bitmask DP — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Interval DP: iterating `i` then `j` in increasing order uses ranges that are not computed yet; iterate by **length** (or `i` descending). - Burst balloons: thinking about the *first* balloon burst makes subproblems depend on each other. - Bitmask: operator precedence (`mask & 1 << i == 0` is wrong; parenthesise). - 2ⁿ blows up quickly: n = 20 is ~1M states (fine), n = 30 is ~1B (not). - Storing redundant state: often something (e.g. "which worker is next") is implied by the mask.

passages.title: Interval DP and bitmask DP — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - "Merge/split a sequence optimally", parenthesisation, palindromes → interval DP. - "Visit/assign every item exactly once", n ≤ ~20 → bitmask DP. - Assignment for large n → Hungarian algorithm (O(n³)). TSP for large n → heuristics / approximation.

passages.title: Knapsack DP (0/1 and unbounded) — Intuition
passages.text: You have a bag with a weight limit and items with weights and values. Which items maximise the value? Trying every subset is 2ⁿ. The DP insight: when deciding about one item, all that matters about the earlier decisions is **how much capacity is left**, not which items used it up. - **0/1:** each item at most once. - **Unbounded:** unlimited copies of each item. A surprising number of problems are knapsack in disguise: subset sum, equal partition, coin change (min coins / number of ways), target sum, rod cutting.

passages.title: Knapsack DP (0/1 and unbounded) — Core math
passages.text: - 0/1: `best[i][c] = max(best[i-1][c], best[i-1][c - wᵢ] + vᵢ)` - Unbounded: `best[i][c] = max(best[i-1][c], best[i][c - wᵢ] + vᵢ)` (note `i`, not `i-1`) - In the 1D array the *only* difference is loop direction: - capacity **descending** → reads old values → each item once (0/1); - capacity **ascending** → reads values already updated with this item → reuse (unbounded). - Counting variants replace `max` with `+`; feasibility variants replace it with `or`. - Combinations vs permutations: **items outer** loop counts combinations; **capacity outer** loop counts ordered sequences.

passages.title: Knapsack DP (0/1 and unbounded) — Complexity
passages.text: O(n · W) time, O(W) space (O(n · W) if you need to reconstruct the chosen items). This is **pseudo-polynomial**: polynomial in the numeric value W, exponential in the number of bits of W. Knapsack is NP-hard in general.

passages.title: Knapsack DP (0/1 and unbounded) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Wrong loop direction in the 1D version (silently turns 0/1 into unbounded or vice versa). - Greedy by value/weight ratio is optimal only for the *fractional* knapsack. - Swapping the loop order when counting ways changes the meaning of the answer. - Huge capacity: DP by weight is infeasible; DP over value or meet-in-the-middle may work. - Zero-weight items / zeros in target-sum need care (each zero doubles the number of ways).

passages.title: Knapsack DP (0/1 and unbounded) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - "Pick a subset subject to a budget" with moderate integer budget → knapsack DP. - Fractions allowed → greedy by ratio. - n ≤ ~40 and huge weights → meet-in-the-middle (2^(n/2)). - Many constraints → integer linear programming / branch and bound.

passages.title: Sequence DP: LIS, LCS, edit distance — Intuition
passages.text: - **LIS (longest increasing subsequence):** pick elements, keeping their order, so they strictly increase; make it as long as possible. - **LCS (longest common subsequence):** the longest sequence appearing (in order, not necessarily contiguously) in *both* inputs. This is what `diff` computes. - **Edit distance:** the fewest single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions to turn one string into another. This powers spell-checkers and DNA alignment. LCS and edit distance share one shape: a 2D table over *prefixes* of the two strings, where each cell looks at the last characters and at three neighbours (up, left, diagonal).

passages.title: Sequence DP: LIS, LCS, edit distance — Core math
passages.text: - LIS O(n²): `best[i] = 1 + max(best[j] for j < i if a[j] < a[i])`. - LIS O(n log n): `tails[k]` = smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length k + 1. `tails` is sorted, so each element is placed by binary search (replace the first tail ≥ x). `tails` is **not** itself an LIS; only its length is meaningful. - LCS: `L[i][j] = L[i-1][j-1] + 1` if `a[i-1] == b[j-1]`, else `max(L[i-1][j], L[i][j-1])`. - Edit distance: `D[i][j] = D[i-1][j-1]` if equal, else `1 + min(D[i-1][j], D[i][j-1], D[i-1][j-1])`; base cases `D[i][0] = i`, `D[0][j] = j`.

passages.title: Sequence DP: LIS, LCS, edit distance — Complexity
passages.text: | Problem | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | LIS (patience) | O(n log n) | O(n) | | LIS (classic DP) | O(n²) | O(n) | | LCS, edit distance | O(n · m) | O(n · m), or O(min(n, m)) for the length only |

passages.title: Sequence DP: LIS, LCS, edit distance — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Subsequence (gaps allowed) vs substring (contiguous): different recurrences. - Strict vs non-decreasing LIS: `bisect_left` gives strict, `bisect_right` gives non-decreasing. - Returning `tails` as the answer sequence. - Edit distance base row/column of zeros instead of 0..n. - Space-optimising to one row and then trying to reconstruct the path (you need the full table, or Hirschberg's algorithm).

passages.title: Sequence DP: LIS, LCS, edit distance — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Similarity of two sequences where order matters → LCS / edit distance. - Only substitutions allowed, equal lengths → Hamming distance (O(n)). - Very long strings with few differences → Myers' O(ND) diff or banded DP. - LIS also solves "minimum number of removals to sort", box/envelope nesting (sort, then LIS).

passages.title: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) — Intuition
passages.text: A plain array makes updates O(1) but prefix sums O(n). A prefix-sum array makes prefix sums O(1) but updates O(n). A Fenwick tree meets in the middle: both are O(log n), in about ten lines. Every number is a sum of powers of two (13 = 8 + 4 + 1), so every prefix of length 13 can be cut into blocks of length 8, 4 and 1. The tree stores exactly those power-of-two-sized block sums.

passages.title: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) — Core math
passages.text: - `lowbit(i) = i & -i` = value of the lowest set bit (two's complement trick). - `tree[i]` = sum of the elements `(i - lowbit(i), i]` (1-indexed). - **Query** prefix `i`: add `tree[i]`, then `i -= lowbit(i)`, until 0. - **Update** position `i`: add to `tree[i]`, then `i += lowbit(i)`, until past n. - Range sum = `prefix(hi) - prefix(lo)`, which is why the operation must be invertible.

passages.title: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Build | O(n) | n + 1 | | add, prefix_sum, range_sum | O(log n) | | | find_kth (binary lifting) | O(log n) | | | count_inversions | O(n log n) | O(n) |

passages.title: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - 0-indexing the internal array: `i & -i` is 0 for `i = 0`, causing an infinite loop. - Using it for min/max: you cannot "subtract" a prefix min (only works for prefix-only queries with monotone updates). - `add` adds a delta; to *set* a value, add `new - old`. - For values that are large or negative, coordinate-compress to ranks first.

passages.title: Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Point update + range sum, counting/order statistics, inversions → Fenwick (smallest, fastest). - Range min/max, non-invertible ops, complex lazy updates → segment tree. - No updates → prefix sums.

passages.title: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort, bipartite check — Intuition
passages.text: - **BFS** explores like ripples in a pond: everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, and so on. It uses a queue. Because it reaches nodes in order of distance, it gives shortest paths when every edge costs the same. - **DFS** explores like walking a maze with a ball of string: go as deep as possible, back up when stuck. It uses a stack (or recursion). It is the tool for "explore everything", cycle detection, and ordering by dependencies. - **Topological sort** lines up the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge points forward (prerequisites before courses). - **Bipartite** means the nodes split into two teams with every edge going between teams; equivalently, the graph has no odd-length cycle.

passages.title: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort, bipartite check — Core idea
passages.text: - Kahn: repeatedly output a node with in-degree 0 and delete its outgoing edges. If nodes remain when none has in-degree 0, they form a cycle. - DFS topo: a node finishes only after everything reachable from it has finished, so *reverse finishing order* is a valid ordering. A gray (in-progress) neighbour is a back edge = cycle. - Bipartite: BFS 2-colouring; an edge between same-coloured nodes proves an odd cycle.

passages.title: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort, bipartite check — Complexity
passages.text: All of these are O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space with adjacency lists (an adjacency matrix makes them O(V²)).

passages.title: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort, bipartite check — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Marking nodes visited when **dequeued** instead of when enqueued → duplicates in the queue. - Using DFS for unweighted shortest paths (it finds *a* path, not the shortest). - Directed cycle detection with a single "visited" set: you need the gray/black distinction (a visited node that is already finished is not a cycle). - Forgetting disconnected graphs: loop over all nodes as possible starts. - Recursion depth in Python on long paths; use the iterative version.

passages.title: Graph traversal: BFS, DFS, topological sort, bipartite check — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Unweighted shortest path, levels, "minimum number of moves" → BFS. - Weighted shortest path → Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford (see `shortest_paths`). - Connectivity that grows over time → union-find. - Kahn vs DFS topo: Kahn is iterative and can produce the lexicographically smallest order with a heap; DFS gives finishing times useful for SCCs.

passages.title: Greedy + intervals — Intuition
passages.text: A greedy algorithm makes the choice that looks best *right now* and never reconsiders. It is fast and simple, but only correct when you can argue that the local choice is always part of some optimal answer. Interval problems are the classic home of greedy: sort the intervals (by start or by end), then sweep once. Rule of thumb for which key to sort by: - **Merging / inserting / sweeping coverage** → sort by **start**. - **Selecting the most non-overlapping / fewest points to hit all** → sort by **end**.

passages.title: Greedy + intervals — Core idea — proving a greedy is right
passages.text: **Exchange argument:** take any optimal solution; show you can swap its first choice for the greedy choice without making it worse. Repeat down the line. Example (activity selection): let `g` be the interval that ends first. In any optimal set, the first interval `o` ends no earlier than `g`, so replacing `o` by `g` conflicts with nothing that follows. So some optimal solution contains `g`. **"Greedy stays ahead"** is the other common proof: after each step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other partial solution (jump game: `farthest` reachable index).

passages.title: Greedy + intervals — Complexity
passages.text: | Problem | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | merge, max non-overlapping, min arrows, fractional knapsack | O(n log n) (the sort) | O(n) | | insert into sorted intervals | O(n) | O(n) | | meeting rooms (heap) | O(n log n) | O(n) | | jump game I/II, gas station | O(n) | O(1) |

passages.title: Greedy + intervals — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Applying greedy where it is not valid (0/1 knapsack, coin change with odd denominations). - Sorting by the wrong key: earliest *start* or *shortest* interval both fail for activity selection. - `<` vs `<=` at touching endpoints: decide whether `(1, 3)` and `(3, 5)` overlap for *this* problem. - Meeting rooms: popping every finished meeting is unnecessary; reusing one room per arrival is enough. - Gas station: forgetting the global feasibility check `sum(gas) >= sum(cost)`.

passages.title: Greedy + intervals — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Greedy when an exchange argument exists: scheduling, Huffman coding, MST, Dijkstra. - DP when choices interact (weighted interval scheduling needs DP + binary search). - Sweep line with events (+1 at start, −1 at end) as an alternative for "max overlap".

passages.title: Heap / priority queue — Intuition
passages.text: A heap answers one question fast: "what is the smallest (or largest) item right now?" It is a binary tree where every parent is no bigger than its children, so the minimum sits at the root. It is **not** fully sorted; it does just enough work to keep the best item on top. The tree is *complete* (filled level by level), so it packs into a plain array with no pointers: `parent(i) = (i-1)//2`, `children(i) = 2i+1, 2i+2`.

passages.title: Heap / priority queue — Core idea
passages.text: - **push:** append at the end, then *sift up* (swap with the parent while smaller). - **pop:** take the root, move the last leaf to the root, then *sift down* (swap with the smaller child while larger). - **heapify:** sift down every internal node from the bottom up. Cost is Σ (nodes at height h) × h = Σ n/2^(h+1) × h = O(n).

passages.title: Heap / priority queue — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | |---|---| | peek | O(1) | | push, pop | O(log n) | | heapify | O(n) | | top-k (size-k heap) | O(n log k), O(k) space | | merge k sorted lists (N items total) | O(N log k) | | median of stream: add / median | O(log n) / O(1) |

passages.title: Heap / priority queue — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Top-k **largest** needs a **min**-heap of size k (the root is the one to beat), not a max-heap. - Assuming the array is sorted: only the root is guaranteed. - Python's `heapq` is min-only; negate values (or use a key) for a max-heap. - Putting uncomparable objects in tuples: add a tie-breaker index, e.g. `(priority, i, obj)`. - Median finder: forgetting to rebalance sizes, or letting an item sit in the wrong half.

passages.title: Heap / priority queue — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Repeated "extract best" with inserts in between (Dijkstra, scheduling, k-way merge) → heap. - Need the k-th element once → quickselect is O(n) average. - Need sorted order of everything → just sort. - Need to delete/update arbitrary items or query ranks → balanced BST / indexed heap.

passages.title: LFU cache — Intuition
passages.text: Evict the entry that has been used the **fewest times**. If several entries tie, evict the one used least recently among them. Compared with LRU, a key that is popular over the long run is not pushed out by a short burst of one-off keys.

passages.title: LFU cache — Core idea
passages.text: Bucket keys by frequency: `groups[f]` is an ordered set of the keys used exactly `f` times (oldest first). Using a key moves it from `groups[f]` to `groups[f + 1]`. Track `min_freq` so the victim is always "the oldest key in `groups[min_freq]`". Why `min_freq` is O(1) to maintain: - inserting a new key ⇒ `min_freq = 1`; - bumping the last key out of `groups[min_freq]` ⇒ that key is now in `groups[min_freq + 1]`, so the new minimum is exactly `min_freq + 1`; - eviction is always followed by an insert, which resets it to 1.

passages.title: LFU cache — Complexity
passages.text: `get`, `put`: O(1). Space O(capacity). (A heap-based LFU would be O(log n) per operation.)

passages.title: LFU cache — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Forgetting the LRU tie-break inside a frequency group. - Not updating `min_freq` when a group becomes empty. - `put` on an existing key must also count as a use. - Capacity 0 must not crash. - **Cache pollution:** a key that was hot long ago keeps a high count forever. Real systems decay counts over time (e.g. TinyLFU, Redis's approximate LFU).

passages.title: LFU cache — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - LFU: stable popularity distribution (CDN objects, hot database rows). - LRU: popularity shifts quickly; simpler; usually the default. - ARC / TinyLFU / W-TinyLFU: adaptive blends used in production caches.

passages.title: Linked list operations — Intuition
passages.text: A linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a pointer to the next node. You cannot jump to position `i`; you can only walk. In exchange, inserting or removing a node is just re-pointing one or two links: O(1) once you are standing next to it. Three tools solve almost every linked-list problem: 1. **Dummy head:** a fake node before the real head so "delete/insert at the head" is not a special case. 2. **Slow/fast pointers:** find the middle, detect a cycle, find the k-th from the end. 3. **In-place reversal:** walk the list flipping each `next` pointer backward.

passages.title: Linked list operations — Core math (Floyd cycle detection)
passages.text: Let `a` = steps from head to the cycle start, `c` = cycle length. When slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps) meet, fast has walked exactly twice as far, and their difference is a multiple of `c`. So `(a + b) ≡ 0 (mod c)` where `b` is the meeting offset inside the cycle. Starting one pointer at head and one at the meeting point and stepping both by 1, they meet after `a` steps at the cycle start.

passages.title: Linked list operations — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Extra space | |---|---|---| | reverse, middle, cycle, merge, remove n-th, reverse k-group | O(n) | O(1) (recursive reverse: O(n) stack) | | sort_list (merge sort) | O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | | access by index | O(n) | |

passages.title: Linked list operations — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Losing the rest of the list: save `cur.next` before overwriting it. - Forgetting the dummy node, then crashing when the head itself is removed. - `while fast and fast.next` — checking only `fast.next` crashes on an empty list. - In `sort_list`, splitting at the second middle makes a 2-node list recurse forever. - Comparing nodes with `==` on values instead of identity (`is`) in cycle problems.

passages.title: Linked list operations — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Linked list: O(1) insert/delete given the node (LRU cache), no reallocation, splice lists. - Array: random access, cache-friendly, binary search. Usually faster in practice. - Sorting: merge sort suits linked lists (no random access needed); quicksort suits arrays.

passages.title: LRU cache — Intuition
passages.text: A cache has limited room. When it is full, throw out the entry that has gone the longest without being touched ("least recently used"), on the bet that recently used things will be used again. We need two things in O(1): *find* an entry by key, and *reorder* entries by recency. No single structure does both, so combine two: - a **hash map** from key to node (fast lookup), - a **doubly linked list** ordered by recency (fast move-to-front and remove-from-back).

passages.title: LRU cache — Core idea
passages.text: - `get(k)`: look up the node, unlink it, push it to the front. - `put(k, v)`: if present, update and move to front. Otherwise, if full, unlink the node before the tail and delete its key from the map; then insert the new node at the front. - Sentinel head/tail nodes mean every real node always has both neighbours, so unlink is two pointer assignments with no `if`.

passages.title: LRU cache — Complexity
passages.text: `get`, `put`: O(1) time. Space O(capacity).

passages.title: LRU cache — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Not storing the **key** inside the node: when evicting from the list you must also delete from the map, and you only have the node. - Forgetting that `get` changes recency. - Updating an existing key but not moving it to the front. - Singly linked list: cannot unlink a middle node in O(1) without its predecessor. - Not thread-safe: real caches need a lock around the map + list update.

passages.title: LRU cache — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - LRU: workloads with temporal locality (recent ⇒ likely again). Simple and the common default. - LFU: some items are popular over the long run and should survive bursts of one-off keys. - FIFO / random eviction: cheaper bookkeeping, worse hit rate. - In Python practice: `functools.lru_cache` or `OrderedDict.move_to_end`.

passages.title: Minimum spanning tree: Prim and Kruskal — Intuition
passages.text: Connect all the towns with roads as cheaply as possible. The result has no cycles (a cycle means one road is redundant), so it is a tree with exactly V − 1 edges. - **Kruskal:** look at roads from cheapest to most expensive; build a road unless the two towns are already connected. Thinks in terms of *edges* and merges components (union-find). - **Prim:** start in one town and repeatedly build the cheapest road from the connected region to a new town. Thinks in terms of *growing one tree* (heap).

passages.title: Minimum spanning tree: Prim and Kruskal — Core math
passages.text: **Cut property:** split the nodes into two non-empty groups; the lightest edge crossing the split belongs to some MST. (If an MST did not use it, adding it creates a cycle that crosses the cut a second time through a heavier-or-equal edge; swapping them does not increase the weight.) Both algorithms repeatedly apply this property with different cuts. **Cycle property:** the heaviest edge on any cycle is not needed.

passages.title: Minimum spanning tree: Prim and Kruskal — Complexity
passages.text: | Algorithm | Time | Space | Best for | |---|---|---|---| | Kruskal | O(E log E) | O(V + E) | sparse graphs, edge lists | | Prim (binary heap) | O(E log V) | O(V + E) | dense graphs, adjacency lists | | Prim (array, no heap) | O(V²) | O(V) | very dense graphs |

passages.title: Minimum spanning tree: Prim and Kruskal — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Confusing MST with shortest paths: the MST minimises *total* weight, not the distance between any particular pair. - Prim: not skipping heap entries whose endpoint is already in the tree. - Disconnected graphs: there is no spanning tree, only a spanning forest. - MSTs are for **undirected** graphs (the directed analogue is the harder arborescence problem). - The MST is unique only if all edge weights are distinct.

passages.title: Minimum spanning tree: Prim and Kruskal — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Network design, clustering (remove the k − 1 heaviest MST edges → k clusters, which is single-linkage clustering), approximating TSP. - Edges already sorted or easy to sort → Kruskal. Dense graph or implicit edges (points in a plane) → Prim.

passages.title: Prefix sums — Intuition
passages.text: If you know the running total up to every position, the total of any stretch in the middle is "total up to the end of the stretch" minus "total up to its start". Pay O(n) once, then answer every range-sum question in O(1).

passages.title: Prefix sums — Core math
passages.text: - `prefix[0] = 0`, `prefix[i] = nums[0] + ... + nums[i-1]`. - `sum(nums[lo:hi]) = prefix[hi] - prefix[lo]`. - 2D (inclusion-exclusion): `S = P[r2][c2] - P[r1][c2] - P[r2][c1] + P[r1][c1]`. - **Difference array** is the inverse: store `d[i] = a[i] - a[i-1]`; a range add becomes two point updates, and a prefix sum of `d` recovers `a`. - **Prefix + hash map:** `sum(i..j) = k` iff `prefix[i] = prefix[j] - k`, turning "count subarrays" into "count earlier prefixes with a given value".

passages.title: Prefix sums — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Build 1D / 2D | O(n) / O(rows·cols) | same | | Range query | O(1) | | | subarray_sum_equals_k, longest_subarray_with_sum | O(n) | O(n) | | m range updates via difference array | O(n + m) | O(n) |

passages.title: Prefix sums — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Off-by-one: using a prefix array of length n instead of n + 1 (the leading 0 removes all edge cases). - Forgetting to seed the hash map with the empty prefix (`{0: 1}` or `{0: -1}`). - For "longest", overwriting the stored index instead of keeping the earliest. - Prefix sums are for **static** arrays; any update costs O(n) to repair.

passages.title: Prefix sums — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Static array, many range sums → prefix sums. - Updates mixed with queries → Fenwick tree or segment tree (O(log n) both). - Range min/max (not invertible, cannot "subtract") → sparse table or segment tree. - All-positive numbers with a sum constraint → sliding window uses O(1) space.

passages.title: Queue, deque, monotonic queue — Intuition
passages.text: - **Queue:** first in, first out, like a line at a shop. Used for BFS and scheduling. - **Deque:** a line where people can join or leave at *both* ends. - **Monotonic queue:** a deque kept sorted by throwing out elements that can never matter again. For "max of every window": if a newer element is bigger than an older one, the older one will leave the window first *and* is smaller, so it is useless. Evict it.

passages.title: Queue, deque, monotonic queue — Core idea
passages.text: Ring buffer: store items in a fixed array, track `head` and `size`; position of item `i` is `(head + i) % capacity`. No shifting is ever needed, so both ends are O(1). When full, copy into an array twice the size (amortized O(1), same argument as a dynamic array). Two-stack queue: each element is pushed to `inbox` once, moved to `outbox` once, popped once → at most 3 operations per element → amortized O(1).

passages.title: Queue, deque, monotonic queue — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | |---|---| | Deque append / appendleft / pop / popleft / index | O(1) amortized | | Two-stack queue push / pop | O(1) amortized (single pop can be O(n)) | | sliding_window_max, shortest_subarray_sum_at_least | O(n) time, O(k) / O(n) space |

passages.title: Queue, deque, monotonic queue — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using `list.pop(0)` as a queue: it is O(n) because every element shifts. - Ring buffer growth: copying the raw array instead of unrolling from `head`. - Monotonic deque storing values instead of indices (you need indices to know when the front expires). - Evicting with `<` vs `<=`: with `<`, equal values pile up (still correct, just bigger).

passages.title: Queue, deque, monotonic queue — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Window max/min → monotonic deque O(n); a heap also works but is O(n log n). - Shortest subarray with sum ≥ k: positives only → sliding window; negatives allowed → prefix sums + monotonic deque. - Need priority rather than arrival order → heap.

passages.title: Quickselect — Intuition
passages.text: To find the k-th smallest element you do not need the whole array sorted; you only need the element that *would* land at position k. Partition around a pivot as in quicksort: the pivot ends up at its final sorted position. If that position is k, done. Otherwise the answer is entirely on one side, so **throw the other side away** and repeat.

passages.title: Quickselect — Core math
passages.text: - Average case with a random pivot: each round keeps about half → n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≤ 2n = O(n). - Worst case (always the smallest/largest pivot): n + (n−1) + … = O(n²). - **Median of medians:** split into groups of 5, take each group's median, recursively take the median of those. That pivot is ≥ about 3n/10 elements and ≤ about 3n/10, so T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n). Since 1/5 + 7/10 < 1, T(n) = O(n) guaranteed.

passages.title: Quickselect — Complexity
passages.text: | Method | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Sort then index | O(n log n) | O(1)–O(n) | | Heap of size k | O(n log k) | O(k) | | Quickselect (random pivot) | O(n) average, O(n²) worst | O(1) in place (O(n) here for the copy) | | Median of medians | O(n) worst case (large constant) | O(n) |

passages.title: Quickselect — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Off-by-one between "k-th smallest (1-based)", "index k (0-based)" and "k-th largest". - Fixed pivot (first/last element) → O(n²) on sorted input. - Two-way partition with many duplicates → O(n²); the 3-way partition here returns as soon as k lands in the "equal" block. - Quickselect reorders the array (this implementation copies first so callers are not surprised). - Not suitable for streams: needs all data in memory (use a heap).

passages.title: Quickselect — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - One-off k-th element / median / top-k on in-memory data → quickselect (`numpy.partition`, C++ `nth_element`). - Streaming data or tiny k → heap. - Many different k on the same data → sort once. - Hard real-time guarantee → median of medians or introselect.

passages.title: Segment tree — Intuition
passages.text: Prefix sums answer range queries instantly but break when the array changes. A segment tree stores the answer for a set of **pre-chosen ranges** arranged as a binary tree: the root covers everything, its children cover each half, and so on down to single elements. Any range can be stitched together from at most ~2·log n of those stored pieces, and changing one element only invalidates the log n pieces that contain it.

passages.title: Segment tree — Core idea
passages.text: - Node = combined value of its segment; `node = op(left child, right child)`. - Works for any **associative** `op` with an identity: sum, min, max, gcd, XOR, matrix product. - **Lazy propagation** (for range *updates*): when an update fully covers a node, update the node's own value and leave a note (`lazy`) for the children; push the note down only when a later operation needs to go below that node.

passages.title: Segment tree — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Build | O(n) | 2n (iterative) / 4n (recursive) | | Point update, range query | O(log n) | | | Range update with lazy | O(log n) | |

passages.title: Segment tree — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Allocating 2n for the *recursive* layout when n is not a power of two (needs up to 4n). - Wrong identity element (e.g. 0 for min). - Lazy: forgetting to push down before recursing, or to recompute the parent afterwards. - Lazy sum: the pending add must be multiplied by the segment length. - Combining left and right partial results in the wrong order for non-commutative ops. - Mixing inclusive and exclusive bounds.

passages.title: Segment tree — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Static array, sums → prefix sums (O(1) query). - Point update + prefix/range **sum** → Fenwick tree (same big-O, far less code and memory). - Range min/max with updates, range updates, or custom merges → segment tree. - Static range min → sparse table (O(1) query).

passages.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall — Intuition
passages.text: All three are built on one move, **relaxation**: "if going to `v` through `u` is shorter than the best route to `v` I know, update it". They differ in the *order* they relax edges. - **Dijkstra** (greedy): always finalise the closest unfinished node. Correct only when weights are non-negative, because then a finalised distance can never be beaten later. - **Bellman-Ford** (brute-force DP): relax *every* edge, V − 1 times. Slower, but handles negative edges and detects negative cycles. - **Floyd-Warshall** (DP over intermediates): all pairs at once; allow node 0 as a stopover, then node 1, ...

passages.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall — Core math
passages.text: - Relaxation: `dist[v] = min(dist[v], dist[u] + w(u, v))`. - Bellman-Ford invariant: after `i` passes, `dist[v]` ≤ the shortest path using at most `i` edges. Shortest simple paths have ≤ V − 1 edges. - Floyd-Warshall recurrence: `d_k[i][j] = min(d_{k-1}[i][j], d_{k-1}[i][k] + d_{k-1}[k][j])`.

passages.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall — Complexity
passages.text: | Algorithm | Time | Space | Negative edges | Scope | |---|---|---|---|---| | BFS (unweighted) | O(V + E) | O(V) | n/a | single source | | Dijkstra (binary heap) | O((V + E) log V) | O(V + E) | no | single source | | Bellman-Ford | O(V · E) | O(V) | yes, detects negative cycles | single source | | Floyd-Warshall | O(V³) | O(V²) | yes, detects negative cycles | all pairs |

passages.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Running Dijkstra with negative edges: silently wrong answers. - Not skipping stale heap entries (`if d > dist[u]: continue`) → correct but much slower. - Floyd-Warshall with `k` not as the outermost loop → wrong. - Bellman-Ford: relaxing from nodes whose distance is still infinity; forgetting that only negative cycles *reachable from the source* matter. - `inf + negative` arithmetic in languages with integer infinity sentinels.

passages.title: Shortest paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Unweighted → BFS. Weights 0/1 → 0-1 BFS with a deque. - Non-negative weights → Dijkstra. With a good heuristic toward one target → A*. - Negative weights or need cycle detection (e.g. currency arbitrage) → Bellman-Ford. - Dense graph, all pairs, small V (≤ ~400) → Floyd-Warshall. Sparse all-pairs → Dijkstra from every node (or Johnson's algorithm with negative edges). - DAG → relax in topological order, O(V + E), any weights.

passages.title: Sliding window — Intuition
passages.text: When the question is about a **contiguous** subarray/substring, do not recompute each candidate from scratch. Keep a window `[left, right]`, extend `right` one step at a time, and move `left` forward only when the window breaks a rule. Because adding/removing one element updates the window's summary (sum, counts) in O(1), the whole scan is O(n). - **Fixed size:** add the new element, subtract the one that fell off. - **Variable size, "longest valid":** grow right; while invalid, shrink left. - **Variable size, "shortest valid":** grow right; while valid, record and shrink left.

passages.title: Sliding window — Core idea
passages.text: Works when validity is **monotonic**: if a window is valid, every sub-window is valid (longest problems), or if it is valid, every super-window is valid (shortest problems). Then `left` never needs to move backward, so both pointers move at most n times: 2n steps total.

passages.title: Sliding window — Complexity
passages.text: All functions here: O(n) time. Space O(1) for sums, O(alphabet) for character counts.

passages.title: Sliding window — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using the sum-based window when numbers can be **negative**: shrinking no longer reliably reduces the sum, so monotonicity breaks (use prefix sums + hash map / monotonic deque instead). - `longest_unique_substring`: jumping `left` backward when the previous occurrence is already outside the window (hence the `>= left` check). - Comparing Counters that still contain zero-count keys. - Off-by-one in window length: it is `right - left + 1`.

passages.title: Sliding window — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Contiguous + monotonic validity → sliding window. - Subarray sum equals k with negatives → prefix sums + hash map. - Max/min of every window → monotonic deque (see `queue_deque`). - Non-contiguous subsequence → usually DP.

passages.title: Sorting algorithms — Intuition
passages.text: - **Insertion sort:** sort a hand of cards — pick up one card at a time and slide it into place. - **Merge sort:** split the pile in two, sort each half, then zip the two sorted halves together. - **Quicksort:** pick a pivot, put smaller things left and bigger things right, repeat on each side. - **Heap sort:** build a max-heap, then keep moving the maximum to the end. - **Counting sort:** if values are small integers, just count how many of each there are. - **Radix sort:** sort by the last digit, then the next digit, and so on, using a *stable* sort.

passages.title: Sorting algorithms — Core math
passages.text: - Comparison sorts need Ω(n log n) comparisons: there are n! possible orderings and each comparison at best halves the candidates, so you need log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n comparisons. - Counting/radix sort beat this bound because they do not compare; they index by value. - Merge sort recurrence: T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = O(n log n). - Quicksort: balanced pivots give the same recurrence; a worst pivot every time gives T(n) = T(n−1) + O(n) = O(n²). A random pivot makes the expected cost O(n log n) on any input.

passages.title: Sorting algorithms — Complexity
passages.text: | Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Insertion | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes | | Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | yes | | Quick (random pivot, 3-way) | O(n) (all equal) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(log n) | no | | Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(1) | no | | Counting | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | O(n + k) | yes | | Radix (LSD) | O(d(n + b)) | same | same | O(n + b) | yes | `k` = value range, `d` = number of digits, `b` = base.

passages.title: Sorting algorithms — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Quicksort with the first element as pivot on sorted input → O(n²) and deep recursion. - Two-way partition with many duplicates → O(n²); use three-way partitioning. - Merge using `<` instead of `<=` loses stability. - Counting sort when the range is huge (k ≫ n) wastes memory. - Radix sort with an unstable inner sort gives wrong results; negatives need special handling.

passages.title: Sorting algorithms — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - General purpose: use the library sort (Python's Timsort = merge + insertion, stable, O(n) on already-sorted runs). - Need guaranteed O(n log n) and O(1) space → heap sort. Need stability / linked lists / external (on-disk) sorting → merge sort. Best average speed in place → quicksort. - Small integer keys → counting sort; fixed-width integers or strings → radix sort. - Only the k smallest → heap or quickselect, not a full sort.

passages.title: Stack & monotonic stack — Intuition
passages.text: A **stack** is "last in, first out": the most recent unfinished thing is the first to be finished. That is exactly the shape of nested structures (brackets, function calls, undo). A **monotonic stack** keeps its contents sorted (always increasing or always decreasing) by popping anything that would break the order before pushing. The items on the stack are "still waiting for an answer"; the moment a new element pops one, that new element *is* its answer (next greater / next smaller element).

passages.title: Stack & monotonic stack — Core idea
passages.text: For next-greater: the stack holds indices with **decreasing** values. When `x` arrives, every index on top with a smaller value has just met its first greater element. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once → O(n) total even though there is a `while` inside the `for`. Histogram: an **increasing** stack. When bar `i` is shorter than the top, the popped bar's rectangle extends from just after the new top to just before `i`.

passages.title: Stack & monotonic stack — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | push / pop / peek / get_min | O(1) | O(n) total | | valid parentheses, RPN | O(n) | O(n) | | next greater, daily temperatures, largest rectangle | O(n) amortized | O(n) |

passages.title: Stack & monotonic stack — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Storing values instead of **indices** (you usually need distances or to write into `out[i]`). - `<` vs `<=` when popping: decides how ties/duplicates are handled. - Forgetting to flush the stack at the end (the sentinel `0` in the histogram does this). - RPN operand order: the first pop is the *right* operand. Python `//` floors; C-style division truncates. - Popping from an empty stack on input like `")"`.

passages.title: Stack & monotonic stack — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Matching/nesting, expression evaluation, DFS without recursion → plain stack. - "Next/previous greater/smaller", spans, histogram areas → monotonic stack. - Sliding-window max/min → monotonic **deque** (needs removal from the front too).

passages.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp — Intuition
passages.text: Naive search tries the pattern at every position and, after a mismatch, starts over one position later, re-reading text it already looked at: O(n·m) in the worst case. - **KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt):** never re-read the text. When a mismatch happens after matching some characters, those characters are known (they equal the start of the pattern). Precompute, for each prefix of the pattern, how much of it can be *reused* as the start of a new attempt. - **Rabin-Karp:** compare fingerprints (hashes) instead of strings. A **rolling hash** updates the window's fingerprint in O(1) as it slides, and real comparison happens only when fingerprints agree.

passages.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp — Core math
passages.text: - Prefix function: `lps[i]` = longest proper prefix of `p[:i+1]` that is also its suffix (a "border"). On a mismatch with `k` characters matched, set `k = lps[k-1]` and retry. - Polynomial hash: `H(s) = Σ s[i] · B^(m-1-i) mod M`. - Rolling update: `H(next) = ((H − s[out]·B^(m-1)) · B + s[in]) mod M`. - Collision probability per comparison is about 1/M for a random base; a large prime modulus (2⁶¹ − 1 here) makes false positives very rare, and verification makes them harmless. - Period from a border: if the longest border of `s` has length `b`, `s` has period `n − b`.

passages.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp — Complexity
passages.text: | Algorithm | Preprocess | Search | Worst case | Extra space | |---|---|---|---|---| | Naive | – | O(n·m) | O(n·m) | O(1) | | KMP | O(m) | O(n) | O(n + m) | O(m) | | Rabin-Karp | O(m) | O(n) expected | O(n·m) (all windows collide) | O(1) |

passages.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - KMP: confusing *proper* prefix (must be shorter than the string) — `lps[0]` is always 0. - KMP: after a full match, forgetting `k = lps[k-1]` and missing overlapping occurrences. - Rabin-Karp: skipping verification (wrong answers on collisions); tiny modulus; negative values after subtraction in languages where `%` can be negative. - Using Python's built-in `hash()` as a rolling hash (it cannot be rolled). - Empty pattern conventions (here: matches at every position, like `str.find`).

passages.title: String matching: KMP and Rabin-Karp — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Single pattern, guaranteed linear time → KMP (or the Z-algorithm, same power). - Many patterns of the same length, 2D matching, plagiarism detection, longest repeated substring via binary search → Rabin-Karp's rolling hash. - Many patterns of different lengths → Aho-Corasick (KMP on a trie). - In practice: library `find` (Boyer-Moore-Horspool / two-way) is sublinear on typical text.

passages.title: Tarjan's strongly connected components — Intuition
passages.text: In a directed graph, a **strongly connected component** (SCC) is a group of nodes where everyone can reach everyone else (think: a set of web pages that all link around to each other). Shrinking each SCC to a single dot always leaves a DAG, which is why SCCs are the first step for many directed-graph problems. Tarjan finds them in one DFS. As DFS walks, it numbers nodes in discovery order and asks of each node: "what is the *oldest* still-open node my subtree can get back to?" If the answer is the node itself, then nothing below it escapes upward, and everything left on the stack above it forms one complete SCC.

passages.title: Tarjan's strongly connected components — Core idea
passages.text: - `index[u]` = discovery time; `low[u]` = min discovery time reachable from u's subtree via at most one back/cross edge to a node **still on the stack**. - Tree edge `u → v`: after returning, `low[u] = min(low[u], low[v])`. - Edge to a node on the stack: `low[u] = min(low[u], index[v])`. - Edge to a node already popped: ignore (that SCC is finished; it cannot reach back or it would not have been popped). - `low[u] == index[u]` ⇒ pop the stack down to `u`: that is an SCC. - **Bridges** (undirected): tree edge `(u, v)` is a bridge iff `low[v] > index[u]`.

passages.title: Tarjan's strongly connected components — Complexity
passages.text: O(V + E) time, O(V) space. One DFS (Kosaraju needs two passes and the reversed graph).

passages.title: Tarjan's strongly connected components — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Updating `low` from nodes that are visited but **not on the stack** → merges separate SCCs. - Popping the stack at the wrong time (must be after all of `u`'s edges are processed). - Bridges: skipping the *parent node* rather than the *parent edge* breaks on parallel edges. - Deep recursion in Python on big graphs (raise the limit or convert to an explicit stack).

passages.title: Tarjan's strongly connected components — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Tarjan: one pass, also yields reverse topological order of the SCC DAG. - Kosaraju: easier to remember (DFS for finish order, then DFS on the reversed graph). - Applications: 2-SAT, deadlock detection, finding cyclic dependency groups, dominance in "who can reach whom" queries, critical network links (bridges / articulation points).

passages.title: Trees: traversals, BST, LCA, serialization — Intuition
passages.text: A tree problem is almost always: "solve it for the left subtree, solve it for the right subtree, combine at the node". The traversal order just says *when* you handle the node: - **preorder** (node, left, right): top-down work, copying/serializing a tree; - **inorder** (left, node, right): sorted order for a BST; - **postorder** (left, right, node): bottom-up work, e.g. heights, deleting; - **level order** (BFS): shortest depth, per-level answers. A **BST** keeps `left < node < right` everywhere, so each comparison discards a whole subtree — binary search in tree form.

passages.title: Trees: traversals, BST, LCA, serialization — Core idea
passages.text: - Iterative traversal = the recursion's call stack made explicit. - BST delete with two children: replace the value with the inorder successor (min of the right subtree), then delete the successor, which has at most one child. - LCA (general): the first node where `p` and `q` end up in different subtrees. LCA (BST): the first node whose value lies between `p` and `q`. - Serialization: preorder alone is ambiguous; preorder **with null markers** is not.

passages.title: Trees: traversals, BST, LCA, serialization — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Any traversal | O(n) | O(h) stack (O(w) queue for BFS) | | BST search / insert / delete | O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate | O(h) recursive | | LCA general / BST | O(n) / O(h) | O(h) / O(1) | | serialize / deserialize | O(n) | O(n) | `h` = height, `w` = max width. The recursive traversals here build lists with `+`, which is simple but O(n·h) copying; the iterative versions are the efficient ones.

passages.title: Trees: traversals, BST, LCA, serialization — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Validating a BST by comparing only with direct children (must respect bounds from *all* ancestors). - Inserting sorted data into a plain BST gives a linked list (height n). Real libraries self-balance (red-black, AVL). - Deep recursion in Python (~1000 frames): prefer iterative on skewed trees. - Forgetting to reattach the returned subtree: `root.left = bst_delete(root.left, v)`. - Level order: reading `len(queue)` *inside* the loop condition instead of once per level.

passages.title: Trees: traversals, BST, LCA, serialization — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - BST: ordered data with inserts/deletes plus range/rank queries. - Hash map: only exact lookups (faster, unordered). - Heap: only need min/max. - Many LCA queries on one tree: binary lifting or Euler tour + sparse table.

passages.title: Trie (prefix tree) — Intuition
passages.text: Store words letter by letter along paths of a tree. Words with a common beginning share the beginning of their path, like a dictionary's guide words. To check whether any word starts with "pre", just follow p → r → e; you never look at the other words at all.

passages.title: Trie (prefix tree) — Core idea
passages.text: - Each node has a map `char -> child` and a flag "a word ends here". - `insert` / `search` / `starts_with` all walk one node per character. - `pass_count` on each node (how many words go through it) gives prefix counts in O(L) and makes deletion easy: decrement along the path and cut the branch when a count hits 0.

passages.title: Trie (prefix tree) — Complexity
passages.text: `L` = word length, `N` = number of words, `Σ` = alphabet size. | Operation | Time | |---|---| | insert / search / starts_with / count_prefix / delete | O(L) | | words_with_prefix | O(L + size of the matching subtree) | | wildcard search | O(L) with no dots, up to O(Σ^dots · L) | | Space | O(total characters) worst case; node overhead is significant |

passages.title: Trie (prefix tree) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Confusing "is a prefix" with "is a word" (need the `is_word` flag). - Memory: one dict per node is heavy; a fixed array of 26 is faster but wasteful for sparse nodes. - Deleting without pruning (leaks nodes) or pruning nodes still used by other words. - Inserting a duplicate and double-counting `pass_count`.

passages.title: Trie (prefix tree) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Trie: prefix queries, autocomplete, word-search on a grid, longest common prefix, IP routing (bitwise trie), max XOR pair. - Hash set: exact membership only — simpler, less memory. - Sorted array + binary search: prefix ranges on static data with far less memory. - Radix/compressed trie: merges single-child chains to cut memory.

passages.title: Two pointers — Intuition
passages.text: Keep two indices into the same sequence and move them according to a rule that lets you *throw away* candidates without checking them. Each pointer only moves forward (or only inward), so the total work is O(n) instead of the O(n²) of trying every pair. Three flavours: - **Opposite ends** moving inward (sorted pair sum, palindrome, container, rain water). - **Slow / fast** in the same direction (in-place dedupe, partitioning, cycle detection). - **Three-way partition** (Dutch national flag).

passages.title: Two pointers — Core idea
passages.text: The proof is always an *invariant*: "the answer is never in the region I skipped". For sorted two-sum with pointers `i < j`: if `a[i] + a[j] < target`, then `a[i]` paired with *anything* still in range is too small (since `a[j]` is the largest), so `i` can be discarded.

passages.title: Two pointers — Complexity
passages.text: | Problem | Time | Extra space | |---|---|---| | palindrome, two_sum_sorted, container, dedupe, sort_colors, rain water | O(n) | O(1) | | three_sum | O(n²) (sort + n two-pointer passes) | O(1) besides output |

passages.title: Two pointers — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using opposite-end pointers on **unsorted** data (the discard argument needs order). - `three_sum`: forgetting to skip duplicates at *both* the outer loop and the inner pointer. - `sort_colors`: advancing `mid` after swapping with `hi` (the swapped-in value is unchecked). - Off-by-one: `while i < j` vs `while i <= j` (use `<=` only when a single element still matters).

passages.title: Two pointers — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Sorted input or you can afford to sort, and need O(1) extra space: two pointers. - Unsorted and need original indices: hash map (see `arrays_hashing`). - Contiguous subarray with a constraint: sliding window (a same-direction two-pointer).

passages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union) — Intuition
passages.text: Keep track of which items belong to the same group when groups only ever **merge**. Each group elects a representative ("root"). Two items are in the same group iff they have the same root. Merging two groups = making one root point at the other.

passages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union) — Core idea
passages.text: - `find(x)`: follow parent pointers to the root. - **Path compression:** after finding the root, re-point every node on the path directly at it, so the next `find` is one hop. - **Union by rank (or size):** hang the shorter tree under the taller one, so trees stay shallow (height ≤ log₂ n even without compression). - With both, m operations cost O(m · α(n)), where α is the inverse Ackermann function (≤ 4 for any n that fits in the universe) — effectively constant.

passages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union) — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | find / union / connected | O(α(n)) amortized | O(n) | | count components / detect cycle over E edges | O(E · α(n)) | O(n) |

passages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Unioning the raw nodes instead of their **roots** (`parent[a] = b` is wrong). - Forgetting to update size/rank only at the root. - Expecting to *split* groups: union-find cannot undo merges (needs offline tricks / rollback DSU). - Using it on **directed** reachability: it models undirected connectivity only. - Recursive `find` hitting Python's recursion limit on long chains (iterative here).

passages.title: Union-find (disjoint set union) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Edges arrive over time and you ask "connected yet?" → union-find. - One-off components on a fixed graph → BFS/DFS is just as good. - Kruskal's MST, cycle detection in undirected graphs, merging equivalent items, percolation. - Need shortest paths or the actual path → BFS/DFS, not union-find.

passages.title: Numerical gradient checking — Intuition
passages.text: A derivative is "how much does the output change if I nudge the input a tiny bit?". So you can *measure* a gradient without any calculus: nudge each input up and down by a small ε, see how the output changes, divide. It is far too slow for training (one or two function calls **per parameter**), but it is the gold standard for **testing** a hand-written backward pass. If backprop says the gradient is `g` and the measured slope disagrees, backprop has a bug.

passages.title: Numerical gradient checking — Core math
passages.text: - Forward difference: `(f(x+ε) − f(x)) / ε = f'(x) + O(ε)`. - Central difference: `(f(x+ε) − f(x−ε)) / 2ε = f'(x) + O(ε²)` (the odd Taylor terms cancel). - Two error sources pull in opposite directions: - truncation error ∝ ε² (shrinks as ε shrinks), - floating-point round-off ∝ machine_eps / ε (grows as ε shrinks). The sweet spot for float64 central differences is ε ≈ 1e-5 … 1e-6. - Relative error: `|a − n| / (|a| + |n|)`. Rough guide in float64: < 1e-7 correct; 1e-4…1e-2 suspicious; > 1e-2 wrong.

passages.title: Numerical gradient checking — Complexity
passages.text: `2 · (number of parameters)` function evaluations for one gradient: O(P · cost(f)). Backprop gets the same gradient in about the cost of **one** extra evaluation, which is why numerical gradients are only for checking.

passages.title: Numerical gradient checking — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using float32: round-off dominates and correct gradients look wrong. Check in float64. - Non-differentiable points (ReLU at 0, max-pool ties) give misleading differences; nudge the inputs away from kinks. - Randomness inside `f` (dropout, sampling): fix the seed/mask so both evaluations match. - Forgetting a term of the loss (e.g. the regulariser) in either the analytic or numeric side. - Checking only at initialisation where some paths are inactive; also check after a few steps. - Comparing with absolute error: tiny gradients trivially "match". - Integer arrays: adding 1e-5 to an int does nothing.

passages.title: Numerical gradient checking — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Unit-testing any custom backward pass, layer, or loss (used throughout sections 3–5 here). - Automatic differentiation (PyTorch/JAX) is exact and fast: use it for real training, and use finite differences to test *it* when you write custom autograd functions. - Complex-step differentiation avoids cancellation entirely when `f` supports complex inputs.

passages.title: Gradient descent variants — Intuition
passages.text: You are on a foggy hillside and want to reach the valley. You cannot see far, but you can feel the slope under your feet. The **gradient** points uphill, so step the other way. Repeat. - **Batch GD:** measure the slope using *all* the data. Accurate but slow per step. - **SGD / mini-batch:** estimate the slope from a few random samples. Noisy but cheap, so you take many more steps for the same cost; the noise even helps escape shallow traps. - **Momentum:** a heavy ball. It builds speed where the slope keeps pointing the same way and cancels out zig-zagging across a narrow valley. - **RMSProp:** give each parameter its own step size: small where gradients are large, large where they are small. - **Adam:** momentum + RMSProp + a correction for starting the averages at zero. The default choice in deep learning.

passages.title: Gradient descent variants — Core math
passages.text: ``` GD x ← x − η g Momentum v ← μ v + g ; x ← x − η v RMSProp s ← ρ s + (1−ρ) g² ; x ← x − η g / (√s + ε) Adam m ← β₁ m + (1−β₁) g ; v ← β₂ v + (1−β₂) g² m̂ = m / (1−β₁ᵗ) ; v̂ = v / (1−β₂ᵗ) x ← x − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) ``` - For a quadratic with largest curvature L, GD converges iff `η < 2/L`. - Convergence speed depends on the **condition number** κ = L/μ: GD needs O(κ) steps, momentum O(√κ). - Mini-batch gradient is an unbiased estimate of the full gradient; its variance shrinks like 1/batch_size.

passages.title: Gradient descent variants — Complexity
passages.text: Per step: O(cost of one gradient) + O(d) for the update. Memory: SGD 0 extra, momentum and RMSProp d, Adam 2d (d = number of parameters).

passages.title: Gradient descent variants — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Learning rate too high → divergence/NaN; too low → looks like "no learning". - Unscaled features make the loss surface a long narrow valley (bad κ): standardise inputs. - Forgetting to shuffle each epoch (ordered data biases SGD). - Different libraries define momentum/RMSProp slightly differently (dampening, ε inside or outside the square root) — matters when reproducing results. - Adam + L2 penalty is not the same as weight decay; use AdamW (decoupled decay). - Convex guarantees do not apply to neural nets: you get *a* good minimum, not *the* minimum.

passages.title: Gradient descent variants — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Adam/AdamW: default for deep nets, transformers, sparse gradients; little tuning. - SGD + momentum: often generalises better for vision models with a tuned schedule. - Small problems with exact solutions (linear regression) → closed form / Newton / L-BFGS. - Second-order methods (Newton) use curvature and converge in few steps but cost O(d³).

passages.title: Vector and matrix operations — Intuition
passages.text: - A **vector** is a list of numbers: a point, or an arrow from the origin. - The **dot product** measures how much two arrows point the same way. Zero means perpendicular. - A **matrix** is a function that transforms vectors (rotate, stretch, project). Multiplying matrices composes the functions. - **Solving `Ax = b`** asks: which input does the transformation send to `b`? - An **eigenvector** is a direction the matrix only stretches (does not rotate); the **eigenvalue** is the stretch factor. Almost all of ML is these operations: a linear layer is `Wx + b`, similarity search is a dot product, linear regression is least squares, PCA is an eigen-decomposition.

passages.title: Vector and matrix operations — Core math
passages.text: - `u · v = Σ uᵢvᵢ = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ`; cosine similarity = `u · v / (‖u‖‖v‖)`. - Norms: `‖v‖₁ = Σ|vᵢ|`, `‖v‖₂ = √Σvᵢ²`, `‖v‖∞ = max|vᵢ|`. - Projection of u on v: `(u·v / v·v) v`. - `(AB)ᵢⱼ = Σₖ AᵢₖBₖⱼ`; `(AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ`; `(AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹`. - Gaussian elimination: row operations reduce `[A | b]` to `[I | x]`. The determinant is the product of pivots (sign flipped per row swap). - QR: `A = QR`, `QᵀQ = I`, `R` upper triangular. Least squares: `Rx = Qᵀb`. - Normal equations: `AᵀA x = Aᵀb` (same solution, worse conditioning). - Power iteration: `v ← Av / ‖Av‖` converges at rate `|λ₂/λ₁|` per step.

passages.title: Vector and matrix operations — Complexity
passages.text: | Operation | Time | |---|---| | dot, norm | O(n) | | matmul (n×m by m×p) | O(n·m·p); O(n³) for square | | solve / inverse / determinant / rank (elimination) | O(n³) | | QR, least squares (m×n) | O(m·n²) | | power iteration | O(n²) per step |

passages.title: Vector and matrix operations — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Computing `inverse(A) @ b` instead of `solve(A, b)`: slower and less accurate. - No pivoting: a zero or tiny pivot ruins elimination even for well-behaved matrices. - Comparing floats with `==`; use a tolerance. "Singular" in floating point is a judgment call. - Classical (unmodified) Gram-Schmidt loses orthogonality on ill-conditioned inputs. - Shape bugs: (n,) vs (n,1) vs (1,n); matrix multiplication is not commutative. - Power iteration stalls when the top two eigenvalues have (nearly) equal magnitude.

passages.title: Vector and matrix operations — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Square system → LU/elimination. Over-determined system → QR least squares (or SVD if rank-deficient). Symmetric positive-definite → Cholesky (half the work). - All eigenvalues → QR algorithm (`numpy.linalg.eigh`). Just the top one or huge sparse matrices → power iteration / Lanczos (this is how PageRank works). - In real code always use NumPy/BLAS: same math, 100–1000× faster.

passages.title: PCA via SVD and via eigendecomposition — Intuition
passages.text: You have data with many features, and many of them move together. PCA finds new axes for the data: the first axis points along the direction where the data is **most spread out**, the second is the most spread-out direction perpendicular to the first, and so on. Keep only the first few axes and you have a lower-dimensional version of the data that loses as little information (variance) as possible. Picture a cloud of points shaped like a flattened rugby ball: PCA finds the long axis, then the medium axis, then the short one. Dropping the short one barely changes the cloud.

passages.title: PCA via SVD and via eigendecomposition — Core math
passages.text: 1. Centre: `Xc = X − mean`. 2. Covariance: `C = XcᵀXc / (n − 1)` (d × d). 3. **Eigen route:** `C v = λ v`. Eigenvectors `v` = principal directions, eigenvalues `λ` = variance along them. 4. **SVD route:** `Xc = U S Vᵀ`. Then `C = V (S²/(n−1)) Vᵀ`, so the right singular vectors are the same directions and `λᵢ = sᵢ² / (n − 1)`. 5. Project: `Z = Xc Vₖ` (n × k). Reconstruct: `X̂ = Z Vₖᵀ + mean`. 6. Explained variance ratio of component i: `λᵢ / Σ λ`. 7. Optimality (Eckart-Young): among all rank-k linear projections, PCA minimises the squared reconstruction error, which equals `(n − 1) · Σ_{i>k} λᵢ`.

passages.title: PCA via SVD and via eigendecomposition — Complexity
passages.text: | Route | Time | Notes | |---|---|---| | Covariance + eigh | O(n d² + d³) | fine when d is small | | SVD of Xc | O(min(n d², n² d)) | more accurate; no `XᵀX` | | Randomized / truncated SVD | ~O(n d k) | large data, small k |

passages.title: PCA via SVD and via eigendecomposition — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Not centring** the data: the first component just points at the mean. - **Not scaling** features with different units: the feature with the largest numbers dominates. Standardise first unless the units are comparable. - Signs of components are arbitrary (`v` and `−v` are both valid); compare up to sign. - Fitting PCA on train + test together leaks information; fit on train, apply to test. - PCA is linear and variance-based: high variance ≠ useful for the label, and curved structure (a spiral) is not captured. - Forming `XᵀX` squares the condition number; tiny eigenvalues come out inaccurate or negative.

passages.title: PCA via SVD and via eigendecomposition — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Compression, denoising, decorrelating features, speeding up downstream models, 2D plots. - Visualising clusters / nonlinear structure → t-SNE, UMAP. - Supervised dimensionality reduction → LDA. Non-negative parts → NMF. Nonlinear → kernel PCA, autoencoders (a linear autoencoder with squared loss learns the PCA subspace).

passages.title: Basic probability: MLE and Bayes — Intuition
passages.text: **Bayes' rule** is how to update a belief when evidence arrives: *new belief ∝ old belief × how well the hypothesis explains the evidence*. The famous surprise: a 99%-accurate test for a rare disease still produces mostly false alarms, because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones. **Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE)** answers "which parameter value makes the data I saw most probable?" Flip a coin 10 times and see 7 heads: the bias that best explains that is 0.7. Training almost any ML model is MLE in disguise: minimising cross-entropy = maximising the likelihood of the labels; minimising squared error = MLE under Gaussian noise. **MAP** adds a prior belief about the parameter; it is MLE plus a regulariser.

passages.title: Basic probability: MLE and Bayes — Core math
passages.text: - Bayes: `P(H|E) = P(E|H) P(H) / P(E)`, with `P(E) = Σ_h P(E|h) P(h)`. posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. - Likelihood of i.i.d. data: `L(θ) = Π p(xᵢ | θ)`; work with `log L = Σ log p(xᵢ | θ)` (sums are stable and easy to differentiate). - MLE: `θ̂ = argmax log L(θ)`; solve `∂ log L / ∂θ = 0`. | Model | MLE | |---|---| | Bernoulli(p) | `p̂ = mean(x)` | | Gaussian(μ, σ²) | `μ̂ = mean(x)`, `σ̂² = mean((x − μ̂)²)` (divisor n: biased) | | Poisson(λ) | `λ̂ = mean(x)` | | Exponential(rate) | `1 / mean(x)` | | Categorical | normalised counts | - MAP: `θ̂ = argmax [log L(θ) + log p(θ)]`. Gaussian prior ⇒ L2 penalty; Laplace prior ⇒ L1. - Conjugacy: Beta(a, b) prior + h heads, t tails ⇒ Beta(a + h, b + t) posterior. Mean `a/(a+b)`, mode `(a−1)/(a+b−2)`.

passages.title: Basic probability: MLE and Bayes — Complexity
passages.text: Closed-form MLEs are O(n). When no closed form exists (logistic regression, neural nets), maximise the log-likelihood with gradient descent.

passages.title: Basic probability: MLE and Bayes — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Base-rate neglect:** confusing `P(positive | sick)` with `P(sick | positive)`. - Multiplying many probabilities underflows to 0: add logs instead. - MLE with little data overfits: zero counts give probability 0 (then `log 0 = −∞`). Use smoothing / a prior. - MLE variance uses divisor n (biased); the unbiased estimator uses n − 1. - Assuming independence (i.i.d.) when samples are correlated. - Likelihood is a function of θ, not a probability distribution over θ.

passages.title: Basic probability: MLE and Bayes — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - MLE: plenty of data, want a simple point estimate (the default in ML). - MAP: want regularisation / have prior knowledge; still a point estimate. - Full Bayesian posterior: need uncertainty (small data, decision-making, A/B tests, Thompson sampling in `s6_rl/bandits`).

passages.title: Softmax / log-sum-exp stability — Intuition
passages.text: **Softmax** turns a list of arbitrary scores ("logits") into probabilities: exponentiate so everything is positive, then divide by the total so it sums to 1. Bigger score → bigger share. The catch: computers store numbers with limited range. `exp(1000)` is "infinity" in float64, and `inf / inf` is `nan`. `exp(-1000)` is exactly `0`, and `log(0)` is `-inf`. A model that was training fine suddenly prints `nan` — this is very often the reason. The fixes are small algebra tricks that give the *same* math with *safe* intermediate numbers.

passages.title: Softmax / log-sum-exp stability — Core math
passages.text: - `softmax(z)ᵢ = e^{zᵢ} / Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}`. Adding a constant to all logits changes nothing, so subtract `m = max(z)`: every exponent is ≤ 0 and at least one term is `e⁰ = 1`. - `logsumexp(z) = m + log Σ e^{zᵢ − m}`. It is a smooth version of `max`: `max(z) ≤ LSE(z) ≤ max(z) + log n`. - `log_softmax(z) = z − logsumexp(z)` (never compute `log(softmax(z))` in two steps). - Cross-entropy from logits: `L = −log_softmax(z)[y]`; gradient `∂L/∂z = softmax(z) − onehot(y)`. - `∇ logsumexp(z) = softmax(z)`. - Stable sigmoid: `1/(1+e^{−x})` for `x ≥ 0`, `e^{x}/(1+e^{x})` for `x < 0`. - BCE from logits: `max(x, 0) − x·y + log(1 + e^{−|x|})`. - `log1p(t)` computes `log(1 + t)` accurately for tiny `t`.

passages.title: Softmax / log-sum-exp stability — Complexity
