passages.text: O(n) per vector; the stable forms cost one extra `max` pass.

passages.title: Softmax / log-sum-exp stability — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Applying softmax and then a loss that expects logits (PyTorch `CrossEntropyLoss` does log-softmax internally): double softmax silently hurts training. - `log(softmax(z))` or `log(sigmoid(x))` in two steps → `-inf` and then `nan` gradients. - Clipping probabilities (`p.clip(1e-12)`) hides the problem and biases the loss; work in log space. - Wrong `axis` on batched inputs (normalising across the batch instead of across classes). - Mixed precision / float32 overflows much earlier (`exp(89)`).

passages.title: Softmax / log-sum-exp stability — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Multi-class, exactly one label → softmax + cross-entropy. - Multi-label (independent yes/no per class) → sigmoid + BCE per class. - Any sum of probabilities in log space (HMM forward algorithm, mixture likelihoods, CTC, attention masks with `-inf`) → logsumexp. - Temperature `softmax(z / T)`: T < 1 sharpens, T > 1 flattens (used in sampling, distillation).

passages.title: AdaBoost — Intuition
passages.text: Train a sequence of very simple classifiers ("weak learners", usually one-question decision stumps). After each one, **turn up the importance of the examples it got wrong**, so the next one is forced to focus on them. At the end, let all of them vote, with more accurate ones getting a louder voice. A study-group analogy: after each practice exam you spend the next session on the questions you missed. No single session covers everything, but together they do.

passages.title: AdaBoost — Core math
passages.text: With sample weights `wᵢ` (sum to 1) and learner `hₘ`: - Weighted error: `εₘ = Σ wᵢ · 1[hₘ(xᵢ) ≠ yᵢ]`. - Learner weight (SAMME, K classes): `αₘ = η [ln((1 − εₘ)/εₘ) + ln(K − 1)]`. (Classic binary AdaBoost uses `½ ln((1 − ε)/ε)`; same model, different scaling.) - Reweight: `wᵢ ← wᵢ · exp(αₘ · 1[wrong])`, then normalise. After the update, the samples the learner got wrong hold exactly half of the total weight (for K = 2). - Prediction: `argmax_k Σₘ αₘ · 1[hₘ(x) = k]`. - AdaBoost is forward stagewise additive modelling under the **exponential loss** `L = exp(−y F(x))`. - Training error bound: `≤ Πₘ 2√(εₘ(1 − εₘ))`, which shrinks exponentially as long as every learner is a bit better than chance.

passages.title: AdaBoost — Complexity
passages.text: O(M · cost of fitting one weak learner). With stumps: O(M · d · n log n). Predict: O(M).

passages.title: AdaBoost — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Sensitive to label noise and outliers:** mislabelled points keep gaining weight exponentially until the model contorts to fit them. - Weak learner must beat random guessing (ε < 1 − 1/K) or the round is useless/harmful. - Weak learner too strong (deep trees) → ε = 0 on the first round and boosting does nothing. - The weak learner must actually *use* the sample weights (or be trained on a weighted resample). - Output scores are not calibrated probabilities.

passages.title: AdaBoost — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Historically important, simple, few hyperparameters, good on clean tabular data and for face detection (Viola-Jones). - Gradient boosting generalises the idea to any differentiable loss and is more robust; it is the usual choice today. - Noisy labels → random forest or gradient boosting with a robust loss.

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — Intuition
passages.text: Imagine re-collecting the training data many times and refitting the same kind of model. - **Bias:** how far the *average* fitted model is from the truth. A straight line fitted to a sine wave is wrong no matter how much data you get. Too-simple models have high bias. - **Variance:** how much the fitted model jumps around between datasets. A degree-12 polynomial through 30 noisy points wiggles wildly and differently every time. Too-flexible models have high variance. - **Noise:** randomness in the labels that no model can predict. Test error = bias² + variance + noise. Making a model more flexible trades bias for variance; the best model sits at the bottom of the U-shaped test-error curve. **Regularisation** is a dial that moves along the same trade-off without changing the model family.

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — Core math
passages.text: For squared loss at an input x, with `f` the truth and `f̂_D` the model trained on dataset D: `E_D,ε[(y − f̂_D(x))²] = (E_D[f̂_D(x)] − f(x))² + Var_D[f̂_D(x)] + σ²`. The demo estimates each term by Monte Carlo over 200 training sets (`impl.py`), and checks that they add up to a directly measured test error. Regularisation demo: ridge on degree-12 polynomial features. As α grows, training error rises monotonically and the weight norm shrinks; validation error first falls (less variance) then rises (more bias).

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — Results (from the tests / plots)
passages.text: - Degree 1: high bias, tiny variance. Degree 4: both small (best). Degree 12: variance dominates. - Validation-optimal α lies strictly inside the swept range and cuts validation MSE by > 30% versus both extremes.

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — Complexity
passages.text: Monte Carlo cost: `n_datasets × cost(fit)`.

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Confusing training error with test error (training error only falls with complexity). - Believing more data fixes bias (it fixes variance; bias needs a richer model). - Thinking the decomposition is exact for 0-1 loss (it is cleanest for squared loss). - Deep networks show "double descent" where very over-parameterised models generalise again; the classic U-curve is not the whole story there.

passages.title: Bias-variance and regularisation demos — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Diagnose with learning curves: big train/val gap → variance (more data, regularise, simpler model, bagging); both errors high → bias (richer model, better features, boosting).

passages.title: DBSCAN — Intuition
passages.text: Clusters are **crowded regions** separated by empty space. Pick a radius `eps`. A point with at least `min_samples` neighbours inside that radius is in a crowd (a *core* point). Crowds that touch merge into one cluster, so a cluster can snake around in any shape. Points near a crowd but not crowded themselves join as *border* points. Everything else is *noise*. You never say how many clusters there are; DBSCAN discovers it.

passages.title: DBSCAN — Core math
passages.text: - ε-neighbourhood: `N(p) = {q : ‖p − q‖ ≤ ε}` (includes p). - Core point: `|N(p)| ≥ min_samples`. - Directly density-reachable: q ∈ N(p) and p is core. A cluster = all points density-reachable from a core point (BFS/DFS over core points). - Border points may be reachable from two clusters; which one claims them depends on visit order (core points and noise are deterministic).

passages.title: DBSCAN — Complexity
passages.text: Brute force: O(n²) time and memory for the neighbour table. With a spatial index (KD-tree, ball tree) roughly O(n log n) in low dimensions.

passages.title: DBSCAN — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Choosing `eps`: plot each point's distance to its k-th nearest neighbour (k = min_samples), sorted, and pick the "knee". - One global `eps` cannot handle clusters of very different densities (use HDBSCAN/OPTICS). - Feature scaling changes every distance. - High dimensions: distances concentrate and density loses meaning. - Border point assignment is order-dependent.

passages.title: DBSCAN — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Arbitrary-shaped clusters, unknown number of clusters, outlier detection, geospatial data. - Compact spherical clusters → k-means (faster). Varying density → HDBSCAN. Soft/probabilistic → GMM.

passages.title: Decision tree (CART, gini + entropy) — Intuition
passages.text: A decision tree is a game of twenty questions. At each step it asks one yes/no question about one feature ("is petal length ≤ 2.45?"), sending the data left or right. It keeps asking until the group that remains is (mostly) one class, then predicts that class. For regression it predicts the group's average. How does it pick the question? It tries *every* feature and *every* threshold and keeps the one that makes the two resulting groups as "pure" as possible. It does this greedily, one split at a time, never looking ahead.

passages.title: Decision tree (CART, gini + entropy) — Core math
passages.text: - Gini impurity: `G = 1 − Σₖ pₖ²`. Entropy: `H = −Σₖ pₖ log₂ pₖ`. Both are 0 for a pure node and maximal for a uniform mix. - Regression impurity: variance of the targets (so splits minimise squared error). - Quality of a split: weighted child impurity `(n_L/n)·I(L) + (n_R/n)·I(R)`; **information gain** = parent impurity − that. - CART = binary splits, threshold at the midpoint between consecutive sorted values. - Efficient search: sort a feature once, then a running (cumulative) class count gives the impurity of every split position in O(n).

passages.title: Decision tree (CART, gini + entropy) — Complexity
passages.text: | | Time | Space | |---|---|---| | Train | O(d · n log n) per level → O(d · n log n · depth) | O(n) + tree | | Predict | O(depth) per sample | | Depth is O(log n) for a balanced tree, up to O(n) for a degenerate one.

passages.title: Decision tree (CART, gini + entropy) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Overfitting:** an unrestricted tree memorises the training set. Limit `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, or prune (cost-complexity pruning). - **High variance:** small changes in data can change the top split and thus the whole tree. This is exactly what bagging / random forests fix. - Greedy splitting cannot see XOR-like interactions at depth 1. - Axis-aligned splits approximate diagonal boundaries with a staircase. - Impurity-based feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality features. - Trees cannot extrapolate: regression predictions are capped by training target values.

passages.title: Decision tree (CART, gini + entropy) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Mixed feature types, no scaling needed, non-linear interactions, need an explainable model. - Single trees are rarely the most accurate: use random forests (lower variance) or gradient boosting (lower bias) for accuracy. - Smooth/linear relationships → linear models are more data-efficient.

passages.title: Gaussian mixture model with EM — Intuition
passages.text: Imagine the data was made by first secretly rolling a weighted die to pick one of K "blob makers", then drawing a point from that maker's bell-shaped (Gaussian) cloud. A GMM tries to recover the makers: their centres, shapes (covariances), and how often each was picked. Unlike k-means, every point is assigned **softly**: "70% blob A, 30% blob B". And blobs may be stretched ellipses of different sizes, not just equal circles. **EM** (expectation-maximisation) is the chicken-and-egg solver: - **E-step:** given the current blobs, how responsible is each blob for each point? - **M-step:** given those responsibilities, refit each blob as a weighted average.

passages.title: Gaussian mixture model with EM — Core math
passages.text: - `p(x) = Σₖ πₖ N(x; μₖ, Σₖ)`. - E-step: `rᵢₖ = πₖ N(xᵢ; μₖ, Σₖ) / Σⱼ πⱼ N(xᵢ; μⱼ, Σⱼ)` (compute in log space with log-sum-exp). - M-step with `Nₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ`: `πₖ = Nₖ/n`, `μₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ xᵢ / Nₖ`, `Σₖ = Σᵢ rᵢₖ (xᵢ − μₖ)(xᵢ − μₖ)ᵀ / Nₖ`. - EM maximises a lower bound on the log-likelihood (the ELBO); each iteration never decreases `log p(X)`. It converges to a local optimum. - Log-density via Cholesky `Σ = LLᵀ`: Mahalanobis distance `‖L⁻¹(x − μ)‖²`, `log|Σ| = 2Σ log Lᵢᵢ`. - Model selection: BIC `= −2 log L + p log n`.

passages.title: Gaussian mixture model with EM — Complexity
passages.text: O(n · K · d²) per iteration for the E-step (plus O(K · d³) for the factorisations); memory O(n·K).

passages.title: Gaussian mixture model with EM — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Singular covariances:** a component collapses onto one point and the likelihood goes to infinity. Add a small value to the diagonal (`reg_covar`). - Local optima: initialise from k-means and/or use several restarts. - Underflow when multiplying tiny densities: stay in log space. - Too many parameters in high dimensions with full covariances; use diagonal/tied covariances. - K must be chosen (BIC/AIC, held-out likelihood).

passages.title: Gaussian mixture model with EM — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Soft clustering, elliptical clusters of different sizes, density estimation, anomaly detection (low `p(x)`), generative sampling. - Hard, spherical clusters and speed → k-means. Arbitrary shapes → DBSCAN / spectral. - Complex high-dimensional densities → normalising flows, VAEs.

passages.title: Gradient boosting (regression + classification) — Intuition
passages.text: Build a team of small trees **one after another**, where each new tree is trained on the *mistakes of the team so far*. 1. Start with a constant guess (the mean). 2. Look at the errors (residuals): where is the current model too low or too high? 3. Fit a small tree that predicts those errors. 4. Add a *fraction* of that tree's output (the learning rate) to the model. 5. Repeat. Each tree is weak (shallow), so it has high bias; adding hundreds of corrections drives the bias down. This is the opposite strategy to a random forest, which averages many strong trees to reduce variance.

passages.title: Gradient boosting (regression + classification) — Core math
passages.text: - Model: `F_M(x) = F₀ + η Σₘ hₘ(x)`. - At round m compute **pseudo-residuals** `rᵢ = −∂L(yᵢ, F(xᵢ)) / ∂F(xᵢ)` and fit `hₘ` to them. This is gradient descent where the "parameter" is the prediction for each training point. - Squared loss `½(y − F)²`: `r = y − F` (ordinary residuals); `F₀ = mean(y)`. - Log-loss with `p = σ(F)`: `r = y − p`; `F₀ = log(p̄ / (1 − p̄))`; leaf values use a Newton step `γ = Σ r / Σ p(1 − p)` over the samples in the leaf. - Regularisation: learning rate `η` (shrinkage), number of trees, tree depth, row subsampling (stochastic GB), plus L1/L2 on leaf values in XGBoost-style implementations.

passages.title: Gradient boosting (regression + classification) — Complexity
passages.text: Train: O(M · d · n log n · depth), sequential across trees (cannot be parallelised over trees). Predict: O(M · depth). Histogram-based versions (LightGBM, XGBoost `hist`) bin features so a split search costs O(#bins) instead of O(n).

passages.title: Gradient boosting (regression + classification) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Overfitting with too many trees** (unlike random forests): use early stopping on a validation set. - Learning rate and number of trees trade off: smaller η needs more trees but generalises better. - Deep trees in boosting overfit quickly; depth 3–8 is typical. - Sensitive to noisy labels/outliers with squared loss (each round chases the big residuals); use Huber or absolute loss. - For classification, forgetting the leaf-value Newton step gives a slow, poorly scaled model. - Like all trees: no extrapolation.

passages.title: Gradient boosting (regression + classification) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - State of the art for tabular data (XGBoost / LightGBM / CatBoost), ranking, and many Kaggle problems. - Random forest: easier to tune, parallel, harder to overfit; a bit less accurate. - Linear models: tiny data, need for extrapolation or coefficients. - Deep learning: unstructured data (images, text, audio).

passages.title: Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering — Intuition
passages.text: Start with every point as its own cluster. Repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until only one is left. The history of merges is a tree (a **dendrogram**): cut it at any height to get any number of clusters, without re-running anything. "Closest clusters" needs a definition (the **linkage**): - **single:** distance between their closest points — follows chains, finds snakes, but can link distinct groups through a thin bridge of points. - **complete:** distance between their farthest points — compact, similar-diameter clusters. - **average:** mean distance over all pairs — a compromise. - **ward:** merge the pair that increases total within-cluster variance the least — k-means-like round clusters.

passages.title: Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering — Core math
passages.text: Lance-Williams update: after merging i and j, the distance to any other cluster k is a formula of the old distances only: - single `min(d_ik, d_jk)`; complete `max(d_ik, d_jk)`; average `(nᵢ d_ik + nⱼ d_jk)/(nᵢ + nⱼ)`; - ward `√[((nᵢ+n_k)d_ik² + (nⱼ+n_k)d_jk² − n_k d_ij²) / (nᵢ+nⱼ+n_k)]`. Single linkage = the minimum spanning tree with its longest edges removed (Kruskal order).

passages.title: Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering — Complexity
passages.text: Naive: O(n³) time, O(n²) memory (the version here). Priority-queue versions O(n² log n); single linkage via MST O(n²). Not practical beyond ~10⁴ points.

passages.title: Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Quadratic memory for the distance matrix. - Greedy merges are final; an early bad merge is never undone. - Single linkage "chaining"; Ward only makes sense with Euclidean distance. - Ties in distances make the tree non-unique. - Scale your features.

passages.title: Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Small/medium data, need a hierarchy (taxonomies, phylogenetics, document topics), or want to explore several k at once. - Large data → k-means / mini-batch k-means. Density-shaped clusters with noise → DBSCAN/HDBSCAN.

passages.title: k-means and k-means++ — Intuition
passages.text: Drop k pins on the map. Every point joins its nearest pin. Move each pin to the centre of its group. Repeat until nothing moves. The result is k compact, roughly round clusters. The start matters: two pins dropped in the same blob may never separate. **k-means++** chooses starting pins one at a time, preferring points far from the pins already placed, so they start spread out.

passages.title: k-means and k-means++ — Core math
passages.text: - Objective (inertia): `J = Σᵢ ‖xᵢ − μ_{c(i)}‖²`. - Assignment step: `c(i) = argmin_k ‖xᵢ − μₖ‖²` (minimises J for fixed centres). - Update step: `μₖ = mean of points in cluster k` (minimises J for fixed assignments). - Each step can only decrease J, and there are finitely many partitions ⇒ convergence to a **local** minimum. Finding the global minimum is NP-hard. - k-means++: next centre chosen with probability `∝ D(x)²` (squared distance to the nearest chosen centre). Guarantees expected cost within O(log k) of optimal. - k-means is EM for a Gaussian mixture with equal, spherical covariances and hard assignments.

passages.title: k-means and k-means++ — Complexity
passages.text: O(n · k · d) per iteration, times iterations, times `n_init`. Memory O(n·k) for the distance table.

passages.title: k-means and k-means++ — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Unscaled features dominate the distance. - Choosing k: inertia always falls as k grows; use the elbow, silhouette score, or a downstream metric. - Assumes convex, similarly sized, roughly spherical clusters; fails on rings and moons (use DBSCAN / spectral clustering) and on clusters of very different spread (use GMM). - Sensitive to outliers (means get dragged); k-medoids is more robust. - Empty clusters: handle them (keep the old centre or re-seed). - Labels are arbitrary: compare clusterings with permutation-invariant scores (ARI, NMI).

passages.title: k-means and k-means++ — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Fast, scalable default for compact clusters, vector quantisation, image colour compression, initialising GMMs, building IVF indexes (see `s5_nlp/dense_retrieval`). - Soft assignments / elliptical clusters → GMM. Arbitrary shapes + noise → DBSCAN. A hierarchy of clusters → agglomerative clustering. Huge data → mini-batch k-means.

passages.title: k-nearest neighbours — Intuition
passages.text: "Tell me who your neighbours are and I will tell you who you are." To label a new point, find the `k` training points closest to it and let them vote (classification) or average their values (regression). There is no training step at all: the model *is* the data. - Small `k`: wiggly boundary, follows noise (low bias, high variance). `k = 1` memorises. - Large `k`: smooth boundary, may blur real structure (high bias, low variance). `k = n` always predicts the majority class.

passages.title: k-nearest neighbours — Core math
passages.text: - Distance, usually Euclidean: `d(a, b) = √Σ(aᵢ − bᵢ)²`. Minkowski: `(Σ|aᵢ − bᵢ|ᵖ)^{1/p}`. - Vectorised trick: `‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² − 2a·b + ‖b‖²`. - Classification: `ŷ = argmax_c Σ_{i ∈ N_k(x)} wᵢ · 1[yᵢ = c]`; regression: weighted mean. - Weights: uniform (`wᵢ = 1`) or inverse distance (`wᵢ = 1/dᵢ`). - Asymptotically, 1-NN's error is at most twice the Bayes-optimal error.

passages.title: k-nearest neighbours — Complexity
passages.text: | Step | Brute force | KD-tree / ball tree | |---|---|---| | Fit | O(1) (store) | O(n log n) | | Query | O(n·d) per point | ~O(log n) in low d, degrades to O(n) in high d | | Memory | O(n·d) | O(n·d) |

passages.title: k-nearest neighbours — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Feature scaling:** a feature measured in thousands dominates one measured in fractions. Always standardise. - **Curse of dimensionality:** in high dimensions all points are almost equally far apart, so "nearest" loses meaning. Reduce dimension first. - Irrelevant features add noise to every distance. - Slow prediction and large memory on big datasets (the opposite of most models). - Ties in votes (use odd `k` for binary problems) and ties in distance. - Imbalanced classes: the majority class crowds the vote; use distance weighting.

passages.title: k-nearest neighbours — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Small/medium, low-dimensional data with irregular decision boundaries; quick baseline; recommender-style "similar items". - Large n or high d → approximate nearest neighbours (HNSW, IVF; see `s5_nlp/dense_retrieval`). - Need fast inference or interpretability → trees, linear models.

passages.title: Linear regression (closed form + gradient descent) — Intuition
passages.text: Draw the straight line (or flat plane, with several features) that passes as close as possible to the data points. "Close" means the sum of squared vertical gaps between the points and the line is as small as possible. Each coefficient says "if this feature goes up by one unit, and the others stay fixed, the prediction changes by this much".

passages.title: Linear regression (closed form + gradient descent) — Core math
passages.text: - Model: `ŷ = Xw + b`. Absorb `b` by adding a column of ones to `X`. - Loss: `L(w) = (1/n) ‖Xw − y‖²`. - Gradient: `∇L = (2/n) Xᵀ(Xw − y)`. - Setting the gradient to zero gives the **normal equations** `XᵀX w = Xᵀy`, so `w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy`. - Geometric view: `Xw` is the projection of `y` onto the column space of `X`; the residual is orthogonal to every feature column. - Gradient descent: `w ← w − η ∇L`. Converges iff `η < 2 / λ_max(2XᵀX/n)`. - Probabilistic view: least squares is the MLE when `y = Xw + Gaussian noise`. - `R² = 1 − SS_res / SS_tot`.

passages.title: Linear regression (closed form + gradient descent) — Complexity
passages.text: | Method | Time | Notes | |---|---|---| | Normal equations / QR / SVD | O(n d² + d³) | exact; needs all data in memory | | Batch gradient descent | O(n d) per iteration | iterations grow with the condition number | | SGD | O(d) per sample | scales to huge n and streaming data |

passages.title: Linear regression (closed form + gradient descent) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Inverting `XᵀX` when features are collinear (singular matrix): use `lstsq`/pseudo-inverse or ridge. - Gradient descent on unscaled features: slow or divergent. Standardise first. - Forgetting the intercept. - Reading coefficients as importance when features have different scales or are correlated. - Outliers dominate squared error; consider Huber loss. - A high training R² says nothing about generalisation; evaluate on held-out data. - Extrapolating far outside the range of the training data.

passages.title: Linear regression (closed form + gradient descent) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - First baseline for any regression task; interpretable; fast. - Many/collinear features → ridge. Want feature selection → lasso. - Nonlinear relationships → add polynomial/interaction features, or trees/boosting. - Closed form when d is modest (up to ~10⁴); (S)GD when d or n is huge.

passages.title: Logistic regression (binary + multinomial) — Intuition
passages.text: Despite the name, it is a **classifier**. Take a linear score `w·x + b` (any real number) and squash it through an S-shaped curve (the sigmoid) so it becomes a probability between 0 and 1. A score of 0 means 50/50; large positive means "almost surely class 1". The linear score is the **log-odds**: each feature adds or subtracts evidence, and a weight of 0.7 means "one more unit of this feature multiplies the odds by e^0.7 ≈ 2". With more than two classes, compute one score per class and use **softmax** instead of sigmoid. It is exactly a neural network with no hidden layer.

passages.title: Logistic regression (binary + multinomial) — Core math
passages.text: - Binary: `p = σ(w·x + b)`, `σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^{−z})`. - Loss (negative log-likelihood / log-loss / cross-entropy): `L = −(1/n) Σ [y log p + (1−y) log(1−p)]`. - Gradient: `∇_w L = (1/n) Xᵀ(p − y)`, `∂L/∂b = mean(p − y)`. Same form as linear regression. - The loss is **convex**: one global minimum, but no closed form → iterate (GD, Newton/IRLS, L-BFGS). - Multinomial: `P = softmax(XW + b)`, `∇_W L = (1/n) Xᵀ(P − Y)` with one-hot `Y`. - L2 penalty `(λ/2)‖w‖²` adds `λw` to the gradient. - Decision boundary: `w·x + b = 0`, a hyperplane.

passages.title: Logistic regression (binary + multinomial) — Complexity
passages.text: O(n·d) per gradient step (O(n·d·K) for K classes). Prediction O(d). Newton's method costs O(n·d² + d³) per step but needs very few steps.

passages.title: Logistic regression (binary + multinomial) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Perfectly separable data + no regularisation:** weights grow forever (the likelihood keeps improving as `‖w‖ → ∞`). Always use some L2 or early stopping. - Using squared error with a sigmoid: non-convex and gives vanishing gradients when confidently wrong. - Computing `log(sigmoid(z))` naively → `log(0)`. Use the logits formulation. - Unscaled features → slow convergence and uneven regularisation. - Reading accuracy at threshold 0.5 on imbalanced data; choose the threshold from ROC/PR curves. - Softmax weights are not unique without regularisation (adding a constant vector to every class changes nothing).

passages.title: Logistic regression (binary + multinomial) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Strong, fast, interpretable baseline; gives calibrated probabilities; scales to huge sparse data (text, ads). - Nonlinear boundaries → feature engineering, kernels, trees, neural nets. - Max-margin with few support vectors → linear SVM (hinge loss). Generative alternative → naive Bayes / LDA (better with very little data).

passages.title: Classification metrics — Intuition
passages.text: Accuracy alone lies when classes are imbalanced: on a dataset with 1% fraud, "never fraud" is 99% accurate and useless. Other metrics ask sharper questions: - **Confusion matrix:** the full table of (true class, predicted class) counts. - **Precision:** of the alarms we raised, how many were real? (cost of false alarms) - **Recall:** of the real cases, how many did we catch? (cost of misses) - **F1:** harmonic mean; high only if both are high. - **ROC curve / AUC:** sweep the threshold; plot true-positive rate vs false-positive rate. AUC = probability a random positive is scored above a random negative. Threshold-free. - **PR curve / average precision:** precision vs recall over thresholds; much more informative than ROC when positives are rare. - **Calibration:** when the model says 70%, does it happen 70% of the time?

passages.title: Classification metrics — Core math
passages.text: - `P = TP/(TP+FP)`, `R = TP/(TP+FN)`, `F1 = 2PR/(P+R)`, `FPR = FP/(FP+TN)`. - Macro F1 = mean over classes; micro F1 = pooled counts (= accuracy for single-label); weighted = support-weighted mean. - `AUC = (Σ ranks of positives − n₊(n₊+1)/2) / (n₊n₋)` (Mann-Whitney U), ties count half. - `AP = Σₖ (Rₖ − Rₖ₋₁) Pₖ`; a random classifier's AP ≈ prevalence (ROC-AUC = 0.5). - ECE `= Σ_b (n_b/n) |acc_b − conf_b|`; Brier `= mean((p − y)²)`.

passages.title: Classification metrics — Complexity
passages.text: O(n) for counts; O(n log n) for curves/AUC (sorting).

passages.title: Classification metrics — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Accuracy on imbalanced data; ROC-AUC looking great while precision at useful thresholds is poor. - Forgetting that ties in scores must move together along the curve. - Comparing AP across datasets with different prevalence. - Picking the threshold on the test set. - Macro vs micro averaging give very different stories with rare classes. - Treating high AUC as good calibration (AUC only measures ranking).

passages.title: Classification metrics — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Balanced classes, equal error costs → accuracy is fine. - Costs of FP vs FN differ → precision/recall at a chosen threshold, or expected cost. - Ranking quality → ROC-AUC (balanced) or PR-AUC (rare positives). - Probabilities used for decisions → calibration curve, ECE, Brier, log-loss.

passages.title: Model selection: splits, k-fold CV, grid search — Intuition
passages.text: A model's score on the data it trained on is optimistic, like grading a student on questions they saw in advance. To estimate real-world performance we must test on data the model never saw. - **Train / validation / test:** fit on train, compare settings on validation, report test **once** at the end. If you look at test to make decisions, it is no longer a fair exam. - **k-fold cross-validation:** with little data, holding out one fixed chunk is wasteful and noisy. Split into k folds; train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining one, k times; average. - **Stratified k-fold:** keep class proportions the same in every fold (vital for imbalance). - **Grid search:** try every combination of hyperparameters, score each with CV, keep the best.

passages.title: Model selection: splits, k-fold CV, grid search — Core math
passages.text: - CV estimate: `CV = (1/k) Σⱼ score(model trained without fold j, fold j)`. - Bias/variance of the estimate: larger k → less pessimistic (more training data per fit) but more compute and correlated folds; k = 5 or 10 is standard. Leave-one-out is k = n. - Grid size = product of the number of values per hyperparameter (grows exponentially).

passages.title: Model selection: splits, k-fold CV, grid search — Complexity
passages.text: Grid search: `(#combinations) × k × cost(fit)`.

passages.title: Model selection: splits, k-fold CV, grid search — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Data leakage:** scaling/PCA/feature selection fitted on the full data before splitting. Fit preprocessing inside each fold. - Reporting the best CV score as the final performance (it is optimistically biased by the selection itself; use a held-out test set or nested CV). - Shuffling time series (use forward-chaining splits) or splitting correlated samples (the same patient in train and test → group k-fold). - Different folds for different candidates → scores not comparable. - Grid search over many dimensions: random search is usually more efficient.

passages.title: Model selection: splits, k-fold CV, grid search — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Large data: a single train/val/test split is enough. - Small data: k-fold (stratified for classification); nested CV for an unbiased estimate. - Many hyperparameters/expensive models: random search, Bayesian optimisation, Hyperband.

passages.title: Naive Bayes (Gaussian + multinomial) — Intuition
passages.text: A **generative** classifier: instead of learning a boundary directly, learn what each class "looks like", then ask which class would most plausibly have produced the new example. Bayes' rule turns "how likely is this email given spam?" into "how likely is spam given this email?". The **naive** part is assuming the features are independent once you know the class (the word "free" tells you nothing about the word "money" beyond what the label already does). That is rarely true, yet the classifier works well, because classification only needs the right class to come out on top, not accurate probabilities. - **Gaussian NB:** continuous features; a bell curve per (class, feature). - **Multinomial NB:** counts (word frequencies); a word distribution per class.

passages.title: Naive Bayes (Gaussian + multinomial) — Core math
passages.text: - `P(c | x) ∝ P(c) · Πⱼ P(xⱼ | c)`; work in logs: `log P(c) + Σⱼ log P(xⱼ | c)`. - Gaussian: `log P(xⱼ | c) = −½ log(2πσ²_{cj}) − (xⱼ − μ_{cj})² / (2σ²_{cj})`. - Multinomial: `P(word j | c) = (N_{cj} + α) / (N_c + α·V)` with Laplace smoothing `α`; score `= log P(c) + Σⱼ xⱼ log P(j | c)`, which is **linear in the counts**. - Normalise with log-sum-exp to get posteriors. - Fitting is MLE (or MAP with smoothing) by counting: no iterative optimisation.

passages.title: Naive Bayes (Gaussian + multinomial) — Complexity
passages.text: Fit: O(n·d), a single pass. Predict: O(d·K) per example. Memory: O(d·K).

passages.title: Naive Bayes (Gaussian + multinomial) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Zero counts** without smoothing: one unseen word makes the whole class probability zero. - Multiplying probabilities instead of summing logs: underflow on long documents. - **Probabilities are poorly calibrated** (pushed toward 0 and 1) because correlated features are counted as independent evidence; trust the ranking, not the number. - Gaussian NB on features that are far from normal (heavy skew, multi-modal). - Multinomial NB requires non-negative features; TF-IDF works in practice, standardised features do not.

passages.title: Naive Bayes (Gaussian + multinomial) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Text classification baselines (spam, sentiment, topic), very high-dimensional sparse data, tiny training sets, streaming/online updates (just update the counts). - Enough data and correlated features → logistic regression usually wins (discriminative). - Need calibrated probabilities → logistic regression or calibrate NB afterwards.

passages.title: PCA as a model — Intuition
passages.text: Rotate the data so the first axis follows the biggest spread, the second the next biggest, and so on; then drop the axes with little spread. Used as a **preprocessing step**: fewer, uncorrelated features that keep most of the information.

passages.title: PCA as a model — Core math
passages.text: - Fit on training data only: mean `μ`, components `Vₖ` (rows), variances `λ`. - `transform(x) = (x − μ) Vₖᵀ`; with **whitening** divide each coordinate by `√λᵢ`, so every output feature has unit variance and they are uncorrelated (covariance = identity). - `inverse_transform(z) = z Vₖ + μ` (undo whitening first). - Choosing k by a variance target τ: smallest k with `Σᵢ≤ₖ λᵢ / Σλ ≥ τ`.

passages.title: PCA as a model — Complexity
passages.text: Fit O(min(n d², n² d)); transform O(n d k).

passages.title: PCA as a model — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Fitting PCA on all data before the train/test split (leakage). - Whitening amplifies noise in low-variance directions. - Interpreting components as "real" factors; they are just orthogonal variance directions. - Forgetting to standardise features with different units (do it before PCA). - Signs of components flip between libraries/runs.

passages.title: PCA as a model — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Speed up / regularise models on many correlated features; compress images; denoise; 2D plots. - Visualising non-linear structure → t-SNE / UMAP. Sparse non-negative data → NMF / truncated SVD.

passages.title: Random forest — Intuition
passages.text: One deep decision tree is a nervous expert: it fits its training data perfectly and changes its mind completely if the data changes a little (high variance). A random forest asks **hundreds of such experts, each trained a bit differently, and averages their answers**. Individual mistakes point in different directions and cancel; what they agree on survives. Two sources of deliberate randomness make the trees different: 1. **Bagging** (bootstrap aggregating): each tree trains on a random sample of rows drawn with replacement. 2. **Random feature subsets:** at every split a tree may only choose among a random handful of features (typically √d). This stops every tree from using the same strong feature at the top, which would make them all alike.

passages.title: Random forest — Core math
passages.text: - Averaging B identically distributed predictors with variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ: `Var(average) = ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B`. More trees shrink the second term; **decorrelating** trees (feature subsampling) shrinks the first. Bias stays about the same as one tree. - A bootstrap sample of size n contains each row with probability `1 − (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → 1 − 1/e ≈ 63.2%`. - **Out-of-bag (OOB) estimate:** predict each row using only trees that did not train on it; behaves like built-in cross-validation. - Classification: average class probabilities (soft vote). Regression: average predictions.

passages.title: Random forest — Complexity
passages.text: Train: O(B · m · n log n · depth) with m features tried per split; trees are independent, so training parallelises perfectly. Predict: O(B · depth). Memory: B full trees.

passages.title: Random forest — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Expecting more trees to overfit: they do not; error plateaus. (Deeper trees can.) - Setting `max_features = d`: that is plain bagging; trees become correlated. - Impurity-based feature importances favour high-cardinality/continuous features and split credit among correlated ones; prefer permutation importance. - Poor extrapolation (cannot predict beyond the training target range). - Large models and slow inference versus a single linear model. - Imbalanced data: use class weights or balanced bootstraps.

passages.title: Random forest — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Excellent default for tabular data: little tuning, robust to outliers and unscaled or irrelevant features, handles non-linear interactions. - Gradient boosting usually edges it out in accuracy when carefully tuned, but is more sensitive to hyperparameters and trains sequentially. - Very high-dimensional sparse data (text) → linear models. Images/audio/text → deep learning.

passages.title: Ridge and lasso regression — Intuition
passages.text: Plain linear regression will happily use huge positive and negative weights to chase noise, especially with many or correlated features. **Regularisation** adds a cost for large weights, so the model only uses a big weight when the data strongly demands it. - **Ridge (L2):** penalise the *squared* weights. Shrinks every weight toward zero a bit, spreads weight across correlated features. Nothing becomes exactly zero. - **Lasso (L1):** penalise the *absolute* weights. Pushes many weights to **exactly zero**, so it also selects features. Why the difference? The L2 penalty's pull (`2αw`) fades as a weight gets small, so weights never quite reach zero. The L1 penalty pulls with constant force `α` however small the weight is, so weak features get pushed all the way to zero. Geometrically, the L1 ball is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the loss contours tend to touch it at a corner.

passages.title: Ridge and lasso regression — Core math
passages.text: - Ridge: `min ‖y − Xw‖² + α‖w‖²` ⇒ `w = (XᵀX + αI)⁻¹Xᵀy`. In SVD terms each direction is shrunk by `s² / (s² + α)`: weak directions are damped most. - Lasso: `min (1/2n)‖y − Xw‖² + α‖w‖₁`. Coordinate update: `wⱼ = S(ρⱼ, α) / zⱼ`, with `ρⱼ = (1/n) xⱼᵀ(y − X₋ⱼw₋ⱼ)`, `zⱼ = (1/n)‖xⱼ‖²`, and soft threshold `S(ρ, α) = sign(ρ) · max(|ρ| − α, 0)`. - All weights are zero when `α ≥ α_max = max|Xᵀy| / n`. - Bayesian view: ridge = MAP with a Gaussian prior on `w`; lasso = MAP with a Laplace prior. - Elastic net = both penalties together.

passages.title: Ridge and lasso regression — Complexity
passages.text: | Model | Time | |---|---| | Ridge closed form | O(n d² + d³) | | Lasso coordinate descent | O(n d) per sweep; usually tens of sweeps |

passages.title: Ridge and lasso regression — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Not standardising features: the penalty treats all weights alike, so features on large scales are penalised less. - Penalising the intercept (shifts predictions for no reason). - Different libraries scale the objective differently (`1/2n` or not), so "α = 1" is not portable. - Lasso with correlated features picks one almost arbitrarily; selection is unstable. - Treating lasso's selected features as causal/important without checking stability. - Choosing α on the test set; use cross-validation.

passages.title: Ridge and lasso regression — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Ridge: many correlated features, d > n, you want stable predictions. - Lasso: you believe only a few features matter, or you want a compact, interpretable model. - Elastic net: correlated groups *and* sparsity. - Nonlinear interactions → tree ensembles.

passages.title: Support vector machines (subgradient + SMO, kernel trick) — Intuition
passages.text: Many lines can separate two classes. The SVM picks the one with the **widest empty street** between the classes (the *margin*). A wide street means small wobbles in the data do not flip predictions, so it generalises well. Only the points touching the edge of the street matter; they are the **support vectors**. Delete any other point and the answer does not change. Real data is messy, so the **soft margin** lets some points sit inside the street or on the wrong side, for a penalty controlled by `C` (large C = few violations tolerated, narrow street). The **kernel trick**: if no straight line works, map the data to a richer space where one does. The dual problem only ever uses dot products `xᵢ·xⱼ`, so replacing them with a kernel function `K(xᵢ, xⱼ)` works *as if* we had mapped to a huge (even infinite) feature space, without ever computing the mapping.

passages.title: Support vector machines (subgradient + SMO, kernel trick) — Core math
passages.text: - Primal: `min ½‖w‖² + C Σ ξᵢ` s.t. `yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ`, `ξᵢ ≥ 0`. Equivalently hinge loss: `min (λ/2)‖w‖² + (1/n) Σ max(0, 1 − yᵢ f(xᵢ))` with `C = 1/(λn)`. - Margin width = `2 / ‖w‖`. - Subgradient of hinge: `−yᵢxᵢ` if `yᵢ f(xᵢ) < 1`, else 0. - Dual: `max Σαᵢ − ½ ΣΣ αᵢαⱼyᵢyⱼK(xᵢ, xⱼ)` s.t. `0 ≤ αᵢ ≤ C`, `Σαᵢyᵢ = 0`. - Decision function: `f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ, x) + b`. - KKT conditions: `αᵢ = 0 ⇒ yᵢfᵢ ≥ 1`; `0 < αᵢ < C ⇒ yᵢfᵢ = 1`; `αᵢ = C ⇒ yᵢfᵢ ≤ 1`. - SMO: update two multipliers at a time (the smallest move that keeps `Σαᵢyᵢ = 0`); the two-variable problem is a clipped 1D quadratic. - Kernels: linear `a·b`; polynomial `(γ a·b + c)ᵈ`; RBF `exp(−γ‖a − b‖²)`.

passages.title: Support vector machines (subgradient + SMO, kernel trick) — Complexity
passages.text: | | Train | Predict | |---|---|---| | Linear (subgradient / coordinate descent) | O(n·d) per pass | O(d) | | Kernel SMO | between O(n²) and O(n³); kernel matrix is O(n²) memory | O(#SV · d) |

passages.title: Support vector machines (subgradient + SMO, kernel trick) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Feature scaling is essential** (distances and dot products). - RBF `γ` too large → every point is its own island (overfit); too small → nearly linear. Tune `C` and `γ` together on a log grid. - Kernel SVMs do not scale past ~10⁵ samples. - Outputs are scores, not probabilities (Platt scaling adds them afterwards). - Multi-class needs one-vs-rest or one-vs-one wrappers. - Subgradient descent is not monotone: keep the best iterate or average.

passages.title: Support vector machines (subgradient + SMO, kernel trick) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Small/medium datasets, high-dimensional features (text with a linear kernel), clear margin. - Large tabular data → gradient boosting. Need probabilities → logistic regression. - Unstructured data at scale → neural networks (which largely displaced kernel SVMs).

passages.title: t-SNE (small-scale, exact) — Intuition
passages.text: t-SNE draws a 2D map of high-dimensional data where **points that were neighbours stay neighbours**. It does not try to preserve large distances, only "who is close to whom". 1. In the original space, turn distances into probabilities: "if point i picked a neighbour at random, favouring close ones, how likely is j?" 2. In the 2D map, define the same kind of probabilities. 3. Move the 2D points until the two sets of probabilities match. The 2D similarities use a heavy-tailed Student-t curve instead of a Gaussian. In 2D there is not enough room for every moderately-close point to stay moderately close (the "crowding problem"); heavy tails let such points sit farther apart, which separates clusters cleanly.

passages.title: t-SNE (small-scale, exact) — Core math
passages.text: - `p_{j|i} = exp(−‖xᵢ − xⱼ‖²/2σᵢ²) / Σₖ exp(−‖xᵢ − xₖ‖²/2σᵢ²)`, σᵢ found by binary search so the perplexity `2^{H(Pᵢ)}` equals the user's value (≈ effective number of neighbours). - Symmetrise: `pᵢⱼ = (p_{j|i} + p_{i|j}) / 2n`. - `qᵢⱼ = (1 + ‖yᵢ − yⱼ‖²)⁻¹ / Σ_{k≠l} (1 + ‖y_k − y_l‖²)⁻¹`. - Cost `C = KL(P‖Q) = Σ pᵢⱼ log(pᵢⱼ/qᵢⱼ)`; gradient `∂C/∂yᵢ = 4 Σⱼ (pᵢⱼ − qᵢⱼ)(yᵢ − yⱼ)(1 + ‖yᵢ − yⱼ‖²)⁻¹`. - Tricks: early exaggeration (multiply P by ~12 at first), momentum, adaptive gains.

passages.title: t-SNE (small-scale, exact) — Complexity
passages.text: Exact: O(n²) time and memory per iteration (fine up to a few thousand points). Barnes-Hut: O(n log n). FFT-accelerated (openTSNE/FIt-SNE): ~O(n).

passages.title: t-SNE (small-scale, exact) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Reading too much into the map:** cluster sizes and between-cluster distances are not meaningful; only local neighbourhoods are. - Perplexity changes the picture a lot; try several (5–50). - Different runs/seeds give different layouts. - Cannot embed new points (no `transform`); it is for visualisation, not features. - Run PCA to ~50 dimensions first on very high-dimensional data.

passages.title: t-SNE (small-scale, exact) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Visualising clusters in embeddings, images, single-cell data. - UMAP: faster, preserves more global structure, can transform new points. - PCA: linear, deterministic, meaningful distances, but misses non-linear structure.

passages.title: Autoencoder — Intuition
passages.text: Squeeze the data through a narrow bottleneck and ask the network to rebuild it on the other side. To succeed, the 8 numbers in the middle must capture what matters about each digit (stroke shape, thickness, slant) and drop what doesn't. The encoder half becomes a learned compressor and feature extractor, without any labels. - **Linear autoencoder** ⇔ PCA: same subspace, same error. - **Non-linear** autoencoders can follow curved structure in the data, so the same 8 numbers keep more. - **Denoising** autoencoders get a corrupted input but must output the clean one, so they learn what real digits look like rather than copying pixels.

passages.title: Autoencoder — Core math
passages.text: - `z = f_enc(x)`, `x̂ = f_dec(z)`, loss `‖x − x̂‖²` (or BCE for [0,1] pixels). - Linear case: optimum spans the top-k principal subspace (Baldi & Hornik), error = sum of the discarded eigenvalues. - Denoising: minimise `E‖x − f(x + ε)‖²`; with small Gaussian noise the optimal `f(x̃) − x̃` points along the gradient of the data log-density (the link to score matching / diffusion models).

passages.title: Autoencoder — Complexity
passages.text: Same as an MLP of the same size: O(batch · parameters) per step.

passages.title: Autoencoder — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - A bottleneck that is too wide (or an overcomplete AE without regularisation) learns the identity. - Comparing reconstruction losses computed with different reductions (sum vs mean). - The latent space of a plain AE is not organised for *sampling*: random codes decode to garbage (that is what the VAE fixes). - Sigmoid outputs with MSE learn slowly near saturation; BCE is a common alternative.

passages.title: Autoencoder — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Dimensionality reduction with non-linear structure, anomaly detection (high reconstruction error = unusual), denoising, unsupervised pre-training of features. - Linear structure → PCA (closed form, no tuning). Generating new samples → VAE, GAN, diffusion.

passages.title: Scalar autograd engine (micrograd-style) — Intuition
passages.text: Backpropagation is just the chain rule, applied automatically. Each `Value` is a number that remembers *how it was made* (which inputs, which operation). Computing a loss therefore builds a graph. To get gradients, start at the loss with gradient 1 and walk the graph backwards; every node passes gradient to its inputs, multiplied by its own local derivative. Every node only needs to know its **local** rule: - `+` copies the gradient to both inputs; - `*` sends each input the gradient times the *other* input; - `tanh` multiplies by `1 − tanh²`; and so on.

passages.title: Scalar autograd engine (micrograd-style) — Core math
passages.text: - Chain rule: if `L` depends on `x` through `y`, `∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · ∂y/∂x`. - If `x` is used in several places, contributions **add**: `∂L/∂x = Σ_paths …` — hence `+=`. - Reverse topological order ensures a node's gradient is complete before it is propagated. - Reverse mode costs about one extra forward pass regardless of the number of parameters, which is why it (not forward mode or finite differences) is used for training.

passages.title: Scalar autograd engine (micrograd-style) — Complexity
passages.text: Forward and backward are each O(number of graph nodes). Memory O(nodes): the whole graph is kept until `backward`. Scalar graphs are *very* slow (one Python object per multiply), which is the motivation for the tensor engine in the next folder.

passages.title: Scalar autograd engine (micrograd-style) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Overwriting (`=`) instead of accumulating (`+=`) gradients: wrong when a value is reused. - Forgetting `zero_grad()` between steps: gradients from previous steps pile up. - Recursive topological sort overflows Python's stack on deep graphs (iterative here). - Using `relu`'s derivative at exactly 0 (we choose 0). - Mutating `.data` of a value after building the graph changes what backward sees.

passages.title: Scalar autograd engine (micrograd-style) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - For learning and testing ideas only. Real work: PyTorch / JAX (tensor-level autograd, GPU, fused kernels). Symbolic differentiation (SymPy) gives formulas but blows up in size.

passages.title: Tensor autograd engine (NumPy) — Intuition
passages.text: The scalar engine works but needs one Python object per number. A tensor engine keeps the same graph-and-chain-rule idea, but each node holds a whole array, so `X @ W` is one node instead of millions. The backward rule for each operation becomes a *matrix* formula. The one genuinely new idea is **broadcasting**: adding a bias of shape `(10,)` to activations of shape `(batch, 10)` silently copies the bias across the batch. In reverse, every copy received some gradient, so the bias's gradient is the **sum over the batch axis**. `_unbroadcast` does that for any shapes.

passages.title: Tensor autograd engine (NumPy) — Core math (backward rules, `G` = upstream gradient)
passages.text: | forward | gradient to inputs | |---|---| | `C = A + B` | `G`, `G` (then unbroadcast) | | `C = A * B` | `G * B`, `G * A` | | `C = A @ B` | `G @ Bᵀ`, `Aᵀ @ G` | | `y = sum(x, axis)` | broadcast `G` back over `axis` | | `y = max(x, axis)` | `G` to the arg-max positions only | | `y = x[idx]` | scatter-add `G` into zeros (`np.add.at` handles repeated indices) | | `y = f(x)` elementwise | `G * f'(x)` | | `log_softmax(x)` | `x − logsumexp(x)`; built from the ops above, with the max subtracted | Optimisers: SGD with momentum and L2 weight decay; Adam with decoupled weight decay (AdamW). Both are tested step-for-step against PyTorch.

passages.title: Tensor autograd engine (NumPy) — Complexity
passages.text: Backward costs roughly the same as forward (about 2× FLOPs for matmul). Memory holds every intermediate array until `backward`, which is why activation memory dominates training.

passages.title: Tensor autograd engine (NumPy) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Forgetting to unbroadcast → gradient with the wrong shape (or silently wrong values). - Using `g[idx] += …` instead of `np.add.at` → repeated indices count once. - Computing gradients for constants (wasted memory); `requires_grad` controls this. - Shape conventions of matmul with 1D operands. - In-place modification of arrays that the backward pass still needs.

passages.title: Tensor autograd engine (NumPy) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Educational, and fine for small CPU models. PyTorch adds GPU kernels, fused ops, memory planning, mixed precision, and higher-order gradients.

passages.title: Character-level language model (NumPy LSTM) — Intuition
passages.text: Read text one character at a time and, at every position, guess the next character. The LSTM's hidden state is the model's memory of what it has read so far. Training pushes up the probability of the character that actually came next. To generate, feed the model its own guesses one at a time. **Temperature** reshapes the guess distribution before sampling: below 1 it plays safe (repetitive text), above 1 it takes risks (creative but misspelled); 0 means always take the most likely character.

passages.title: Character-level language model (NumPy LSTM) — Core math
passages.text: - `P(c_{t+1} | c_{≤t}) = softmax(W_out hₜ + b)`, loss = mean `−log P(true next char)` (nats/char); perplexity = `e^{loss}`, bits/char = `loss / ln 2`. - Embedding backward: rows of `E` receive the *sum* of gradients from every position that used them. - **Truncated BPTT:** train on random 64-character windows instead of the full 300k-long sequence. - **Gradient clipping:** if `‖g‖ > τ`, rescale `g ← g·τ/‖g‖` (direction kept, size capped). - Sampling: `p = softmax(logits / T)`.

passages.title: Character-level language model (NumPy LSTM) — Complexity
passages.text: Per step O(T · N · H · (D + H + V)); generation is O(H · (D + H + V)) per character, strictly sequential.

passages.title: Character-level language model (NumPy LSTM) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Off-by-one between inputs and targets (targets are inputs shifted by one). - Evaluating on windows that overlap the training text (use a held-out tail). - Exploding gradients early in training without clipping. - Comparing losses in nats vs bits. - Sampling with temperature 0 loops forever on a repeated phrase.

passages.title: Character-level language model (NumPy LSTM) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Character-level models need no tokenizer and handle any spelling, but sequences are long. - Subword tokens (BPE, `s5_nlp/tokenization`) + transformers (`s5_nlp/gpt`) are the modern default: shorter sequences, parallel training, far better long-range modelling.

passages.title: CNN: conv2d (im2col), pooling, a small CNN on digits — Intuition
passages.text: A convolution slides a small filter (say 3×3) over the image and, at every position, computes a weighted sum of the pixels under it. The *same* weights are used everywhere, so a filter that detects "a vertical edge" detects it anywhere in the image. Stacking conv layers builds features from small (edges) to large (strokes, digits). **Pooling** keeps the strongest response in each small window, shrinking the image and making the output less sensitive to exact positions. **im2col** is the speed trick: copy every 3×3 patch into a column of a big matrix, and the whole convolution becomes a single matrix multiplication (which BLAS does very fast).

passages.title: CNN: conv2d (im2col), pooling, a small CNN on digits — Core math
passages.text: - Output size: `⌊(H + 2·pad − k)/stride⌋ + 1`. - `out[n,f,r,c] = b_f + Σ_{c',i,j} W[f,c',i,j] · x[n,c',r·s+i,c·s+j]`. - im2col: `cols` of shape `(N, C·k·k, L)`; `out = W_flat @ cols + b`. - Backward: `∂W = Σₙ Gₙ colsₙᵀ`, `∂b = Σ G`, `∂x = col2im(W_flatᵀ G)`; `col2im` scatter-*adds* because overlapping patches share pixels (it is the adjoint of im2col; tested). - Max pool: gradient goes only to the arg-max of each window; avg pool spreads it evenly. - Parameters: `C_out·C_in·k² + C_out`, independent of image size.

passages.title: CNN: conv2d (im2col), pooling, a small CNN on digits — Complexity
passages.text: Conv forward: O(N · C_out · C_in · k² · H_out · W_out) multiply-adds. im2col memory: O(N · C_in · k² · H_out · W_out) — k² times the input, the price of the single big matmul.

passages.title: CNN: conv2d (im2col), pooling, a small CNN on digits — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Off-by-one output sizes with stride/padding. - In col2im, assigning instead of adding when patches overlap. - Mixing up (N, C, H, W) and (N, H, W, C) layouts. - Max-pool gradients with ties (we pick the first max, like PyTorch). - CNNs are translation-*equivariant* by design but not rotation/scale invariant; augment the data.

passages.title: CNN: conv2d (im2col), pooling, a small CNN on digits — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Images, audio spectrograms, any grid data with local structure → CNNs. - Very large datasets / long-range relationships in images → vision transformers. - Tiny or tabular inputs → MLP or trees (as the centred-digits result shows).

passages.title: GAN on 2D toy data — Intuition
passages.text: Two networks play a game. The **generator** turns random noise into fake data points. The **discriminator** looks at a point and guesses "real or fake?". The discriminator is trained to catch fakes; the generator is trained to fool the discriminator. If both play well, the fakes become indistinguishable from real data. At that point the discriminator can only guess, its output is ½ everywhere, and its loss is `2 log 2 ≈ 1.39` (the dashed line).

passages.title: GAN on 2D toy data — Core math
passages.text: - Minimax objective: `min_G max_D E_x[log D(x)] + E_z[log(1 − D(G(z)))]`. - For a fixed G the optimal discriminator is `D*(x) = p_data / (p_data + p_G)`; plugging it in, G minimises `2·JS(p_data ‖ p_G) − log 4`. - **Non-saturating generator loss** `−log D(G(z))`: same fixed point, but it gives big gradients when D confidently rejects the fakes (early training), where `log(1 − D(G(z)))` is flat. - Alternating updates; `fake.detach()` for the D step so G is not updated by D's loss.

passages.title: GAN on 2D toy data — Complexity
passages.text: Two forward/backward passes per step; no likelihood is computed.

passages.title: GAN on 2D toy data — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Mode collapse:** G produces only a few modes that currently fool D. Diagnose with coverage metrics like `mode_metrics`; mitigate with minibatch discrimination, WGAN-GP, unrolled D. - Losses do not tell you sample quality; they oscillate around an equilibrium (left plot). - D too strong → vanishing G gradients (use non-saturating loss); D too weak → G learns nothing. - Forgetting `detach()` (G is pushed to help D) or using BatchNorm carelessly in D. - Very sensitive to learning rates, β₁, and architecture.

passages.title: GAN on 2D toy data — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Sharp image synthesis, image-to-image translation, super-resolution (historically). - Today diffusion models usually win on quality and stability; VAEs give likelihoods and smooth latents; normalising flows give exact likelihoods.

passages.title: MLP with backprop, activations, Xavier/He initialisation — Intuition
passages.text: An MLP is a stack of "linear map, then bend": `Linear → activation → Linear → activation → …`. Without the bends (activations) the whole stack collapses into one linear map; with them it can carve curved decision boundaries (the moons test shows a linear model failing where a two-hidden-layer net succeeds). Backprop by hand: each layer stores what it saw in the forward pass, and in the backward pass turns "gradient w.r.t. my output" into "gradient w.r.t. my input" (plus gradients for its own weights). Chaining the layers in reverse gives every gradient in one sweep. **Initialisation matters** because signals are multiplied by a weight matrix at every layer. If weights are slightly too small the signal shrinks exponentially with depth (vanishing); slightly too big and it explodes. Xavier and He pick the variance that keeps the signal's scale constant.

passages.title: MLP with backprop, activations, Xavier/He initialisation — Core math
passages.text: - Linear `y = xW + b`: `∂W = xᵀG`, `∂b = Σ_batch G`, `∂x = GWᵀ`. - Activations (`∂x = G ⊙ f'(x)`): ReLU `1[x>0]`; leaky ReLU `1` or `α`; tanh `1 − tanh²`; sigmoid `σ(1 − σ)`; GELU (tanh approx.) derivative in `impl.py`. - Softmax + cross-entropy: `∂logits = (softmax − onehot)/batch`. - Variance propagation: `Var(y) = fan_in · Var(w) · Var(x)` (times ½ after ReLU). - Xavier: `Var(w) = 2/(fan_in + fan_out)` — tanh/sigmoid/linear. - He: `Var(w) = 2/fan_in` — ReLU family. - Test: 20 ReLU layers keep activation std ≈ 1 with He init but shrink ~100× with Xavier.

passages.title: MLP with backprop, activations, Xavier/He initialisation — Complexity
passages.text: Forward and backward: O(batch · Σ fan_in·fan_out) each. Memory: activations of every layer.

passages.title: MLP with backprop, activations, Xavier/He initialisation — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - All-zero initialisation: every hidden unit stays identical forever (symmetry is never broken). - Sigmoid/tanh in deep nets: derivatives ≤ 0.25 / ≤ 1 multiply up → vanishing gradients. - Dead ReLUs: a unit whose input is always negative never updates (leaky ReLU, lower lr, He init). - Forgetting to sum the bias gradient over the batch. - Applying softmax before a loss that expects logits. - Learning rate too high with momentum → divergence.

passages.title: MLP with backprop, activations, Xavier/He initialisation — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Tabular data where boosting is not available or as a component in bigger models. - Images → CNNs; sequences → RNNs/transformers; small tabular data → gradient boosting usually wins.

passages.title: Batch norm and layer norm — Intuition
passages.text: As earlier layers learn, the distribution of inputs to later layers keeps shifting and can drift to very large or very small scales. Normalisation re-centres and re-scales activations at every layer so each layer always sees inputs with a sensible scale, then lets the network learn its own preferred scale and offset (`γ`, `β`). - **Batch norm:** for each feature, normalise using the mean and variance **across the batch**. - **Layer norm:** for each sample, normalise **across its features**. No dependence on other samples, identical at training and test time.

passages.title: Batch norm and layer norm — Core math
passages.text: `x̂ = (x − μ)/√(σ² + ε)`, `y = γ x̂ + β`. - BN: μ, σ² over the batch axis (per feature); running averages `r ← (1 − m) r + m · stat` used at evaluation (unbiased variance, as in PyTorch). - LN: μ, σ² over the feature axis (per sample). - Backward (both, means over the normalised axis): `∂x = (1/σ)·(g − mean(g) − x̂·mean(g·x̂))` with `g = ∂y · γ`; `∂γ = Σ ∂y·x̂`, `∂β = Σ ∂y`. Verified against PyTorch and finite differences.

passages.title: Batch norm and layer norm — Complexity
passages.text: O(activations) for both passes; negligible next to the matmuls.

passages.title: Batch norm and layer norm — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - BN at evaluation must use running statistics (`model.eval()`); forgetting this gives batch-dependent predictions. - BN with tiny batches: noisy statistics (use LayerNorm/GroupNorm). - Forgetting the `ε`, or computing the backward pass as if μ and σ were constants (that is only correct in eval mode). - Weight decay on `γ`/`β` usually hurts; exclude them. - BN + dropout ordering can shift variance between train and test.

passages.title: Batch norm and layer norm — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - CNNs with reasonable batch sizes → BatchNorm. Transformers/RNNs, batch size 1, or online inference → LayerNorm (or RMSNorm, which drops the mean subtraction). Small-batch vision → GroupNorm.

passages.title: Dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules — Intuition
passages.text: A big network can memorise a small training set (training loss → 0) and then generalise worse. Regularisation makes memorising harder or less attractive: - **Dropout:** randomly switch off units during training, so the network cannot rely on any one unit and must spread knowledge redundantly. It behaves like averaging many thinned networks. - **Weight decay:** add a small pull toward zero on every weight; large weights are needed to fit noise sharply, so the network prefers smoother functions. - **Learning-rate schedules:** big steps early to make progress, small steps late to settle. Warm-up starts small because the first updates on random weights are unreliable.

passages.title: Dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules — Core math
passages.text: - Inverted dropout: `mask ~ Bernoulli(1 − p)`, `y = x · mask / (1 − p)` so `E[y] = x`; at test time `y = x`. Backward multiplies by the same mask. - Weight decay: minimise `L + (λ/2)‖W‖²` ⇒ gradient `g + λW` ⇒ update `W ← (1 − ηλ)W − ηg`. With Adam use decoupled weight decay (AdamW; see `autograd_tensor`). - Schedules: step `η₀ γ^⌊t/k⌋`; exponential `η₀ γᵗ`; cosine with warm-up `η₀ (t+1)/w` then `η_min + ½(η₀ − η_min)(1 + cos(π·progress))` (matches PyTorch, tested).

passages.title: Dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules — Complexity
passages.text: Dropout: O(activations) per step for the mask. Weight decay: O(parameters). Schedules: O(1).

passages.title: Dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Leaving dropout on at evaluation (call `model.eval()`), or using non-inverted dropout without rescaling at test time. - Decaying biases and normalisation parameters (usually excluded). - L2 inside Adam ≠ weight decay; use AdamW. - Too much dropout on small layers or before batch norm (variance shift). - Comparing runs with different schedules for different numbers of steps.

passages.title: Dropout, weight decay, learning-rate schedules — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Weight decay: almost always (small value). Dropout: large fully-connected layers, transformers (attention/residual dropout), less common in modern CNNs (batch norm + augmentation instead). - Other regularisers: data augmentation, early stopping, label smoothing, mixup, smaller models. - Schedules: cosine + warm-up for transformers; step decay / one-cycle for CNNs.

passages.title: ResNet block (PyTorch) — Intuition
passages.text: Making a network deeper should never hurt: the extra layers could just copy their input. In practice plain deep networks train *worse* than shallow ones (the "degradation problem"), because learning an exact identity through convolutions and ReLUs is hard, and gradients get badly scaled as they pass through dozens of layers. A residual block adds its input back to its output: `out = F(x) + x`. Now "do nothing" just means `F(x) = 0`, which is easy. And in the backward pass the `+ x` path gives the gradient a direct route to every earlier layer. Surprise from this experiment: with batch norm, the plain net's gradients did not *vanish*, they **exploded** going backwards (batch norm in deep plain nets is known to cause this). Either way, the gradient scale varies over orders of magnitude, and skip connections fix it.

passages.title: ResNet block (PyTorch) — Core math
passages.text: - `y = ReLU(F(x) + S(x))`, with `S` = identity, or a 1×1 conv + BN when the shape changes. - Backward: `∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · (∂F/∂x + I)`; the `I` term means the gradient can always flow through unchanged, so a stack of blocks has Jacobian `Π (I + ∂Fₖ/∂x)` instead of `Π ∂Fₖ/∂x`. - Zero-init trick: setting the last BN's γ to 0 makes every block start as the identity (tested). - Global average pooling before the classifier removes the dependence on spatial size.

passages.title: ResNet block (PyTorch) — Complexity
passages.text: Same as a plain CNN of the same depth; the identity shortcut is free, a projection shortcut adds a 1×1 conv.

passages.title: ResNet block (PyTorch) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Adding tensors with different shapes: use a projection shortcut when channels/stride change. - Putting the ReLU before the addition on the identity path (changes the "pre-activation" design). - Conv bias before BN is redundant (BN subtracts the mean). - Comparing plain vs residual with different optimisers/epochs.

passages.title: ResNet block (PyTorch) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Any deep network: skip connections are now everywhere (ResNets, U-Nets, transformers' residual stream). Variants: bottleneck blocks (1×1–3×3–1×1) for deeper ResNets, pre-activation ResNets, DenseNets (concatenate instead of add).

passages.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU: forward and backward (NumPy) — Intuition
passages.text: An RNN reads a sequence one step at a time and keeps a running **hidden state**: a summary of everything seen so far. The same weights are used at every step. Training unrolls the loop into a long chain and backpropagates through it (**BPTT**). The problem: the gradient from step 60 back to step 1 is multiplied by the recurrent weight matrix and the tanh slope **60 times**. That product almost always shrinks to nothing (vanishing) or blows up (exploding), so plain RNNs forget long-range information. The **LSTM** adds a separate memory lane, the cell state `c`, which is updated by *adding* new information instead of re-multiplying it through a weight matrix. Gates (numbers between 0 and 1) decide what to write, what to forget, and what to show. Along the memory lane the gradient is only scaled by the forget gate, so with `f ≈ 1` it survives many steps. The **GRU** is a lighter version with two gates and no separate cell.

passages.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU: forward and backward (NumPy) — Core math
passages.text: - RNN: `hₜ = tanh(W_ih xₜ + W_hh hₜ₋₁ + b)`. BPTT: `δₜ = (gₜ + δₜ₊₁ W_hh) ⊙ (1 − hₜ²)` → the product of Jacobians `Πₖ W_hhᵀ diag(1 − hₖ²)`. - LSTM (i, f, g, o): `cₜ = f ⊙ cₜ₋₁ + i ⊙ g`, `hₜ = o ⊙ tanh(cₜ)`; `∂cₜ₋₁ = ∂cₜ ⊙ f` (the additive "constant error carousel"). - GRU (r, z, n): `n = tanh(W_in x + r ⊙ (W_hn h + b_hn))`, `hₜ = (1 − z) ⊙ n + z ⊙ hₜ₋₁`. - Parameters: RNN `H(D + H + 2)`, GRU 3×, LSTM 4×.

passages.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU: forward and backward (NumPy) — Complexity
passages.text: O(T · N · H · (D + H)) per pass; **sequential in T** (cannot parallelise over time steps). Memory O(T · N · H) for the cached states (truncated BPTT limits T).

passages.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU: forward and backward (NumPy) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Exploding gradients: clip the global gradient norm (see `char_lm`). - Forgetting the gradient coming from the *next* time step (`dh_next`) — the most common BPTT bug. - Gate order differs between libraries (PyTorch LSTM is i, f, g, o). - PyTorch's GRU applies the reset gate *after* the hidden matmul (`r ⊙ (W_hn h + b_hn)`); the original paper applies it before. - Zero forget bias: the LSTM starts out forgetting; initialise it to ~1–3. - Carrying hidden state across batches without detaching (graph grows forever).

passages.title: RNN, LSTM, GRU: forward and backward (NumPy) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Streaming/online sequence processing, small models, low latency per step → GRU/LSTM. - Long-range dependencies with lots of data and parallel hardware → transformers. - Very long sequences with linear cost → state-space models (Mamba/S4) and linear attention.

passages.title: Siamese network with contrastive loss — Intuition
passages.text: Instead of a classifier with a fixed set of labels, learn a **similarity**: map every input to a point in space so that same-class inputs land close together and different-class inputs far apart. Then "are these two the same person/signature/digit?" is just "is the distance small?". New classes need no retraining: you can store one example (one-shot) and compare against it. "Siamese" means both inputs of a pair go through **the same network with the same weights**, so the distance is symmetric and meaningful.

passages.title: Siamese network with contrastive loss — Core math
passages.text: - Distance `d = ‖f(a) − f(b)‖₂`. - Contrastive loss (Hadsell et al. 2006), per pair: `½ d²` if same, `½ max(0, m − d)²` if different. The margin `m` stops pushing pairs already far apart. - Triplet loss alternative: `max(0, d(a, p) − d(a, n) + m)` with anchor, positive, negative. - Evaluation: ROC-AUC of `−d` as a score for "same".

passages.title: Siamese network with contrastive loss — Complexity
passages.text: Each training example is a pair (two forward passes through the shared network). There are O(n²) possible pairs, so pairs are sampled; mining hard pairs speeds learning.

passages.title: Siamese network with contrastive loss — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - **Collapse:** with only "same" pairs the network maps everything to one point; the negative term and margin prevent this. - Unbalanced pair sampling (random pairs are mostly "different"). - Easy negatives contribute zero loss once past the margin: hard-negative mining helps, too-hard (noisy) negatives hurt. - Evaluating only on seen classes overstates how well the embedding transfers (as the table shows).

passages.title: Siamese network with contrastive loss — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Face/signature verification, one-shot learning, image retrieval, deduplication, recommendation. - Fixed, known classes with plenty of labels → a plain classifier. Modern embedding learning → triplet loss with hard mining, or InfoNCE / CLIP-style contrastive learning over large batches.

passages.title: U-Net on a synthetic segmentation task — Intuition
passages.text: Segmentation means classifying **every pixel**. You need two kinds of information at once: - **context** — "this bright pixel is part of a round blob, not a square" — which needs a wide view, obtained by repeatedly downsampling; - **precision** — exactly where the blob's edge is — which downsampling destroys. A U-Net has an encoder that shrinks the image while widening the channels (context), a decoder that grows it back (upsampling), and **skip connections** that hand each decoder level the encoder's full-resolution features from the same level. The decoder then combines "what" (from below) with "where" (from the skip). The ablation shows it: without skips, the boundaries come out blurry and IoU drops.

passages.title: U-Net on a synthetic segmentation task — Core math
passages.text: - Encoder level: two 3×3 conv–BN–ReLU, then 2×2 max-pool. Decoder level: 2×2 transposed conv (stride 2) upsampling, concatenate the skip, two 3×3 conv–BN–ReLU. Final 1×1 conv → per-pixel logit. - Transposed conv with kernel 2, stride 2: each input pixel paints a learned 2×2 patch. - Loss: pixel-wise BCE + soft Dice, `1 − (2Σpy + ε)/(Σp + Σy + ε)`; Dice ignores the huge number of easy background pixels. - IoU = `|A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|` (Jaccard). Dice = `2|A ∩ B|/(|A| + |B|)`; `Dice = 2·IoU/(1 + IoU)`.

passages.title: U-Net on a synthetic segmentation task — Complexity
passages.text: Convolutional cost at each resolution; most FLOPs are in the full-resolution levels. Memory is dominated by the stored encoder activations needed for the skips.

passages.title: U-Net on a synthetic segmentation task — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Pixel accuracy looks great when most pixels are background; report IoU/Dice. - Spatial size mismatches when concatenating (odd sizes after pooling); pad or crop. - Checkerboard artefacts from transposed convs (alternatively upsample + conv). - Class imbalance: combine BCE with Dice or use focal loss. - Augmentations must transform image and mask identically.

passages.title: U-Net on a synthetic segmentation task — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Medical imaging, satellite imagery, any dense prediction with limited data (U-Nets train well on small datasets); also the denoiser inside diffusion models. - Instance segmentation (separate objects) → Mask R-CNN; large-scale semantic segmentation → DeepLab / transformer-based models (SegFormer, SAM).

passages.title: Variational autoencoder — Intuition
passages.text: A plain autoencoder's codes are scattered with gaps, so a random code decodes to nonsense. A VAE forces the codes to fill a known shape, a standard normal cloud, so that *any* point in it decodes to something plausible. 1. The encoder outputs a small **cloud** (mean and spread) for each image, not a single point. 2. We decode a random point from that cloud, so nearby codes must decode to similar images. 3. A **KL penalty** pulls every cloud toward the standard normal, packing the codes together without holes. Generating = sample from the standard normal, decode.

passages.title: Variational autoencoder — Core math
passages.text: - ELBO: `log p(x) ≥ E_{q(z|x)}[log p(x|z)] − KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z))`; train by minimising `−ELBO`. - Gaussian KL in closed form: `½ Σ (μ² + σ² − log σ² − 1)`. - **Reparameterisation:** `z = μ + σ ⊙ ε`, `ε ~ N(0, I)`, so `∂z/∂μ = 1`, `∂z/∂σ = ε`. - Gap: `log p(x) − ELBO = KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z|x))`; importance weighting with k samples tightens it: `log p(x) ≈ logsumexp_i[log p(x|zᵢ) + log p(zᵢ) − log q(zᵢ|x)] − log k`. - β-VAE: weight the KL by β (>1 for more disentangled, blurrier results).

passages.title: Variational autoencoder — Complexity
passages.text: Same as an autoencoder plus O(latent) for sampling and the KL term.

passages.title: Variational autoencoder — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Using the variance instead of the log-variance as the network output (negative variances, instability). - Mismatched reduction: summing reconstruction over pixels but averaging the KL (or vice versa) silently changes β. - **Posterior collapse:** a powerful decoder ignores z and KL → 0; use KL annealing or a weaker decoder. - Blurry samples: Gaussian/Bernoulli likelihoods average over uncertainty. - Reporting the ELBO as if it were the exact log-likelihood.

passages.title: Variational autoencoder — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Smooth, structured latent spaces; representation learning; generation with likelihoods; anomaly detection; as the compressor inside latent diffusion models. - Sharper samples → GANs or diffusion models. Exact likelihood → normalising flows / autoregressive models.

passages.title: Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention — Intuition
passages.text: Attention lets every position in a sequence **look at every other position and decide how much to borrow from each**. Each token produces three vectors: - a **query** — "what am I looking for?" - a **key** — "what do I contain?" - a **value** — "what will I hand over if chosen?"
