A token's output is the average of all values, weighted by how well its query matches each key (softmax of the dot products). Unlike an RNN, any two positions are connected in one step, and all positions are computed in parallel. **Multi-head** attention runs several smaller attentions side by side, each with its own query/key/ value projections, so different heads can track different relationships (the previous word, the subject, a matching bracket...), then concatenates and mixes their outputs.

passages.title: Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention — Core math
passages.text: - `Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(QKᵀ / √d_k + M) V`, `M` = 0 or −∞ (masking). - Why `√d_k`: for random unit-variance vectors, `q·k` has variance `d_k`. At d = 512 the raw scores have std ≈ 22 (softmax almost one-hot, tiny gradients); scaled, std ≈ 1 (tested). - Causal mask: position i may attend only to j ≤ i (language modelling). - Multi-head: `headᵢ = Attention(XW_Qⁱ, XW_Kⁱ, XW_Vⁱ)`, `MHA = Concat(head₁..h) W_O`, `d_head = d/h`. - Self-attention without positions is **permutation-equivariant** (tested): it has no notion of order until positional encodings are added. - Matches `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` and `nn.MultiheadAttention` (weights copied) to float tolerance, including causal masks and key-padding masks; gradcheck passes.

passages.title: Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention — Complexity
passages.text: O(T² · d) time and O(T²) memory per head for the score matrix: quadratic in sequence length. FlashAttention computes the same result in tiles without storing the T×T matrix.

passages.title: Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Mask conventions differ: here `True` = attend; `nn.MultiheadAttention` uses `True` = block. - Fully masked rows: softmax of all −∞ is NaN; handle them (zeros here). - Forgetting the scale factor; applying the mask after the softmax (weights no longer sum to 1). - Shape bugs when splitting heads: view as (B, T, h, d_head) then transpose to (B, h, T, d_head). - Padding tokens must be masked as keys (and ignored in the loss).

passages.title: Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - The core of transformers (`gpt`, `bert_classifier`), cross-attention in seq2seq, vision transformers. - Very long sequences: sparse/local attention, linear attention, state-space models. - Additive (Bahdanau) attention is the older variant used in `seq2seq_attention`.

passages.title: Tiny BERT-style encoder for sentiment — Intuition
passages.text: BERT is the *encoder* half of the transformer: every token attends to every other token, both to its left and its right (no causal mask). That makes it excellent at **understanding** a whole input (classification, tagging, retrieval embeddings) but not at generating text left-to-right. - A special **[CLS]** token is placed first. After the layers it has attended to the whole sentence, so its final vector serves as the sentence summary fed to a small classifier. - **Masked language modelling** pre-training: hide 15% of words and train the model to fill them in from context on both sides. This needs no labels and teaches general language structure; the model is then **fine-tuned** on the labelled task.

passages.title: Tiny BERT-style encoder for sentiment — Core math
passages.text: - Input: `LN(token_emb + position_emb)`; layers: post-norm `LN(x + MHA(x))`, `LN(x + FFN(x))` with padding keys masked. - Classification: `softmax(W₂ tanh(W₁ h_[CLS]))`, cross-entropy. - MLM masking: choose 15% of tokens; 80% → `[MASK]`, 10% → random token, 10% unchanged; loss only on chosen positions. (The 10%/10% stop the model relying on the `[MASK]` symbol, which never appears at fine-tuning time.) - Tested properties: changing a *later* word changes *earlier* positions' representations (bidirectional); changing padding changes nothing.

passages.title: Tiny BERT-style encoder for sentiment — Complexity
passages.text: O(L · (T² d + T d²)) per sentence; one forward pass gives the whole-sentence representation.

passages.title: Tiny BERT-style encoder for sentiment — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Not masking padding in attention (padding tokens then influence real tokens). - Using a causal mask by mistake (turns it into a weak GPT). - Learning rate too high for fine-tuning a pre-trained model (catastrophic forgetting); typical 1e-5–5e-5 for real BERT. - Max length truncation dropping the decisive clause. - Synthetic data is easy to solve perfectly; real sentiment data has sarcasm, noise and label ambiguity.

passages.title: Tiny BERT-style encoder for sentiment — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Classification, named-entity tagging, extractive QA, sentence embeddings for retrieval. - Bag-of-words + linear models: fast baseline when order rarely matters. - Generation tasks → decoder (GPT) or encoder-decoder (T5). Today large decoder LLMs are also used zero-shot for classification, at much higher cost.

passages.title: BM25 — Intuition
passages.text: BM25 is the scoring function behind most keyword search engines (Lucene, Elasticsearch). It ranks a document higher when it contains the query's words, especially **rare** words, with two corrections to plain term counting: - **Saturation:** the first time a document says "kneser" is strong evidence; the 20th adds little. - **Length normalisation:** a long document will contain more matches by chance, so matches in a short document count for more.

passages.title: BM25 — Core math
passages.text: `score(q, d) = Σ_{t ∈ q} idf(t) · tf·(k₁ + 1) / (tf + k₁·(1 − b + b·|d|/avgdl))` - `idf(t) = ln(1 + (N − df + 0.5)/(df + 0.5))` (always positive). - `k₁` ∈ [1.2, 2]: how quickly tf saturates (the tf factor is bounded by `k₁ + 1`, tested). `k₁ = 0` ignores tf entirely. - `b` ∈ [0, 1]: strength of length normalisation (`b = 0` disables it, tested). - Inverted index: `term → {doc: tf}`, so a query touches only documents containing its terms. Scores match a direct implementation of the formula (tested).

passages.title: BM25 — Complexity
passages.text: Indexing O(total tokens). Query O(Σ posting-list lengths of the query terms), far smaller than the corpus for selective terms. Production engines add skip lists and top-k pruning (WAND, MaxScore).

passages.title: BM25 — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Tokenisation mismatch between index and query (case, stemming, stopwords). - Vocabulary mismatch: "car" never matches "automobile" (dense retrieval fixes this; see `dense_retrieval`; or combine both in a hybrid). - Classic idf goes negative for terms in more than half the documents; use the +1 form. - Very short documents dominate if b is too high.

passages.title: BM25 — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Strong, cheap, explainable first-stage retrieval; works with no training data; great for exact terms (names, codes, error messages). - Semantic matching / paraphrases → dense embeddings. Best results usually come from BM25 + dense hybrid retrieval followed by a cross-encoder reranker.

passages.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF — Intuition
passages.text: **Bag of words:** describe a document by *which words appear and how often*, ignoring order — like tipping the words of a page into a bag and counting them. Simple, fast, and surprisingly strong for topic-level tasks (spam, news category, search). **TF-IDF** fixes the obvious flaw that common words ("the", "and") dominate the counts. Weight each word by how *rare* it is across the collection: a word that appears in every document says nothing about any particular one; a word that appears in few documents is a strong signal.

passages.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF — Core math (sklearn defaults, reproduced exactly)
passages.text: - Tokens: lowercase, regex `\b\w\w+\b` (2+ word characters). Vocabulary sorted alphabetically. - `tf(t, d)` = raw count (or `1 + ln tf` if sublinear). - `idf(t) = ln((1 + n)/(1 + df(t))) + 1` with smoothing, `ln(n/df(t)) + 1` without. - `tfidf = tf · idf`, then each document vector is L2-normalised, so cosine similarity is just a dot product. - n-grams (`ngram_range=(1, 2)`) recover a little word order ("not good").

passages.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF — Complexity
passages.text: Fitting: O(total tokens). The matrix is `documents × vocabulary`, extremely sparse (real implementations use sparse matrices; here dense arrays keep the code readable).

passages.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Fitting the vocabulary/idf on test data (leakage). - Vocabulary explosion with n-grams; control with `min_df`, `max_df`, `max_features`. - Losing negation and order ("not bad" vs "bad"); add bigrams or use embeddings. - Words unseen at training time are silently ignored at test time. - Dense matrices for big corpora run out of memory.

passages.title: Bag-of-words and TF-IDF — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Strong baselines for text classification (with logistic regression or naive Bayes), keyword search, and document similarity; interpretable features. - BM25 (`s5_nlp/bm25`) is the better-tuned version for search ranking. - Semantic similarity (synonyms, paraphrases) → dense embeddings (`word2vec`, `dense_retrieval`).

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — Results
passages.text: **Vector index** (20,000 clustered unit vectors in 32-d, 200 queries, top-10, IVF with 64 cells): | n_probe | recall vs exact | vectors compared per query | |---|---|---| | 1 | 0.90 | 348 (1.7%) | | 4 | 1.00 | 1,313 (6.6%) | | 64 (all cells) | 1.00 (= brute force) | 20,000 | **Embedding model:** a dual encoder (mean of learned word embeddings → linear → unit vector, 128-d) trained from scratch for 1,500 steps with InfoNCE and in-batch negatives on self-supervised pairs from the notes corpus (a sentence of a passage ↔ another passage of the same topic; no queries used). On the 430 held-out interview questions over 432 passages (numbers from [`results.txt`](results.txt), written by the slow test), MRR@10: | | MRR@10 | |---|---| | untrained encoder (random embeddings, averaged) | 0.29 | | **trained dual encoder** | **0.42** | | BM25 (`s5_nlp/bm25`) | **0.69** | | reciprocal-rank fusion of BM25 + dense (top 50 each, k = 60) | 0.57 | **Why this number has moved:** the corpus is the repository's own notes, so it grows as topics are added (and when these notes are edited). The trained encoder's MRR was 0.33 when first measured (401 passages, 400 training steps, 64-d), 0.40 after tuning to 1,500 steps and 128-d (406 passages), and is 0.42 on the final corpus (432 passages). The conclusion has not changed at any point: training helps, and BM25 stays far ahead. **Honest finding:** training helps, but a dense model learned from ~400 passages is far behind BM25, and fusing it in hurts. Its training loss goes to ~0: it memorises the 86 topics rather than learning general meaning. Dense retrieval wins when the encoder is **pre-trained on huge corpora** (e.g. sentence-transformers, E5) and tested on paraphrased queries. Here the questions share many exact terms with the notes, which suits BM25.

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — Intuition
passages.text: Turn every passage and every query into a vector so that "relevant" means "close". Search is then a nearest-neighbour lookup, and the vectors can capture meaning beyond exact words ("automobile" near "car"), *if* the encoder has learned language from enough data. **Brute force** compares the query with every vector: exact but O(N). **IVF** (inverted file) groups the vectors into clusters with k-means; a query only scans the few clusters whose centres are nearest. A true neighbour sitting just across a cluster border is missed, so `n_probe` trades recall for speed.

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — Core math
passages.text: - Encoder: `f(text) = normalize(W · mean(E[tokens]))`; similarity = cosine = dot product of unit vectors. - InfoNCE: `L = −(1/B) Σᵢ log( exp(qᵢ·pᵢ/τ) / Σⱼ exp(qᵢ·pⱼ/τ) )`, τ = 0.05; the other passages in the batch are the negatives. (One pair per topic per batch avoids false negatives.) - IVF: k-means centroids `c₁..c_L`; query cost ≈ `L + (n_probe/L)·N` vector comparisons. - Recall vs exact = `|ANN top-k ∩ exact top-k| / k`.

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — Complexity
passages.text: Brute force O(N·d) per query (fast with BLAS for up to ~10⁶ vectors). IVF build = k-means O(iters·N·L·d); query ~O((L + N·n_probe/L)·d). Memory O(N·d) for both (product quantisation compresses it).

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Comparing unnormalised vectors with dot product (long vectors win) or mixing metrics. - IVF with too few training points per cell, or `n_probe = 1` on borderline queries. - Evaluating a dense retriever on queries that overlap its training pairs (leakage). - Small in-batch negatives make contrastive training too easy; hard negatives help. - Expecting a from-scratch encoder on a tiny corpus to beat BM25 (it did not here).

passages.title: Dense retrieval: an embedding model and vector indexes (brute force + IVF) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Semantic search, RAG, recommendation, deduplication — with a pre-trained embedding model. - Exact/rare terms, no training data → BM25. Best practice: hybrid retrieval plus a reranker. - Larger indexes: IVF-PQ (FAISS), HNSW graphs (hnswlib, most vector databases), ScaNN.

passages.title: Evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, exact match, recall@k, MRR, NDCG — Intuition
passages.text: - **BLEU** (translation): what fraction of the output's 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-word chunks appear in a reference translation? Plus a penalty for outputs that are too short. Precision-oriented. - **ROUGE-L** (summarisation): how long is the longest sequence of words that appears, in order, in both the output and the reference? Recall-oriented. - **Exact match / token F1** (question answering): is the answer string right after normalising case, punctuation and articles? F1 gives partial credit for overlapping words. - **Recall@k:** did the relevant documents make it into the top k? - **MRR:** how high is the *first* relevant result? (1 for rank 1, ½ for rank 2, ...) - **NDCG:** graded relevance with a logarithmic discount for lower positions, divided by the best possible score.

passages.title: Evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, exact match, recall@k, MRR, NDCG — Core math
passages.text: - BLEU = `BP · exp((1/N) Σₙ log pₙ)`, `pₙ` = clipped n-gram precision (each n-gram counted at most as often as in the best reference), `BP = min(1, exp(1 − r/c))` with r the closest reference length. - ROUGE-L: `P = LCS/|hyp|`, `R = LCS/|ref|`, `F = (1 + β²)PR / (R + β²P)`. - EM / F1: SQuAD normalisation, F1 over token multisets. - `recall@k = |top-k ∩ relevant| / |relevant|`, `RR = 1/rank_first_relevant`, MRR = mean RR. - `DCG@k = Σᵢ relᵢ / log₂(i + 1)`, `NDCG = DCG / IDCG` (matches `sklearn.metrics.ndcg_score`, tested).

passages.title: Evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, exact match, recall@k, MRR, NDCG — Complexity
passages.text: BLEU O(N · L) with hashing; ROUGE-L O(L_hyp · L_ref) (LCS DP); ranking metrics O(k).

passages.title: Evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, exact match, recall@k, MRR, NDCG — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Sentence-level BLEU of 0 because one n-gram order has no match (use smoothing, or corpus BLEU). - Different tokenisation/normalisation makes BLEU numbers incomparable (sacreBLEU standardises it). - n-gram metrics reward surface overlap: correct paraphrases score low, fluent nonsense can score well. - Recall@k with k ≥ corpus size is trivially 1. - NDCG with all-zero relevance (undefined; treat as 0).

passages.title: Evaluation metrics: BLEU, ROUGE-L, exact match, recall@k, MRR, NDCG — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - BLEU: machine translation benchmarks. ROUGE: summarisation. EM/F1: extractive QA. - Ranking: recall@k for first-stage retrieval (what reaches the reranker), MRR when one answer matters, NDCG for graded relevance. - Open-ended generation: human evaluation, model-based judges, embedding similarity (BERTScore).

passages.title: GloVe (small) — Intuition
passages.text: word2vec learns from one (word, context) pair at a time. GloVe first counts how often every pair of words co-occurs in the whole corpus, then finds vectors whose dot products reproduce the **logarithm of those counts**. The key observation (Pennington et al.) is that *ratios* of co-occurrence probabilities carry meaning: `P(solid | ice) / P(solid | steam)` is large, `P(water | ice) / P(water | steam)` ≈ 1. Fitting log counts turns ratios into vector differences, which is why analogies show up as straight-line offsets.

passages.title: GloVe (small) — Core math
passages.text: - Co-occurrence `X_ij = Σ 1/distance` within the window. - Objective: `J = Σ_{X_ij > 0} f(X_ij) (wᵢ·c̃ⱼ + bᵢ + b̃ⱼ − log X_ij)²`. - Weighting: `f(x) = (x/x_max)^α` for `x < x_max`, else 1 — down-weights noisy rare pairs and caps frequent ones. - Gradients: with `e_ij = f·(prediction − log X)`, `∂J/∂W = 2EC`, `∂J/∂C = 2EᵀW`, `∂J/∂b = 2Σⱼ e_ij` (finite-difference checked). Final vectors `W + C`. - AdaGrad: `θ ← θ − η g / √(Σ g²)`.

passages.title: GloVe (small) — Complexity
passages.text: Building X: O(tokens × window). Each epoch: O(non-zero entries × d) (here full-batch O(V² d) since V is tiny). Memory O(V²) for X (sparse in practice).

passages.title: GloVe (small) — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Including zero counts (log 0); they must be skipped. - Forgetting the weighting function: frequent pairs like ("the", ·) dominate. - Over-training on small corpora (above). - Comparing W alone vs W + C (W + C is usually slightly better). - Building X for a large vocabulary as a dense matrix.

passages.title: GloVe (small) — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Pre-trained GloVe vectors are a common, cheap feature set. Train-from-scratch: SGNS, fastText, or GloVe depending on tooling; contextual embeddings (BERT) for most modern tasks. - Very small data: PPMI + SVD.

passages.title: Decoder-only transformer (GPT-style) on tiny-shakespeare — Intuition
passages.text: A GPT reads a sequence and, at every position, predicts the next token. Each layer has two parts: 1. **Causal self-attention** — every position gathers information from earlier positions (never later ones, so training on all positions at once is still honest next-token prediction). 2. **MLP** — processes each position's gathered information on its own. Both are wrapped in residual connections with layer norm before them ("pre-norm"), forming a "residual stream" that each layer reads from and writes back to. **Generation** is a loop: predict a distribution, pick a token, append it, repeat. The **KV cache** stores each layer's keys and values for the tokens already processed, so each new token only computes its own query/key/value instead of recomputing the whole prefix (tested: identical output, faster). **Sampling** controls creativity: temperature rescales the logits, top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens, top-p keeps the smallest set whose probabilities sum to p.

passages.title: Decoder-only transformer (GPT-style) on tiny-shakespeare — Core math
passages.text: - Embedding `x₀ = E[tokens]` (positions enter via RoPE inside attention). - Block: `x ← x + Attn(LN(x))`, `x ← x + MLP(LN(x))`, MLP = Linear(d, 4d) → GELU → Linear(4d, d). - Output logits `= LN(x_L) Eᵀ` (weight tying: the same matrix embeds and un-embeds). - Loss: mean cross-entropy over all positions. Init: N(0, 0.02), residual projections scaled by `1/√(2L)` (GPT-2), so loss at init ≈ `ln V` (tested). - KV cache: at step t, `q_t` attends over cached `K_{≤t}, V_{≤t}`; RoPE uses the absolute offset t. - Top-p: sort probabilities, drop a token when the probabilities before it already sum to ≥ p.

passages.title: Decoder-only transformer (GPT-style) on tiny-shakespeare — Complexity
passages.text: Training: O(L · T · d² + L · T² · d) per sequence. Generation without cache: O(T²) work per new token (O(T³) total); with cache O(T) per token, at the cost of O(L · T · d) memory for keys/values.

passages.title: Decoder-only transformer (GPT-style) on tiny-shakespeare — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Off-by-one between inputs and targets; leaking future tokens through the mask (tested causality). - KV cache with the wrong position offset for RoPE (tested against full recompute). - Generating past `block_size` (the model never saw those positions). - Evaluating with dropout on (`model.eval()`). - Weight decay on LayerNorm and bias parameters (excluded here). - Comparing losses across different tokenizers (nats/char vs nats/token).

passages.title: Decoder-only transformer (GPT-style) on tiny-shakespeare — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Any autoregressive generation: text, code, music, even pixels. Encoders (BERT, `bert_classifier`) are better for classification/retrieval embeddings; encoder-decoders (T5) for input → output tasks.

passages.title: LoRA by hand, applied to the tiny GPT — Intuition
passages.text: Fine-tuning a big model normally updates every weight and needs a full copy of the model per task. LoRA's bet: the *change* a task needs is simple, so it can be written as a low-rank matrix `ΔW = B·A`, where A squeezes the input down to r numbers and B expands them back. Freeze the original W, train only A and B. A 128×384 matrix (49k numbers) gets an adapter of 4×(128 + 384) = 2k numbers. One base model can carry many tiny adapters, one per task, and swap them. B starts at zero, so training starts from exactly the pretrained model (tested).

passages.title: LoRA by hand, applied to the tiny GPT — Core math
passages.text: - `h = W x + (α/r) · B A x`, `W ∈ ℝ^{d_out×d_in}` frozen, `A ∈ ℝ^{r×d_in}` (Kaiming init), `B ∈ ℝ^{d_out×r}` (zeros). - `rank(ΔW) ≤ r`; trainable parameters `r(d_in + d_out)` per adapted matrix. - `α/r` scaling keeps the update size roughly independent of r, so the learning rate needn't change with r. - Merge for inference: `W ← W + (α/r) B A`; unmerge to switch adapters. - Gradients flow only into A and B (tested; gradcheck passes).

passages.title: LoRA by hand, applied to the tiny GPT — Complexity
passages.text: Training memory falls sharply (no optimiser state for frozen weights: Adam keeps 2 extra copies of each trainable parameter). Compute per step is about the same as full fine-tuning (the backward pass still runs through the frozen layers). Inference after merging: unchanged.

passages.title: LoRA by hand, applied to the tiny GPT — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Forgetting to freeze the base weights (then it is just full fine-tuning plus extra parameters). - Initialising both A and B randomly: the model no longer starts at the pretrained function. - Rank too small for a big domain shift; target only some layers (here attention) and decide whether to include the MLPs. - Using the full fine-tuning learning rate: LoRA usually wants a larger one (3e-3 vs 1e-3 here). - Merging, then continuing to train the adapter (double counting); unmerge first.

passages.title: LoRA by hand, applied to the tiny GPT — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Adapting large models on limited GPU memory; serving many task-specific variants of one base model. - QLoRA: LoRA on top of a 4-bit quantised base. Other parameter-efficient methods: adapters (small bottleneck MLPs), prefix/prompt tuning, IA³. Full fine-tuning when data is large and compute allows.

passages.title: n-gram language model, smoothing, perplexity — Intuition
passages.text: A language model assigns a probability to the next word given the previous ones. An n-gram model makes a strong simplification: only the last `n − 1` words matter. Then probabilities are just ratios of counts: `P(sat | the cat) = count("the cat sat") / count("the cat")`. The trouble is **sparsity**: most word combinations never appear in training, so their count is 0, and one zero makes a whole sentence impossible (infinite perplexity). **Smoothing** moves a little probability mass from seen to unseen events: - **add-k:** pretend everything was seen k extra times (simple, too crude for large vocabularies); - **interpolation:** mix the trigram, bigram, and unigram estimates; - **Kneser-Ney:** subtract a fixed discount from every seen count and give the freed mass to a lower-order model that asks "*in how many different contexts* does this word appear?" (so "Francisco", which almost only follows "San", is not a good guess after a random word). **Perplexity** = `exp(average negative log-probability per word)`: roughly "how many words the model is choosing between". A uniform guess over V words has perplexity exactly V (tested).

passages.title: n-gram language model, smoothing, perplexity — Core math
passages.text: - MLE: `P(w | h) = c(h, w) / c(h)`. - add-k: `(c(h, w) + k) / (c(h) + kV)`. - Interpolation: `Σₘ λₘ P_MLE^{(m)}(w | h)`, λ tuned on held-out data (weight of an unseen context is passed to the next order down). - Interpolated Kneser-Ney: `P(w|h) = max(c(h,w) − d, 0)/c(h) + d·N₁₊(h•)/c(h) · P_lower(w|h')`, lower orders use continuation counts `N₁₊(•h'w)`, base case uniform `1/V`. - Perplexity: `PP = exp(−(1/N) Σ log P(wᵢ | hᵢ))`.

passages.title: n-gram language model, smoothing, perplexity — Complexity
passages.text: Training: O(tokens · n) counting. Memory: number of distinct n-grams (grows fast with n). Query: O(n) dictionary lookups.

passages.title: n-gram language model, smoothing, perplexity — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Comparing perplexities computed with different vocabularies or `<unk>` handling. - Forgetting the end-of-sentence token (it is a prediction too) or counting start tokens. - Probabilities that do not sum to one after "smoothing" (tested for every method here). - Tuning λ or k on the test set. - Larger n is not automatically better: data sparsity grows exponentially with n.

passages.title: n-gram language model, smoothing, perplexity — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Fast, interpretable baselines; spelling correction, keyboard prediction, speech recognition decoding (historically), counting-based features. - Neural LMs (RNNs, transformers in `s5_nlp/gpt`) generalise across similar contexts and handle long history, at much higher compute.

passages.title: Positional encodings: sinusoidal and RoPE — Intuition
passages.text: Attention by itself has no idea of order: shuffle the words and each word's output is simply shuffled too (tested in `attention`). Something must tell the model *where* each token is. - **Sinusoidal (absolute):** give every position a fixed fingerprint made of sine and cosine waves of many different wavelengths, like the hands of many clocks turning at different speeds, and **add** it to the token embedding. Fast waves distinguish neighbours; slow waves distinguish distant regions. - **RoPE (rotary, relative):** instead of adding anything, **rotate** each query and key vector by an angle proportional to its position (each pair of dimensions at its own speed). When a query at position m meets a key at position n, the two rotations combine into a rotation by `m − n`, so attention scores depend only on the *distance* between tokens. Used by Llama, Mistral, GPT-NeoX.

passages.title: Positional encodings: sinusoidal and RoPE — Core math
passages.text: - Sinusoidal: `PE[p, 2i] = sin(p·ωᵢ)`, `PE[p, 2i+1] = cos(p·ωᵢ)`, `ωᵢ = 10000^(−2i/d)`; wavelengths from 2π to 2π·10000. Each (sin, cos) pair has norm 1. - Shift property: `PE[p + k] = PE[p] · R_k` for a fixed block-diagonal rotation `R_k` (tested), so a linear layer can read relative offsets. - RoPE: for each pair `(x₂ᵢ, x₂ᵢ₊₁)` at position m, rotate by `m·θᵢ`: `(x₂ᵢ cos − x₂ᵢ₊₁ sin, x₂ᵢ sin + x₂ᵢ₊₁ cos)`, i.e. multiply the complex number `x₂ᵢ + i·x₂ᵢ₊₁` by `e^{i m θᵢ}` (both forms implemented and compared). - `⟨R_m q, R_n k⟩ = ⟨q, R_{n−m} k⟩` ⇒ scores depend on `m − n` only (tested: score(5, 2) = score(50, 47)). - Rotations preserve norms; position 0 is the identity.

passages.title: Positional encodings: sinusoidal and RoPE — Complexity
passages.text: O(T·d) to compute/apply; negligible next to attention. Tables are precomputed.

passages.title: Positional encodings: sinusoidal and RoPE — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - RoPE applied to values (it should be queries and keys only). - Interleaved pairs (2i, 2i+1) vs "half split" (i, i + d/2) layouts differ between codebases; weights are not interchangeable. - Forgetting the position offset when decoding with a KV cache (new token is at position t, not 0). - Learned absolute embeddings cannot extrapolate past the training length; RoPE degrades gracefully and can be extended (position interpolation, NTK scaling). - Scaling: embeddings are often multiplied by √d before adding sinusoidal encodings.

passages.title: Positional encodings: sinusoidal and RoPE — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Modern decoder LLMs: RoPE. Original transformer / many encoders: sinusoidal or learned absolute embeddings (BERT, GPT-2). Other relative schemes: ALiBi (linear distance penalty), T5 relative buckets.

passages.title: Minimal RAG loop with an offline extractive answerer — Intuition
passages.text: A language model only knows what it saw in training. **Retrieval-augmented generation** looks things up first: find the passages most relevant to the question, then produce an answer *grounded* in them, with sources. Updating knowledge means updating the index, not retraining the model. Here the "generator" is extractive (it selects a sentence), which keeps everything offline and makes every answer verifiable: it is a quote, and the citation says where it came from.

passages.title: Minimal RAG loop with an offline extractive answerer — Core math / algorithm
passages.text: 1. Retrieve: BM25 top-k (`s5_nlp/bm25`). 2. Candidate sentences from those passages. 3. Score: `Σ_{t ∈ q ∩ s} idf(t) / Σ_{t ∈ q} idf(t) + w · score(passage)/score(top passage)`, w = 1. 4. Answer = best sentence + passage id. Unanswerable (nothing retrieved) → explicit "not found". 5. Evaluate retrieval (topic hit) and answer quality (ROUGE-L, token F1 from `s5_nlp/eval_metrics`).

passages.title: Minimal RAG loop with an offline extractive answerer — Complexity
passages.text: Retrieval O(posting lists); answer selection O(k · sentences · |q|). Index built once, O(corpus).

passages.title: Minimal RAG loop with an offline extractive answerer — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Leakage: indexing the very text the references come from (the interview sections are excluded here). - Chunking: passages too long dilute relevance; too short lose context. - Garbage in: the answer can only be as good as retrieval (the ceiling above). - Ungrounded generation: an LLM generator may ignore the retrieved text; always show citations and check them. - Evaluating only with n-gram overlap: paraphrased correct answers score low.

passages.title: Minimal RAG loop with an offline extractive answerer — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Question answering over private or changing documents, support bots, internal search with answers. - Production: hybrid retrieval + cross-encoder reranking + an LLM generator instructed to cite and to say "not found". Fine-tuning instead of RAG when the knowledge is stable and style matters more than facts.

passages.title: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention — Intuition
passages.text: A plain encoder-decoder reads the whole input, squeezes it into **one** vector, and the decoder must regenerate everything from that vector. That bottleneck is fine for short inputs and fails for long ones (see the "no attention" row). **Attention** removes the bottleneck. The encoder keeps a vector for *every* input position. At each output step the decoder asks "which input positions matter right now?", gets a weight for each, and reads a weighted average (the *context*). For reversal it learns to look at the input from the back to the front.

passages.title: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention — Core math
passages.text: - Encoder states `hⱼ = [→hⱼ; ←hⱼ]` (bidirectional GRU), initial decoder state `s₀ = tanh(W[→h_L; ←h_1])`. - Bahdanau (additive) score: `eₜⱼ = vᵀ tanh(W_s sₜ₋₁ + W_h hⱼ)`; weights `αₜ = softmax(eₜ)` over real (unpadded) positions; context `cₜ = Σⱼ αₜⱼ hⱼ`. - Decoder: `sₜ = GRU([emb(yₜ₋₁); cₜ], sₜ₋₁)`, `P(yₜ) = softmax(W_o [sₜ; cₜ])`. - Training: teacher forcing (true previous token as input), cross-entropy ignoring padding, gradient clipping at norm 1. Inference: greedy decoding with the model's own predictions.

passages.title: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention — Complexity
passages.text: O(T_in · T_out · d) for attention plus the recurrent cost; decoding is sequential in T_out.

passages.title: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Not masking padded encoder positions (attention leaks onto padding). Packed sequences keep padding out of the encoder (tested: extra padding does not change the encoding). - Exposure bias: trained with teacher forcing, tested on its own outputs, so errors compound. - Forgetting the end-of-sequence token, so decoding never knows when to stop. - Measuring token accuracy instead of exact match for tasks where one wrong token ruins the output.

passages.title: Seq2seq with Bahdanau attention — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Historical baseline for translation/summarisation and the direct ancestor of the transformer. - Today: transformer encoder-decoders (T5, BART) or decoder-only LMs; RNN seq2seq still fits small, streaming or low-latency settings.

passages.title: Tokenization: whitespace/regex, BPE from scratch, WordPiece — Intuition
passages.text: Models work on numbers, so text must be cut into pieces (tokens) that each get an id. The choice of pieces is a trade-off: - **Words** are meaningful but there are millions of them, and any new word is "unknown". - **Characters/bytes** never fail, but sequences get very long and each token means little. - **Subwords** (BPE, WordPiece) sit in between: frequent words become single tokens, rare words are spelled out from smaller pieces (`" foxes"` → `" fox" + "e" + "s"` after a few merges). **Byte-pair encoding** starts from single bytes and repeatedly glues together the most frequent adjacent pair, adding it to the vocabulary. **WordPiece** (BERT) is similar but picks the pair whose parts appear together *more than chance*, and encodes greedily by longest match.

passages.title: Tokenization: whitespace/regex, BPE from scratch, WordPiece — Core math / algorithms
passages.text: - **BPE training:** vocab = 256 bytes; repeat `V − 256` times: count adjacent pairs (weighted by word frequency), merge the most frequent pair `(a, b) → new id`. Pre-tokenization (a regex that splits words, numbers, punctuation, attaching a leading space) keeps merges inside words. - **BPE encoding:** within each pre-token, repeatedly apply the *earliest-learned* merge present. - Byte level ⇒ every string is encodable; `decode(encode(s)) == s` (tested on random Unicode). - **WordPiece score:** `count(ab) / (count(a)·count(b))`; encoding = greedy longest-match-first, continuation pieces prefixed `##`; if any position cannot be matched the word is `[UNK]`. - Sennrich et al.'s toy corpus `{low:5, lower:2, newest:6, widest:3}` gives first merges `e s`, `es t`, `est </w>`, `l o` (reproduced in the tests). - On the test corpus: 44 merges cut 4,020 bytes to 1,652 tokens; 144 merges to 871.

passages.title: Tokenization: whitespace/regex, BPE from scratch, WordPiece — Complexity
passages.text: Naive BPE training: O(merges × corpus size). Counting each distinct pre-token once (as here) makes it O(merges × unique words × word length). Encoding a word of length L with this simple loop is O(L²); production tokenizers use priority queues / tries and are written in Rust or C++.

passages.title: Tokenization: whitespace/regex, BPE from scratch, WordPiece — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Different tokenizers for training and inference (ids mean different things). - Whitespace handling: GPT-style tokens include the leading space (`" the"` ≠ `"the"`). - Counting characters instead of tokens for context limits and pricing. - Unicode: splitting a multi-byte character mid-way; byte-level BPE handles it, char-level may not. - Numbers and code tokenize poorly (digits split unevenly), which hurts arithmetic.

passages.title: Tokenization: whitespace/regex, BPE from scratch, WordPiece — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Generative LMs: byte-level BPE (GPT-2/3/4, Llama 3). BERT-family: WordPiece. Many multilingual models: SentencePiece (BPE or unigram LM over raw text, treats space as a symbol). - Classic NLP pipelines / bag-of-words: regex word tokenization + normalisation.

passages.title: word2vec: skip-gram with negative sampling, similarity, analogies — Intuition
passages.text: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps." Words that appear in similar contexts get similar vectors. Skip-gram turns this into a prediction task: from a word, predict the words around it. The vectors that make this prediction work become the embeddings. Predicting the exact neighbour out of the whole vocabulary (a huge softmax) is expensive. **Negative sampling** asks an easier yes/no question: "is this (word, context) pair real, or did I make it up by picking a random context word?" That is logistic regression with a few random "negative" words per real pair. Why analogies work: if `king` ≈ `royal + male + adult` and `queen` ≈ `royal + female + adult` in vector space, then `king − man + woman` lands on `queen`, because the "male" and "female" directions are the same everywhere.

passages.title: word2vec: skip-gram with negative sampling, similarity, analogies — Core math
passages.text: - Score `s = u_o · v_c` (context vector · center vector). - Loss per positive pair with k negatives: `−log σ(u_o·v_c) − Σᵢ log σ(−u_{nᵢ}·v_c)`. - Gradients: `∂L/∂v_c = (σ(s_o) − 1) u_o + Σᵢ σ(s_{nᵢ}) u_{nᵢ}`, `∂L/∂u_o = (σ(s_o) − 1) v_c`, `∂L/∂u_{nᵢ} = σ(s_{nᵢ}) v_c` (finite-difference checked). - Negatives ~ unigram^0.75. SGNS implicitly factorises the shifted PMI matrix `PMI(w, c) − log k` (Levy & Goldberg 2014). - Analogy (3CosAdd): `argmax_d cos(d, b − a + c)` excluding a, b, c.

passages.title: word2vec: skip-gram with negative sampling, similarity, analogies — Complexity
passages.text: O(pairs × k × d) per epoch; independent of vocabulary size (that is the point of negative sampling).

passages.title: word2vec: skip-gram with negative sampling, similarity, analogies — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Not excluding the query words in analogy search (the answer is usually `b` itself). - Using raw frequency for negatives (too many "the"); use the 0.75 power and subsample frequent words. - Comparing un-normalised vectors (use cosine). - Evaluating analogies on a vocabulary that misses the test words. - Expecting embeddings to separate senses: one vector per word mixes meanings ("bank").

passages.title: word2vec: skip-gram with negative sampling, similarity, analogies — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Cheap word features, similarity search, initialising models, studying semantics/bias. - GloVe (co-occurrence factorisation, `s5_nlp/glove`) gives similar quality; fastText adds subword n-grams for rare/misspelled words; contextual embeddings (BERT/GPT) give a vector per occurrence.

passages.title: Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — Intuition
passages.text: You face several slot machines with unknown payout rates and a fixed number of pulls. Every pull spent on a machine you're unsure about is *exploration*; every pull on the current favourite is *exploitation*. Too little exploration and you may get stuck on a mediocre arm; too much and you waste pulls. - **ε-greedy:** usually play the best-looking arm, occasionally a random one. - **UCB:** be optimistic: score each arm by its average *plus* a bonus that is large when it has been tried only a few times; play the highest score. - **Thompson sampling:** keep a belief (a probability distribution) about each arm's rate; imagine one plausible rate per arm by sampling from those beliefs; play the arm whose imagined rate is highest. Uncertain arms sometimes get lucky draws and get explored; clearly bad arms rarely do.

passages.title: Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — Core math
passages.text: - Regret: `R_T = Σₜ (μ* − μ_{aₜ})` (pseudo-regret, using true means). - Incremental mean: `Q ← Q + (r − Q)/n`. - UCB1 (Auer et al. 2002): `aₜ = argmax_a Q_a + √(2 ln t / n_a)`, regret `O(Σ_{a} ln T / Δ_a)`. - Thompson (Beta-Bernoulli): posterior `Beta(1 + successes, 1 + failures)`; sample `θ_a`, play `argmax θ_a`; also logarithmic regret, often the best in practice. - Lai-Robbins lower bound: any consistent strategy needs Ω(log T) regret.

passages.title: Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — Complexity
passages.text: O(k) per step for all three (a Beta sample per arm for Thompson). Memory O(k).

passages.title: Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Fixed ε: linear regret; decay it (e.g. ε ∝ 1/t) or use UCB/Thompson. - Forgetting to try every arm once before UCB (division by zero). - Ties: always picking arm 0 among equal estimates biases ε-greedy; break ties randomly. - Non-stationary rewards: plain averages adapt slowly; use a constant step size or sliding windows. - Measuring regret with realised rewards (noisy) instead of the true means when you know them.

passages.title: Multi-armed bandits: epsilon-greedy, UCB, Thompson sampling — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - A/B/n testing with adaptive traffic, recommendation and ad selection, hyperparameter search, clinical-trial-like allocation. - Context matters (user features) → contextual bandits (LinUCB, neural Thompson). Actions change future states → full reinforcement learning (`dynamic_programming`, `td_learning`).

passages.title: Value iteration and policy iteration — Intuition
passages.text: When you **know the rules** of the world (what each action does, with what probability, and what reward it gives), you don't need trial and error: you can *compute* how good every state is. - **Value of a state:** the total reward you expect from there onward. - **Bellman equation:** a state's value = immediate reward + (discounted) value of where you land. - **Value iteration:** start with all values 0 and repeatedly replace each value by the best one-step lookahead. Information spreads backward from the goal one step per sweep. - **Policy iteration:** pick a policy, compute exactly how good it is, then switch every state to the action that looks best under those values; repeat until nothing changes.

passages.title: Value iteration and policy iteration — Core math
passages.text: - Bellman expectation: `V^π(s) = Σ_{s'} P(s'|s, π(s)) [r + γ V^π(s')]` — a linear system `V = R_π + γ P_π V` (iterative evaluation matches `np.linalg.solve`, tested). - Bellman optimality: `V*(s) = max_a Σ_{s'} P(s'|s,a) [r + γ V*(s')]`; greedy policy `π*(s) = argmax_a Q*(s,a)`. - Value iteration is a γ-contraction: error shrinks by a factor γ per sweep (geometric convergence). - Policy improvement theorem: the greedy policy w.r.t. `V^π` is at least as good as π; finitely many policies ⇒ policy iteration terminates (ties kept to prevent cycling).

passages.title: Value iteration and policy iteration — Complexity
passages.text: One sweep: O(|S|·|A|·branching). Value iteration: O(log(1/ε)/(1 − γ)) sweeps. Policy iteration: few iterations, each needing a full evaluation (O(|S|³) by linear solve, or many sweeps).

passages.title: Value iteration and policy iteration — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Updating terminal states (their value must stay 0). - γ = 1 with policies that never terminate: values diverge (fine here because every optimal path ends). - Policy iteration oscillating between equally good actions: break ties consistently. - Assuming a model: real problems usually don't give you `P` — that's what model-free TD learning is for. - Huge state spaces make tabular DP impossible (function approximation, then deep RL).

passages.title: Value iteration and policy iteration — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Small/medium MDPs with a known model: inventory, routing, games with known rules, planning inside model-based RL. Unknown model → Q-learning / SARSA (`td_learning`); huge state spaces → approximate DP / deep RL.

passages.title: Q-learning and SARSA on a gridworld — Intuition
passages.text: Dynamic programming needs the rules of the world. **Temporal-difference (TD) learning** learns from experience instead: act, see what happens, and nudge your estimate toward "the reward you just got plus what you now think the next state is worth". You learn from a guess about the future, updated one step at a time (bootstrapping), without waiting for the episode to end. - **SARSA** (on-policy) uses the action it will *actually* take next, including random exploratory moves, so it learns the value of its own cautious, exploring behaviour. - **Q-learning** (off-policy) uses the *best* next action, so it learns the value of acting optimally even while behaving randomly some of the time.

passages.title: Q-learning and SARSA on a gridworld — Core math
passages.text: - TD error: `δ = target − Q(s, a)`; update `Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α δ`. - SARSA target: `r + γ Q(s', a')` with `a' ~ ε-greedy(Q)`, the actual next action. - Q-learning target: `r + γ max_b Q(s', b)`. - Terminal transitions: target `= r`. - Convergence (tabular): Q-learning → Q* if every (s, a) is visited infinitely often and α decays suitably; SARSA → Q* if ε also decays to 0 (GLIE).

passages.title: Q-learning and SARSA on a gridworld — Complexity
passages.text: O(1) per step; memory O(|S|·|A|) for the table.

passages.title: Q-learning and SARSA on a gridworld — Common pitfalls
passages.text: - Bootstrapping from the terminal state (its value must be 0). - Using the greedy action instead of the actually-taken a' in SARSA (that turns it into Q-learning). - No exploration (ε = 0 from the start): the agent never discovers better paths. - Fixed learning rate in stochastic environments: estimates keep fluctuating (smaller α helps, as in the slippery experiment). - Judging an agent by its training returns vs its greedy policy: they answer different questions (above).

passages.title: Q-learning and SARSA on a gridworld — When to use vs. alternatives
passages.text: - Small discrete problems without a known model. Known model → DP (`dynamic_programming`). Large/continuous state spaces → function approximation (DQN = Q-learning with a neural net, replay buffer, target network); policy-gradient / actor-critic methods for continuous actions.

queries.text: Why is hash map lookup O(1) on average but O(n) worst case?
queries.answer: With a good hash and bounded load factor each bucket holds O(1) keys on average; adversarial or poor hashing can put all keys in one bucket.

queries.text: Chaining vs. open addressing?
queries.answer: Chaining is simple and tolerates high load; open addressing is cache-friendly and uses no pointers but needs tombstones on delete and degrades near full.

queries.text: Why is appending to a dynamic array / resizing a hash map amortized O(1)?
queries.answer: Doubling means each element is copied O(1) times on average across all inserts.

queries.text: How do you get top-k frequent in O(n)?
queries.answer: Bucket sort by frequency, since frequencies are bounded by n (a heap would give O(n log k)).

queries.text: What makes a good hash function?
queries.answer: Deterministic, fast, and spreads keys uniformly; equal objects must have equal hashes.

queries.text: Backtracking vs brute force?
queries.answer: Same search space, but backtracking abandons partial candidates as soon as they violate a constraint.

queries.text: How do you avoid duplicate permutations/subsets with repeated values?
queries.answer: Sort and skip `nums[i] == nums[i-1]` when the previous one was not chosen at this depth.

queries.text: Why are diagonals `r - c` and `r + c`?
queries.answer: Moving along "\" increases r and c together (difference constant); along "/" one rises as the other falls (sum constant).

queries.text: How do you speed up Sudoku?
queries.answer: Most-constrained-cell ordering, O(1) validity via row/col/box sets (or bitmasks), and constraint propagation.

queries.text: Time complexity of generating all subsets, and can it be better?
queries.answer: O(n · 2ⁿ); no, because the output itself is that large.

queries.text: lower_bound vs upper_bound?
queries.answer: First index with value `>= target` vs `> target`; their difference is the count of `target`.

queries.text: How do you recognise binary search on the answer?
queries.answer: You are asked to optimise a number, a candidate answer can be verified quickly, and feasibility is monotonic.

queries.text: Why does `while lo < hi` terminate?
queries.answer: `mid` is always `< hi`, so `hi = mid` shrinks the range, and `lo = mid + 1` shrinks it too.

queries.text: How does rotated-array search decide which half to keep?
queries.answer: One half is always sorted; check whether the target lies inside that sorted half's endpoints.

queries.text: What breaks with duplicates in a rotated array?
queries.answer: You cannot tell which half is sorted when the ends equal the middle, so you must shrink linearly in the worst case.

queries.text: Top-down vs bottom-up?
queries.answer: Memoization is closest to the recurrence and only visits reachable states; tabulation avoids recursion overhead and makes space optimisation easy.

queries.text: How do you find the recurrence?
queries.answer: Ask what the last step of an optimal solution looks like and what smaller problem remains.

queries.text: Why does Kadane work?
queries.answer: A best subarray ending at i either extends the best one ending at i − 1 or starts at i; a negative running sum can never help.

queries.text: Why can unique-paths use one row?
queries.answer: Each cell needs only the cell above (old value in the same slot) and the cell to the left (already updated).

queries.text: When does greedy fail for coin change?
queries.answer: When the coin system is not "canonical"; DP checks all last-coin choices.

queries.text: Why order interval DP by length?
queries.answer: `[i, j]` depends on strictly shorter ranges inside it.

queries.text: Why "last balloon" rather than "first balloon"?
queries.answer: The last balloon in a range has fixed neighbours (the range boundaries), which decouples the left and right subranges.

queries.text: What does Held-Karp save over brute force?
queries.answer: It forgets the *order* of visited cities and keeps only the set and the current city: O(n² 2ⁿ) vs O(n!).

queries.text: How do you represent and update a set in a bitmask?
queries.answer: Bit i for item i; OR to add, AND with the complement to remove, AND to test.

queries.text: Largest n for bitmask DP?
queries.answer: Roughly 20–22 for O(n · 2ⁿ) within a second or two in a fast language; less in Python.

queries.text: Why iterate capacity backwards for 0/1?
queries.answer: So `best[c - w]` has not yet been updated with the current item; iterating forward would let the item be taken repeatedly.

queries.text: Is O(nW) polynomial?
queries.answer: Pseudo-polynomial: W is exponential in its bit length.

queries.text: How do you recover which items were chosen?
queries.answer: Keep the 2D table and walk backwards: if `best[i][c] != best[i-1][c]`, item i was taken; subtract its weight.

queries.text: How do combinations vs permutations differ in coin change?
queries.answer: Coins-outer fixes an order of coin types (combinations); amount-outer allows any coin last (permutations).

queries.text: Why does greedy fail for 0/1 knapsack?
queries.answer: A high-ratio item can waste capacity; e.g. capacity 10, items (6, $7) and two (5, $5): greedy takes $7, optimal is $10.

queries.text: Explain the O(n log n) LIS.
queries.answer: Maintain the smallest possible tail for each length; binary search where each new element goes. The array's length is the answer.

queries.text: Why is `tails` always sorted?
queries.answer: A longer increasing subsequence's tail must exceed the tail of its own prefix, which is at least the smallest tail of that shorter length.

queries.text: How are LCS and edit distance related?
queries.answer: With only insert/delete allowed, `distance = len(a) + len(b) - 2·LCS(a, b)`.

queries.text: How do you reconstruct the edits?
queries.answer: Walk back from `D[n][m]`, at each cell moving to the neighbour that explains the value.

queries.text: How do you reduce space to O(min(n, m))?
queries.answer: Keep only the previous row; put the shorter string on the column axis.

queries.text: What does `i & -i` compute and why?
queries.answer: The lowest set bit: `-i` is `~i + 1`, which flips all bits above the lowest set bit and preserves that bit.

queries.text: Why are both operations O(log n)?
queries.answer: Query removes one set bit per step; update moves to a strictly higher power-of-two block per step; both are bounded by the number of bits.

queries.text: How do you count inversions with it?
queries.answer: Process elements in order; for each, count previously seen elements with greater rank, then insert its rank.

queries.text: How do you support range updates?
queries.answer: Store the difference array (range add / point query), or two trees for range add / range sum.

queries.text: Fenwick vs segment tree?
queries.answer: Same asymptotics for sums; Fenwick uses n memory and trivial code, but only supports invertible operations.

queries.text: Why does BFS give shortest paths in unweighted graphs?
queries.answer: Nodes are dequeued in non-decreasing distance; the first time a node is reached is via a shortest route.

queries.text: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph?
queries.answer: DFS with three colours (back edge to a gray node), or Kahn's algorithm leaving nodes unprocessed.

queries.text: How is that different for undirected graphs?
queries.answer: Any visited neighbour other than the parent is a cycle; or use union-find.

queries.text: When is a graph bipartite?
queries.answer: Iff it has no odd cycle; test with BFS/DFS 2-colouring.

queries.text: Is the topological order unique?
queries.answer: Only if there is a Hamiltonian path in the DAG (at every step exactly one node has in-degree 0).

queries.text: Why sort by end time for activity selection?
queries.answer: Finishing earliest leaves the most room; the exchange argument shows it is always safe.

queries.text: Give a counterexample for "shortest interval first".
queries.answer: `(0,5), (4,7), (6,11)`: the shortest one, `(4,7)`, blocks both others; optimal picks two.

queries.text: How do you compute the minimum number of meeting rooms?
queries.answer: Max number of simultaneously active intervals: min-heap of end times, or a sweep over sorted start/end events.

queries.text: How do you know a greedy algorithm is correct?
queries.answer: Exchange argument or stays-ahead proof; otherwise test against brute force and look for counterexamples.

queries.text: Why is fractional knapsack greedy but 0/1 knapsack not?
queries.answer: With fractions you can always fill remaining capacity with the best ratio; without them leftover capacity may be wasted.

queries.text: Why is heapify O(n) and not O(n log n)?
queries.answer: Half the nodes are leaves (0 work), a quarter move at most 1 level, and so on; the series sums to O(n).

queries.text: How do you find the k largest of a stream of n items?
queries.answer: Min-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, works online.

queries.text: How does the two-heap median work?
queries.answer: Max-heap for the lower half, min-heap for the upper half, sizes kept within one; the median is at the tops.

queries.text: Heap vs sorted array vs BST for a priority queue?
queries.answer: Sorted array: O(n) insert. BST: O(log n) everything but more overhead. Heap: O(log n) insert/pop, O(1) peek, tiny constant.

queries.text: Is heap sort stable? In place?
queries.answer: In place and O(n log n) worst case, but not stable.

queries.text: How do you get O(1) LFU?
queries.answer: Hash map for values and frequencies, plus one ordered set per frequency and a `min_freq` pointer.

queries.text: Why can `min_freq` just be incremented?
queries.answer: The key leaving the minimum group lands in the group one higher, which is therefore non-empty.

queries.text: LFU vs LRU trade-offs?
queries.answer: LFU protects long-term popular items but adapts slowly and suffers from stale high counts; LRU adapts fast but one scan of cold keys can flush hot ones.

queries.text: How would you fix stale counts?
queries.answer: Periodically halve all counts (aging) or use a time window.

queries.text: What would a heap-based design cost?
queries.answer: O(log n) per access, since each use changes a key's priority.

queries.text: Reverse a linked list iteratively and recursively; space?
queries.answer: Iterative O(1); recursive O(n) call stack.

queries.text: Why do slow/fast pointers detect a cycle?
queries.answer: Inside the cycle the gap between them shrinks by one each step, so fast must land on slow.

queries.text: How do you find where the cycle starts?
queries.answer: After they meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the entry (see math above).

queries.text: Why use a dummy head?
queries.answer: It gives every real node a predecessor, removing head special cases.

queries.text: Why merge sort rather than quicksort for linked lists?
queries.answer: Merging needs only sequential access and O(1) extra space; quicksort's partition relies on random access.

queries.text: Why a doubly linked list and not a singly linked one or an array?
queries.answer: Removing an arbitrary node in O(1) requires access to its predecessor; arrays need O(n) shifting.

queries.text: Why must nodes store keys?
queries.answer: Eviction starts from the list tail; you need the key to remove the map entry.

queries.text: How would you make it thread-safe?
queries.answer: A mutex around get/put; or sharding into several independently locked LRUs to reduce contention.

queries.text: How does `OrderedDict` implement this?
queries.answer: The same way: hash map plus a doubly linked list.

queries.text: How would you add TTL (expiry)?
queries.answer: Store an expiry timestamp in each node; check lazily on `get` and/or sweep periodically.

queries.text: Why is the greedy choice safe?
queries.answer: The cut property: the cheapest edge across any cut is in some MST.

queries.text: Prim vs Kruskal?
queries.answer: Same result; Kruskal sorts edges and uses union-find, Prim grows one component with a heap. Prim's O(V²) form wins on dense graphs.

queries.text: Do negative weights break them?
queries.answer: No; only relative order matters (unlike Dijkstra).

queries.text: How do Prim and Dijkstra differ?
queries.answer: Same skeleton; Prim's key is the single edge weight into the tree, Dijkstra's is the total distance from the source.

queries.text: How would you find the second-best MST or check uniqueness?
queries.answer: For each non-tree edge, add it and remove the heaviest edge on the cycle it forms; take the best such swap.

queries.text: Why does subarray-sum-equals-k need a hash map rather than a sliding window?
queries.answer: With negative numbers the window sum is not monotonic, so shrinking/growing decisions are not safe.

queries.text: Why length n + 1?
queries.answer: So that ranges starting at index 0 need no special case.

queries.text: How do you apply 10⁵ range increments to an array efficiently?
queries.answer: Difference array: two writes per update, then one prefix-sum pass.

queries.text: Can prefix sums answer range minimum?
queries.answer: No: min has no inverse operation. Sum, XOR and (non-zero) product do.

queries.text: Derive the 2D formula.
queries.answer: Add the big rectangle, subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, add back the corner that was subtracted twice.

queries.text: Implement a queue with two stacks; what is the complexity?
queries.answer: Amortized O(1): each element crosses from inbox to outbox exactly once.

queries.text: Why is sliding window max O(n)?
queries.answer: Each index enters and leaves the deque at most once.

queries.text: Why can smaller-and-older elements be discarded?
queries.answer: They expire sooner and are dominated by the newer larger element for every window that contains both.

queries.text: How does a ring buffer avoid shifting?
queries.answer: Head pointer plus modulo arithmetic; removing from the front just advances `head`.

queries.text: Deque vs linked list implementation?
queries.answer: Linked list has true O(1) worst case but poor cache locality and per-node overhead; ring buffer is contiguous and supports O(1) indexing.

queries.text: Why is quickselect O(n) on average while quicksort is O(n log n)?
queries.answer: Quickselect recurses into one side only, giving a geometric series instead of n work per level over log n levels.

queries.text: How do you get a worst-case linear guarantee?
queries.answer: Median-of-medians pivot selection.

queries.text: Why groups of 5?
queries.answer: It is the smallest odd size where the recurrence fractions sum below 1 (groups of 3 give T(n/3) + T(2n/3), which is O(n log n)).

queries.text: Heap vs quickselect for top-k?
queries.answer: Heap: O(n log k), streaming, O(k) memory. Quickselect: O(n) average, needs random access to all data.

queries.text: How do you find the median of an unsorted array in O(n)?
queries.answer: Quickselect for index n//2 (and n//2 − 1 for even n).

queries.text: Why is a query O(log n)?
queries.answer: At each level at most two nodes are partially overlapped; all others are fully inside (used whole) or outside (skipped).

queries.text: What property must `op` have?
queries.answer: Associativity, so partial results can be grouped freely; commutativity is not required if you keep left/right order.

queries.text: What is lazy propagation?
queries.answer: Deferring a range update by tagging the highest fully covered nodes and pushing tags down only on demand.

queries.text: Segment tree vs Fenwick tree?
queries.answer: Fenwick is simpler/faster for invertible ops like sum; segment trees handle min/max and richer range updates.

queries.text: How would you support "range assign" as well as "range add"?
queries.answer: Keep a richer lazy tag and define how tags compose (assign overrides earlier adds).

queries.text: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges?
queries.answer: A node may be finalised and later a cheaper route through a negative edge appears; the greedy choice is no longer safe.

queries.text: Why V − 1 passes in Bellman-Ford?
queries.answer: A shortest path without cycles has at most V − 1 edges and each pass extends correct prefixes by at least one edge.

queries.text: How do you detect a negative cycle?
queries.answer: If any edge can still be relaxed after V − 1 passes (Bellman-Ford), or some `dist[i][i] < 0` (Floyd-Warshall).

queries.text: Dijkstra's complexity without decrease-key?
queries.answer: With lazy deletion the heap holds up to E entries: O(E log E) = O(E log V).

queries.text: How would you find the path, not just the distance?
queries.answer: Store a parent pointer whenever a relaxation succeeds and walk back from the target.

queries.text: Why is a nested `while` inside the `for` still O(n)?
queries.answer: `left` only moves forward and at most n times in total across the entire run (amortized analysis).

queries.text: Why does min-subarray-sum need positive numbers?
queries.answer: So adding an element never decreases the sum and removing never increases it; that monotonicity justifies never moving `left` back.

queries.text: In character replacement, why is a stale `max_count` OK?
queries.answer: The answer only grows when a strictly larger true `max_count` appears; a stale value just keeps the window from shrinking below the best size already achieved.

queries.text: How do you track "window contains all of t" in O(1) per step?
queries.answer: Keep a `missing` counter of still-needed characters instead of comparing whole count tables.

queries.text: Fixed vs. variable window?
queries.answer: Fixed when the size is given; variable when you optimise the size subject to a constraint.

queries.text: Why is comparison sorting Ω(n log n)?
queries.answer: A decision tree distinguishing n! permutations has height at least log₂(n!) = Θ(n log n).

queries.text: What is stability and when does it matter?
queries.answer: Equal keys keep their original order; needed for multi-key sorts (sort by name, then stably by age) and for radix sort passes.

queries.text: Quicksort's worst case and how to avoid it?
queries.answer: Consistently unbalanced pivots; use random or median-of-three pivots, 3-way partitioning, and fall back to heap sort (introsort).

queries.text: Merge sort vs quicksort?
queries.answer: Merge: stable, guaranteed bound, O(n) memory. Quick: in place, cache-friendly, faster on average, not stable.

queries.text: What does Python's `sorted` use?
queries.answer: Timsort: finds existing runs, extends short ones with insertion sort, merges them; stable and adaptive.

queries.text: Why is the monotonic stack O(n) despite the nested loop?
queries.answer: Each element is pushed and popped at most once, so total pops ≤ n.

queries.text: How does MinStack give O(1) min?
queries.answer: Each entry stores the minimum of the stack at the time it was pushed; popping restores the previous minimum for free.

queries.text: Increasing or decreasing stack for "next greater"?
queries.answer: Decreasing: smaller elements wait on the stack until something larger pops them.

queries.text: In the histogram, what are a popped bar's left and right limits?
queries.answer: Right limit is the current index (first shorter bar to the right); left limit is the new stack top (first shorter bar to the left).

queries.text: Stack via list vs linked list?
queries.answer: Both O(1); a dynamic array has better cache behaviour and amortized O(1) push.

queries.text: What does the LPS / failure table store?
queries.answer: For each pattern prefix, the length of its longest proper prefix that is also a suffix: where to resume after a mismatch.

queries.text: Why is KMP O(n + m)?
queries.answer: The text pointer never moves back; `k` increases at most n times in total, so it can decrease at most n times in total (amortized).

queries.text: How does a rolling hash update in O(1)?
queries.answer: Subtract the outgoing character's weighted term, multiply by the base, add the incoming character, all modulo M.

queries.text: What if two different strings hash equal?
queries.answer: Verify with a direct comparison; choose a large prime modulus (or double hashing) to make collisions rare.

queries.text: How do you check if a string is a repetition of a smaller block?
queries.answer: Compute the longest border `b`; it repeats iff `n % (n − b) == 0` and `b > 0`.

queries.text: What is an SCC and why is the condensation a DAG?
queries.answer: A maximal mutually reachable set; if two SCCs lay on a cycle they could reach each other and would be one SCC.

queries.text: What does `low[u] == index[u]` mean?
queries.answer: No node in u's subtree can reach an earlier node on the stack, so u is the first-discovered node of its SCC.

queries.text: Why must cross edges to finished SCCs be ignored?
queries.answer: Those nodes cannot reach back to the current path, so using their index would wrongly lower `low`.

queries.text: Tarjan vs Kosaraju?
queries.answer: Same O(V + E); Tarjan uses one DFS and no reversed graph.

queries.text: How do SCCs solve 2-SAT?
queries.answer: Build the implication graph; the formula is satisfiable iff no variable shares an SCC with its negation.

queries.text: Why does inorder traversal of a BST give sorted output?
queries.answer: By the invariant, everything left is smaller and visited first, everything right is larger and visited after.

queries.text: How do you delete a node with two children?
queries.answer: Swap in its inorder successor (or predecessor) and delete that node instead.

queries.text: Can you rebuild a tree from preorder only?
queries.answer: Not in general; you need null markers, or a second traversal (inorder), or the BST property.

queries.text: What is the worst-case height of a BST and how is it avoided?
queries.answer: n (sorted inserts); self-balancing rotations keep it O(log n).

queries.text: Explain the recursive LCA.
queries.answer: Each call returns p, q, or None from its subtree; a node that receives non-None from both sides is the split point.

queries.text: Trie vs hash set for a dictionary?
queries.answer: Both O(L) lookup; the trie also answers prefix questions and shares prefixes, the hash set has less overhead and better cache behaviour.

queries.text: How would you implement autocomplete with ranking?
queries.answer: Walk to the prefix node, then DFS; or cache the top-k completions at each node for O(L) queries.

queries.text: How do you delete a word safely?
queries.answer: Track pass-through counts (or check for other children / `is_word` while unwinding) and remove only nodes no other word uses.

queries.text: How do tries help the grid word-search problem?
queries.answer: Search all words at once: DFS the grid while walking the trie, pruning as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any word.

queries.text: Space optimisation?
queries.answer: Compressed (radix) tries, arrays instead of dicts, or a DAWG that also shares suffixes.

queries.text: Why is it safe to move the shorter wall in the container problem?
queries.answer: Any container using the shorter wall and a closer partner is narrower and no taller, so it cannot be better.

queries.text: How does three-sum avoid duplicates without a set?
queries.answer: Sort, then skip equal neighbours for the fixed element and for the left pointer after a hit.

queries.text: Two-sum: hash map or two pointers?
queries.answer: Hash map is O(n) on unsorted input with O(n) space; two pointers is O(1) space but needs sorted input (O(n log n) if you must sort).

queries.text: What is the invariant in Dutch national flag?
queries.answer: `[0,lo)` zeros, `[lo,mid)` ones, `(hi,n)` twos, `[mid,hi]` unknown; the loop shrinks the unknown region to nothing.

queries.text: How does the O(1)-space rain water solution work?
queries.answer: Process the side with the smaller boundary; its water level is fixed by its own running max because the other side is at least as tall.

queries.text: What do path compression and union by rank each buy you?
queries.answer: Rank alone gives O(log n); compression alone gives O(log n) amortized; together O(α(n)).

queries.text: How do you detect a cycle in an undirected graph?
queries.answer: For each edge, if both ends already share a root the edge closes a cycle.

queries.text: Why does Kruskal use union-find?
queries.answer: To test in near-constant time whether an edge joins two different components.

queries.text: Can union-find delete an edge?
queries.answer: Not directly; process queries offline in reverse (deletions become unions) or use a rollback structure without path compression.

queries.text: Union-find vs DFS for connected components?
queries.answer: Same result on a static graph; union-find wins when the graph grows incrementally.

queries.text: Why central rather than forward differences?
queries.answer: Error O(ε²) instead of O(ε) for one extra function call.

queries.text: Why not make ε extremely small?
queries.answer: Subtracting nearly equal floats loses precision (catastrophic cancellation); error grows like machine_eps/ε.

queries.text: Why relative error?
queries.answer: It is independent of the gradient's scale.

queries.text: Why not train with numerical gradients?
queries.answer: Cost is proportional to the number of parameters per step; backprop is proportional to one forward pass.

queries.text: Your gradient check fails only for some units. What do you look at?
queries.answer: Kinks (ReLU at 0), a stochastic layer not being frozen, float32, or a broadcasting bug that sums over the wrong axis.

queries.text: Batch vs stochastic vs mini-batch?
queries.answer: Trade gradient accuracy for cost per step; mini-batch is the practical middle and uses vectorised hardware well.

queries.text: Why does momentum help?
queries.answer: It averages gradients, damping oscillation across steep directions and accelerating along consistent ones.

queries.text: Why does Adam need bias correction?
queries.answer: `m` and `v` start at 0, so early averages are too small by a factor `(1 − βᵗ)`; dividing by it fixes the first steps.

queries.text: What happens if the learning rate is too large?
queries.answer: Updates overshoot; on a quadratic the error grows whenever `η > 2/L`.

queries.text: Adam vs SGD?
queries.answer: Adam adapts per-parameter step sizes and converges fast with defaults; SGD with momentum can reach flatter minima and better test accuracy when tuned.

queries.text: Geometric meaning of the dot product?
queries.answer: `‖u‖‖v‖cos θ`: projection length times length; zero iff orthogonal.

queries.text: Why not invert a matrix to solve a linear system?
queries.answer: It costs more and amplifies rounding error; factorise and substitute instead.

queries.text: What does the determinant tell you?
queries.answer: The volume scaling factor of the transformation; zero means the matrix squashes space into a lower dimension and is not invertible.

queries.text: Why is QR preferred to the normal equations?
queries.answer: `cond(AᵀA) = cond(A)²`, so the normal equations lose twice as many digits.

queries.text: What is the rank and why does it matter in ML?
queries.answer: The number of independent directions in the data; low rank means redundant features (collinearity) and enables compression (LoRA, PCA).

queries.text: What do the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the covariance matrix represent?
queries.answer: Directions of maximal variance and the variance along each.

queries.text: Why is PCA usually computed with SVD?
queries.answer: It avoids forming `XᵀX` (better numerical accuracy) and gives the same components.

queries.text: How do you choose k?
queries.answer: Cumulative explained variance (e.g. 95%), a scree-plot elbow, or cross-validating the downstream task.

queries.text: Do you need to standardise before PCA?
queries.answer: Yes when features have different scales/units; otherwise the result reflects units rather than structure.

queries.text: How does PCA relate to an autoencoder?
queries.answer: A linear autoencoder trained with MSE spans the same subspace as the top-k principal components.

queries.text: A test is 99% sensitive with a 5% false-positive rate, prevalence is 1%. P(sick | positive)?
Why maximise the log-likelihood instead of the likelihood?
queries.answer: Same argmax (log is monotonic), products become sums, no underflow, easier derivatives.

queries.text: Derive the MLE for a Bernoulli.
queries.answer: `log L = h log p + t log(1−p)`; derivative `h/p − t/(1−p) = 0` ⇒ `p = h/(h+t)`.

queries.text: MLE vs MAP?
queries.answer: MAP multiplies the likelihood by a prior; with a flat prior they coincide, and with lots of data the prior's influence vanishes.

queries.text: How is cross-entropy loss related to MLE?
queries.answer: Minimising cross-entropy is maximising the log-likelihood of the labels under the model's predicted distribution.

queries.text: How do you make softmax numerically stable?
queries.answer: Subtract the max logit before exponentiating; the result is mathematically identical.

queries.text: Why do frameworks combine log-softmax and NLL into one loss?
queries.answer: To use the log-sum-exp trick and avoid `log(0)`; it also gives the simple gradient `p − y`.

queries.text: What is the gradient of cross-entropy w.r.t. the logits?
queries.answer: `softmax(z) − onehot(y)`.

queries.text: What is logsumexp intuitively?
queries.answer: A smooth, differentiable approximation of `max` whose gradient is the softmax.

queries.text: Softmax vs sigmoid outputs?
queries.answer: Softmax: classes compete, probabilities sum to 1. Sigmoid: independent probabilities per class. For two classes, softmax over `[z, 0]` equals `sigmoid(z)`.

queries.text: How does AdaBoost differ from gradient boosting?
queries.answer: AdaBoost reweights samples and is tied to exponential loss; gradient boosting fits new learners to loss gradients for any loss.

queries.text: What is a weak learner?
queries.answer: A model only slightly better than chance, e.g. a decision stump.

queries.text: Why is AdaBoost sensitive to outliers?
queries.answer: Exponential loss puts enormous weight on badly misclassified points.

queries.text: How are the learner weights chosen?
queries.answer: `α ∝ ln((1 − ε)/ε)`: zero at chance level, growing as the weighted error falls.

queries.text: Does AdaBoost overfit?
queries.answer: Test error often keeps improving after training error hits zero (margins grow), but with noisy data it can overfit badly.

queries.text: Define bias and variance.
queries.answer: Error of the average model vs spread of models across datasets.

queries.text: How do you tell if a model has high bias or high variance?
queries.answer: Compare training and validation error (learning curves).

queries.text: How does regularisation affect the trade-off?
queries.answer: Increases bias, decreases variance.

queries.text: Bagging vs boosting in this language?
queries.answer: Bagging reduces variance; boosting reduces bias.

queries.text: Does more data help a high-bias model?
queries.answer: Not much; it mostly reduces variance.

queries.text: Core, border, noise?
queries.answer: Core: ≥ min_samples within eps. Border: within eps of a core point but not core. Noise: neither.

queries.text: Advantages over k-means?
queries.answer: No k needed, any shape, handles outliers explicitly.

queries.text: How to choose eps and min_samples?
queries.answer: min_samples ≈ 2·d or domain-based; eps from the k-distance plot knee.

queries.text: Main weakness?
queries.answer: A single density threshold fails for clusters of different densities.

queries.text: Is DBSCAN deterministic?
queries.answer: Core and noise points yes; border points can depend on order.

queries.text: Gini vs entropy?
queries.answer: Very similar in practice; gini is slightly cheaper (no log), entropy penalises mixed nodes a little more. They rarely change the chosen split.

queries.text: How does a tree handle continuous features?
queries.answer: Sort the values and test midpoints between consecutive distinct values as thresholds.

queries.text: How do you prevent overfitting?
queries.answer: Pre-pruning (depth, min samples, min impurity decrease) or post-pruning (cost-complexity), validated by cross-validation.

queries.text: Why don't trees need feature scaling?
queries.answer: Splits depend only on the ordering of values, which monotonic rescaling does not change.

queries.text: Why is the algorithm greedy and is it optimal?
queries.answer: Finding the optimal tree is NP-hard; greedy is fast and usually good enough, especially inside ensembles.

queries.text: What do the E and M steps do?
