queries.answer: E computes posterior responsibilities; M re-estimates weights, means, covariances by responsibility-weighted MLE.

queries.text: Why does EM increase the likelihood?
queries.answer: It maximises a lower bound that touches the true log-likelihood at the current parameters, so improving the bound improves the likelihood.

queries.text: GMM vs k-means?
queries.answer: GMM: soft assignments, full covariances, probabilistic; k-means is its hard-assignment, spherical, equal-variance limit.

queries.text: What can go wrong with EM?
queries.answer: Local optima, collapsing components (singular covariance), slow convergence.

queries.text: How do you choose the number of components?
queries.answer: BIC/AIC or held-out log-likelihood.

queries.text: Why is it called *gradient* boosting?
queries.answer: Each tree is fitted to the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions: functional gradient descent.

queries.text: Bagging vs boosting in terms of bias/variance?
queries.answer: Bagging lowers variance of low-bias learners; boosting lowers bias of high-bias (weak) learners.

queries.text: What does the learning rate do?
queries.answer: Shrinks each tree's contribution so later trees can correct it; lower rate + more trees usually generalises better.

queries.text: How does XGBoost differ from classic GBM?
queries.answer: Second-order (Newton) objective, explicit regularisation of leaf weights and tree size, histogram/sparse-aware split finding, parallelism.

queries.text: How do you prevent overfitting?
queries.answer: Early stopping, shrinkage, shallow trees, subsampling rows/columns, min samples per leaf.

queries.text: Agglomerative vs divisive?
queries.answer: Bottom-up merging vs top-down splitting; agglomerative is far more common.

queries.text: How do linkages differ?
queries.answer: Single = nearest points (chaining), complete = farthest (compact), average = mean, ward = variance increase.

queries.text: How do you choose the number of clusters?
queries.answer: Cut the dendrogram at a large gap in merge heights, or use a validity index.

queries.text: Complexity?
queries.answer: O(n²) memory and O(n²)–O(n³) time.

queries.text: Relation to MSTs?
queries.answer: Single-linkage clustering is equivalent to building an MST and removing its k − 1 heaviest edges.

queries.text: Does k-means always converge? To what?
queries.answer: Yes, in finitely many steps, to a local minimum of inertia; hence multiple restarts.

queries.text: Why k-means++?
queries.answer: Spread-out initial centres give faster convergence and provably better expected objective than uniform random starts.

queries.text: How do you pick k?
queries.answer: Elbow on inertia, silhouette, gap statistic, or business/downstream needs.

queries.text: What shapes can it not find?
queries.answer: Non-convex or very unequal-variance clusters.

queries.text: How does it relate to GMM/EM?
queries.answer: It is the hard-assignment, equal-spherical-covariance limit of EM for Gaussian mixtures.

queries.text: How do you choose k?
queries.answer: Cross-validation; small k overfits, large k underfits; odd k avoids binary ties. A common starting point is √n.

queries.text: Why must features be scaled?
queries.answer: Distances add up raw differences, so large-scale features dominate.

queries.text: What is the curse of dimensionality for KNN?
queries.answer: Distances concentrate; the volume to cover grows exponentially, so neighbours are no longer "near".

queries.text: Training and prediction complexity?
queries.answer: Training O(1); brute-force prediction O(n·d) per query: the cost is paid at inference.

queries.text: Is KNN parametric?
queries.answer: No. It is non-parametric and instance-based: model capacity grows with the data.

queries.text: Derive the normal equations.
queries.answer: Differentiate `‖Xw − y‖²` to get `2Xᵀ(Xw − y) = 0`.

queries.text: When is the closed form a bad idea?
queries.answer: Very large d (O(d³)), data that does not fit in memory, or singular `XᵀX`.

queries.text: What are the assumptions of linear regression?
queries.answer: Linearity, independent errors, constant error variance (homoscedasticity), no perfect multicollinearity; normal errors for inference.

queries.text: Why squared error?
queries.answer: Smooth and convex with a closed form, and equals maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise. The downside is sensitivity to outliers.

queries.text: What happens with multicollinearity?
queries.answer: Coefficients become unstable (huge variance) though predictions may still be fine; regularise or drop features.

queries.text: Why not use linear regression for classification?
queries.answer: Outputs are unbounded, squared error is the wrong likelihood, and outliers far on the correct side still shift the boundary.

queries.text: Derive the gradient.
queries.answer: With `p = σ(z)`, `∂L/∂z = p − y`, so `∇_w = Xᵀ(p − y)/n`.

queries.text: Is the loss convex? Is there a closed form?
queries.answer: Convex, yes; closed form, no.

queries.text: What happens on linearly separable data?
queries.answer: MLE does not exist: weights diverge; regularise.

queries.text: How do you interpret a coefficient?
queries.answer: A one-unit increase in the feature multiplies the odds of the positive class by `e^w`, holding the others fixed.

queries.text: Precision vs recall — when do you favour each?
queries.answer: Recall for screening (missing cancer is costly); precision when false alarms are costly (spam filtering of important email).

queries.text: What does ROC-AUC mean probabilistically?
queries.answer: P(score of a random positive > score of a random negative).

queries.text: Why PR-AUC for imbalanced data?
queries.answer: ROC's FPR has a huge TN denominator and hides many false positives; precision exposes them.

queries.text: Macro vs micro F1?
queries.answer: Macro treats classes equally (sensitive to rare classes); micro treats samples equally.

queries.text: How do you check and fix calibration?
queries.answer: Reliability diagram / ECE; fix with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on a validation set.

queries.text: Why separate validation and test sets?
queries.answer: Validation is used to make choices and becomes biased; the test set gives an untouched final estimate.

queries.text: Why stratify?
queries.answer: To keep class ratios stable across folds, reducing variance in the estimate, especially for rare classes.

queries.text: What is data leakage? Give an example.
queries.answer: Information from validation/test reaching training, e.g. standardising with the mean of the whole dataset.

queries.text: Grid vs random search?
queries.answer: Random search covers important dimensions better for the same budget when only a few hyperparameters matter.

queries.text: What is nested CV?
queries.answer: An outer CV for estimating performance and an inner CV for tuning, so the tuning does not bias the estimate.

queries.text: What is the "naive" assumption?
queries.answer: Features are conditionally independent given the class.

queries.text: Why does it work despite the assumption being false?
queries.answer: The argmax can be right even when the probabilities are wrong; errors in dependence often affect all classes similarly.

queries.text: Why Laplace smoothing?
queries.answer: To avoid zero probabilities for unseen feature/class pairs; it is a MAP estimate under a Dirichlet prior.

queries.text: Generative vs discriminative?
queries.answer: NB models `P(x, y)` and converges fast with little data; logistic regression models `P(y | x)` and has lower asymptotic error with more data.

queries.text: Why is multinomial NB a linear classifier?
queries.answer: Its log-posterior is `b_c + w_c·x` with `w_c = log P(feature | c)`.

queries.text: Why fit PCA only on the training set?
queries.answer: Test statistics would leak into the projection.

queries.text: What does whitening do?
queries.answer: Makes the transformed features uncorrelated with unit variance.

queries.text: How many components?
queries.answer: Explained-variance threshold (e.g. 95%), scree elbow, or CV on the downstream task.

queries.text: Does PCA help every model?
queries.answer: No; it can discard low-variance directions that are highly predictive of the label, and tree models do not need decorrelated inputs.

queries.text: What is the reconstruction error?
queries.answer: `(n − 1) Σ_{i>k} λᵢ`: the variance in dropped directions.

queries.text: Bagging vs boosting?
queries.answer: Bagging trains strong learners independently and averages them to cut variance; boosting trains weak learners sequentially to cut bias.

queries.text: Why sample features at each split?
queries.answer: To decorrelate the trees; otherwise a dominant feature makes all trees similar and averaging helps little.

queries.text: What is the OOB error?
queries.answer: Validation error computed on rows left out of each tree's bootstrap sample (~37%), with no extra data.

queries.text: Does a random forest overfit as you add trees?
queries.answer: No; adding trees only reduces variance.

queries.text: Which hyperparameters matter most?
queries.answer: `max_features`, tree size (`max_depth` / `min_samples_leaf`), and enough trees for the error to plateau.

queries.text: Why does L1 give sparsity and L2 not?
queries.answer: L1's gradient has constant magnitude near zero (and the constraint region has corners on the axes); L2's gradient vanishes near zero.

queries.text: How does ridge fix multicollinearity?
queries.answer: `XᵀX + αI` is always invertible and well conditioned; variance of the estimates drops at the cost of some bias.

queries.text: Why can't lasso be solved in closed form or with plain GD?
queries.answer: `|w|` is not differentiable at zero; use coordinate descent, proximal gradient (ISTA), or LARS.

queries.text: What does regularisation do to bias and variance?
queries.answer: Increases bias, decreases variance; the best α balances them (found by cross-validation).

queries.text: What is the Bayesian interpretation?
queries.answer: Penalised least squares is MAP estimation: Gaussian prior ⇒ ridge, Laplace prior ⇒ lasso.

queries.text: What are support vectors?
queries.answer: Training points with `α > 0`: on or inside the margin; they alone define the boundary.

queries.text: What does C control?
queries.answer: The trade-off between a wide margin and few margin violations (inverse of regularisation strength).

queries.text: What is the kernel trick and why does it work?
queries.answer: The dual depends on the data only through inner products, so any positive semi-definite kernel can stand in for an inner product in an implicit feature space.

queries.text: Hinge loss vs log-loss?
queries.answer: Hinge is exactly zero beyond the margin (sparse solutions, no probabilities); log-loss never reaches zero and yields calibrated probabilities.

queries.text: Why does SMO optimise two variables at a time?
queries.answer: The constraint `Σαᵢyᵢ = 0` means one variable cannot move alone; two is the smallest feasible step and has a closed-form solution.

queries.text: Why Student-t in the low-dimensional space?
queries.answer: Heavy tails solve the crowding problem by allowing moderate distances to become large ones.

queries.text: What is perplexity?
queries.answer: A smooth measure of the effective number of neighbours per point; it sets each σᵢ.

queries.text: Can you trust distances between clusters in a t-SNE plot?
queries.answer: No; only local structure is preserved.

queries.text: Why is KL(P‖Q) asymmetric and why does that matter?
queries.answer: It heavily penalises putting neighbours far apart (large p, small q) but barely penalises putting non-neighbours close.

queries.text: t-SNE vs PCA vs UMAP?
queries.answer: PCA is linear/global; t-SNE is non-linear/local and slow; UMAP is non-linear, faster, and keeps more global structure.

queries.text: How is an autoencoder related to PCA?
queries.answer: A linear AE with squared error learns the same subspace as PCA (but not necessarily orthonormal axes).

queries.text: How do you stop an autoencoder learning the identity?
queries.answer: A narrow bottleneck, noise (denoising), sparsity or contractive penalties.

queries.text: How would you use an AE for anomaly detection?
queries.answer: Train on normal data; flag inputs with large reconstruction error.

queries.text: Why can't you sample new data from a plain AE?
queries.answer: Its code space has no known distribution and has holes; random codes are off the data manifold.

queries.text: What does a denoising AE learn?
queries.answer: To map corrupted points back onto the data manifold, which approximates the score (gradient of log-density).

queries.text: What is reverse-mode autodiff and why is it used for neural nets?
queries.answer: It computes the gradient of one scalar w.r.t. all inputs in one backward pass; nets have one loss and millions of inputs.

queries.text: Why accumulate gradients with `+=`?
queries.answer: A variable used in several places receives gradient along every path; the multivariable chain rule sums them.

queries.text: Why topological order?
queries.answer: A node may propagate only after all of its consumers have contributed to its gradient.

queries.text: Autodiff vs numerical vs symbolic differentiation?
queries.answer: Autodiff is exact up to float error and cheap; numerical is approximate and O(#params) evaluations; symbolic produces expressions that can explode in size.

queries.text: What does `zero_grad` do and why is it needed?
queries.answer: Resets accumulated gradients; otherwise each step would use the sum of all previous gradients.

queries.text: Gradient of `A @ B` w.r.t. `A`?
queries.answer: `G @ Bᵀ` (check shapes: `(m,n)·(n,k)ᵀ… → (m,k)(k,n) = (m,n)`).

queries.text: How do you handle broadcasting in backward?
queries.answer: Sum the gradient over the broadcast axes until it matches the input's shape.

queries.text: Why is reverse mode memory-hungry?
queries.answer: It stores all forward activations to use in the backward pass; gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory.

queries.text: Why is `log_softmax` implemented as `x − logsumexp(x)`?
queries.answer: Numerical stability; and its gradient becomes the simple `softmax − one_hot` combination.

queries.text: L2 weight decay vs decoupled weight decay?
queries.answer: Same for SGD; for Adam, L2 in the gradient gets rescaled by the adaptive denominator, so AdamW applies decay directly to the weights.

queries.text: What is perplexity?
queries.answer: `exp(average cross-entropy)`: the effective number of equally likely choices the model is torn between.

queries.text: What does temperature do?
queries.answer: Divides logits before softmax; lower sharpens, higher flattens.

queries.text: Why truncate BPTT?
queries.answer: Memory and compute grow with sequence length; truncation trades very-long-range credit assignment for feasibility.

queries.text: Why clip gradients in RNNs?
queries.answer: Repeated multiplication through time can produce huge gradients that wreck the weights in one step.

queries.text: Character vs word vs subword models?
queries.answer: Characters: tiny vocab, long sequences. Words: short sequences, huge vocab and out-of-vocabulary problems. Subwords: the practical middle ground.

queries.text: Why do CNNs need fewer parameters than MLPs on images?
queries.answer: Local connectivity and weight sharing: one small filter is reused at every position.

queries.text: What is im2col and why use it?
queries.answer: Unrolling patches into columns so convolution becomes one GEMM; costs extra memory.

queries.text: Output size of a conv layer?
What does pooling do?
queries.answer: Downsamples and adds local translation invariance; gradient flows only through the max (max pool).

queries.text: What is the receptive field?
queries.answer: The region of the input that influences one output unit; it grows with depth, kernel size, stride and pooling.

queries.text: What does the discriminator converge to at equilibrium?
queries.answer: `D(x) = ½` everywhere when `p_G = p_data`.

queries.text: Why the non-saturating generator loss?
queries.answer: The original loss has near-zero gradient when D easily rejects fakes; `−log D(G(z))` is steep there.

queries.text: What is mode collapse and how do you detect it?
queries.answer: The generator covers only some modes of the data; measure coverage/diversity (e.g. modes hit, recall metrics).

queries.text: What does the original GAN objective minimise?
queries.answer: Jensen–Shannon divergence (up to constants) when D is optimal.

queries.text: GAN vs VAE?
queries.answer: GANs: sharp samples, no likelihood, unstable training. VAEs: stable, likelihood bound, blurrier samples.

queries.text: Why do neural nets need non-linear activations?
queries.answer: A composition of linear maps is linear.

queries.text: Why not initialise weights to zero?
queries.answer: Hidden units would compute identical outputs and receive identical gradients forever.

queries.text: Xavier vs He?
queries.answer: Xavier assumes a symmetric, roughly linear activation; He doubles the variance to compensate for ReLU zeroing half the inputs.

queries.text: What are vanishing/exploding gradients?
queries.answer: Gradients scale like a product of per-layer factors; if those are < 1 or > 1 the product decays or blows up exponentially with depth.

queries.text: Why is ReLU popular?
queries.answer: Cheap, non-saturating for positive inputs (gradient 1), sparse activations; downside: dead units.

queries.text: BN vs LN?
queries.answer: BN normalises each feature over the batch; LN normalises each sample over its features. LN is batch-independent, identical at train and test.

queries.text: Why the learnable γ and β?
queries.answer: So the layer can undo the normalisation if that is optimal; normalisation should not restrict what the network can represent.

queries.text: What changes between training and inference in BN?
queries.answer: Batch statistics are replaced by running averages accumulated during training.

queries.text: Why does BN allow higher learning rates?
queries.answer: It keeps activations well scaled, so the loss landscape is smoother and updates are less likely to blow up.

queries.text: Why do transformers use LayerNorm?
queries.answer: Variable sequence lengths, small per-device batches, and autoregressive inference make batch statistics impractical.

queries.text: Why scale by 1/(1 − p) in dropout?
queries.answer: So expected activations match between training and test, letting inference skip dropout entirely.

queries.text: How is dropout an ensemble?
queries.answer: Each mask defines a sub-network sharing weights; test-time scaling approximates averaging their predictions.

queries.text: What does weight decay do to the update?
queries.answer: Multiplies weights by `(1 − ηλ)` each step before the gradient step: exponential shrinkage toward zero.

queries.text: Why warm up the learning rate?
queries.answer: Early gradients (and Adam's moment estimates) are noisy and can push weights into bad regions; warm-up stabilises training, especially for transformers.

queries.text: Early stopping as regularisation?
queries.answer: Stopping when validation loss stops improving limits how far weights move from initialisation, similar in effect to L2.

queries.text: What problem do residual connections solve?
queries.answer: Degradation of very deep plain nets: hard optimisation and badly scaled gradients; they make identity mappings easy.

queries.text: Why does `F(x) + x` help gradients?
queries.answer: The derivative contains an identity term, giving a direct path for the gradient through every block.

queries.text: What if input and output shapes differ?
queries.answer: Use a projection shortcut (1×1 conv with stride).

queries.text: Why global average pooling?
queries.answer: Fewer parameters than flattening, and works for any input size.

queries.text: How are transformers related?
queries.answer: Each attention/MLP sublayer is a residual block on the "residual stream" with layer norm.

queries.text: Why do vanilla RNNs suffer from vanishing gradients?
queries.answer: BPTT multiplies T Jacobians whose norms are typically < 1, so the product decays exponentially.

queries.text: How does the LSTM fix it?
queries.answer: The cell state is updated additively and its gradient is scaled only by the forget gate, giving an uninterrupted path for gradient flow.

queries.text: LSTM vs GRU?
queries.answer: GRU merges cell and hidden state and uses two gates; fewer parameters, often similar accuracy.

queries.text: How do you handle exploding gradients?
queries.answer: Gradient norm clipping; careful initialisation.

queries.text: Why did transformers replace RNNs for most NLP?
queries.answer: Attention connects any two positions in one step and trains in parallel across the sequence.

queries.text: Why share weights between the two branches?
queries.answer: Both inputs must be mapped into the same space; sharing also makes the distance symmetric and halves the parameters.

queries.text: What does the margin do?
queries.answer: Dissimilar pairs only incur loss when closer than `m`, so the model does not waste capacity pushing them infinitely apart.

queries.text: Contrastive vs triplet loss?
queries.answer: Contrastive uses absolute distances on pairs; triplet uses relative distances (positive closer than negative by a margin).

queries.text: How do you do one-shot classification with it?
queries.answer: Embed one labelled example per class; label a query with the class of its nearest example.

queries.text: Why might it fail on new classes?
queries.answer: Too few/too similar training classes: the embedding specialises instead of learning general features.

queries.text: Why skip connections in a U-Net?
queries.answer: To restore spatial detail lost during downsampling by giving the decoder high-resolution encoder features.

queries.text: Concatenation vs addition for skips?
queries.answer: U-Net concatenates (decoder can choose how to mix); ResNets add (identity path for gradients).

queries.text: Why Dice loss?
queries.answer: It directly optimises overlap and is robust to class imbalance.

queries.text: IoU vs Dice?
queries.answer: Monotonically related; Dice weights true positives more heavily.

queries.text: What does a transposed convolution do?
queries.answer: Learned upsampling: the adjoint (gradient) of a strided convolution.

queries.text: What is the reparameterisation trick?
queries.answer: Writing `z = μ + σε` so sampling is a differentiable function of the parameters and backprop works.

queries.text: What are the two terms of the ELBO?
queries.answer: Reconstruction (expected log-likelihood) and KL to the prior.

queries.text: Why is the ELBO a lower bound?
queries.answer: `log p(x) = ELBO + KL(q(z|x) ‖ p(z|x))` and KL ≥ 0.

queries.text: What is posterior collapse?
queries.answer: The decoder models the data without using z, so the encoder matches the prior and the KL term vanishes.

queries.text: VAE vs autoencoder?
queries.answer: A VAE is probabilistic and regularised to a prior, so its latent space can be sampled; a plain AE only learns to reconstruct.

queries.text: Why divide by √d_k?
queries.answer: To keep score variance ≈ 1 so the softmax does not saturate and gradients do not vanish.

queries.text: What are Q, K, V?
queries.answer: Learned projections of the inputs: queries are matched against keys, and the matching weights average the values.

queries.text: Why multiple heads?
queries.answer: Each head attends in a different subspace, letting the layer capture several relationships at once for the same cost.

queries.text: What is the complexity of self-attention?
queries.answer: O(T²·d) time, O(T²) memory.

queries.text: What does the causal mask do?
queries.answer: Prevents positions from attending to the future so a model can be trained to predict the next token in parallel.

queries.text: BERT vs GPT?
queries.answer: BERT is a bidirectional encoder trained with masked LM; GPT is a causal decoder trained with next-token prediction. BERT for understanding, GPT for generation.

queries.text: Why the 80/10/10 masking scheme?
queries.answer: To reduce the mismatch between pre-training (which has `[MASK]`) and fine-tuning (which doesn't), and to keep all token representations informative.

queries.text: What is the [CLS] token for?
queries.answer: A position whose final state summarises the sequence for classification.

queries.text: Why does bag-of-words fail on this data?
queries.answer: It discards order, so it cannot tell which adjective "not" modifies or which clause follows "but".

queries.text: Pre-training vs fine-tuning?
queries.answer: Self-supervised learning on unlabelled text, then supervised adaptation of all (or some) weights on a small labelled set.

queries.text: How does BM25 differ from TF-IDF?
queries.answer: Saturating term frequency and explicit document-length normalisation, with tunable k₁ and b.

queries.text: What do k₁ and b control?
queries.answer: k₁ how fast repeated terms stop adding score; b how strongly long documents are penalised.

queries.text: Why an inverted index?
queries.answer: Scoring only documents containing a query term makes search sub-linear in corpus size.

queries.text: When does BM25 beat dense retrieval?
queries.answer: Rare exact terms, out-of-domain data, identifiers; no training needed.

queries.text: How would you evaluate a retriever?
queries.answer: Recall@k (does the answer reach the reranker), MRR/NDCG for ranking quality, on held-out queries with relevance labels.

queries.text: What does IDF do?
queries.answer: Down-weights terms that occur in many documents and up-weights rare, discriminative terms.

queries.text: Why L2-normalise TF-IDF vectors?
queries.answer: So long documents do not get larger scores just for being long, and cosine similarity becomes a dot product.

queries.text: Limitations of bag of words?
queries.answer: No word order, no semantics (synonyms are unrelated dimensions), huge sparse vectors.

queries.text: Why is sublinear tf useful?
queries.answer: The 20th occurrence of a word adds much less evidence than the first; log scaling reflects that.

queries.text: TF-IDF vs BM25?
queries.answer: BM25 saturates term frequency and normalises by document length with tunable parameters; it usually ranks better for search.

queries.text: Bi-encoder vs cross-encoder?
queries.answer: Bi-encoders embed query and document separately (indexable, fast); cross-encoders read them together (more accurate, used to rerank a short list).

queries.text: What are in-batch negatives?
queries.answer: Using the other examples' positives in the batch as negatives, giving B−1 negatives per query for free.

queries.text: How does IVF speed up search and what does it cost?
queries.answer: Scans only the nearest clusters; may miss neighbours in unprobed clusters (lower recall).

queries.text: IVF vs HNSW?
queries.answer: IVF partitions by clustering (cheap memory, tunable n_probe); HNSW navigates a multi-layer proximity graph (excellent recall/latency, more memory, slower builds).

queries.text: Why might BM25 beat dense retrieval?
queries.answer: Domain shift or small training data for the encoder, and queries dominated by exact keywords.

queries.text: Why does BLEU clip n-gram counts?
queries.answer: So repeating a common word cannot inflate precision.

queries.text: Why the brevity penalty?
queries.answer: Precision alone rewards very short outputs.

queries.text: BLEU vs ROUGE?
queries.answer: BLEU is precision-oriented over n-grams; ROUGE(-L) is recall-oriented and LCS allows gaps.

queries.text: MRR vs NDCG?
queries.answer: MRR only cares about the first relevant hit; NDCG uses all hits with graded relevance and position discounting.

queries.text: Limitations of n-gram metrics?
queries.answer: Insensitive to meaning; penalise valid paraphrases; correlate weakly with human judgement for open-ended text.

queries.text: GloVe vs word2vec?
queries.answer: GloVe fits global co-occurrence counts (log-bilinear regression); word2vec learns from local windows by SGD. They are closely related (both factorise PMI-like matrices).

queries.text: Why the weighting function?
queries.answer: Rare co-occurrences are noisy and very frequent ones uninformative; `f` balances them and is 0 for unseen pairs.

queries.text: Why log counts?
queries.answer: So that dot products model log probabilities and ratios become differences.

queries.text: Why add the two vector tables?
queries.answer: The objective is symmetric; summing reduces noise.

queries.text: What is PPMI?
queries.answer: `max(0, log P(i,j)/(P(i)P(j)))`: how much more often two words co-occur than chance.

queries.text: What does the causal mask do and why does it allow parallel training?
queries.answer: Each position sees only the past, so all T next-token predictions are valid simultaneously.

queries.text: What is the KV cache and what does it cost?
queries.answer: Stored keys/values of past tokens; makes each decoding step O(T) instead of recomputing O(T²), using memory proportional to layers × T × d.

queries.text: Pre-norm vs post-norm?
queries.answer: Pre-norm (LN before each sublayer) keeps a clean residual path and trains stably without careful warm-up.

queries.text: Temperature, top-k, top-p?
queries.answer: Temperature sharpens/flattens; top-k truncates to k tokens; top-p truncates to the smallest set with cumulative probability p (adapts to the model's confidence).

queries.text: Why weight tying?
queries.answer: Fewer parameters and a consistent mapping between input and output token spaces; usually improves perplexity for small models.

queries.text: What does LoRA assume?
queries.answer: The weight update needed for adaptation has low intrinsic rank.

queries.text: Why initialise B to zero?
queries.answer: So ΔW = 0 at the start and the adapted model equals the pretrained one.

queries.text: Does LoRA slow down inference?
queries.answer: Not after merging ΔW into W.

queries.text: Where does the memory saving come from?
queries.answer: No gradients/optimiser states for frozen weights; only r(d_in + d_out) parameters per adapted layer are trained and stored per task.

queries.text: What does α do?
queries.answer: Scales the update (`α/r`), decoupling the effective step size from the rank.

queries.text: Define perplexity.
queries.answer: `exp` of the average negative log-likelihood per token; the effective branching factor.

queries.text: Why smooth?
queries.answer: Unseen n-grams get probability 0 under MLE, making test perplexity infinite and overfitting the training counts.

queries.text: Why is add-1 bad for language?
queries.answer: With a large vocabulary it hands most of the probability mass to the huge number of unseen n-grams.

queries.text: What makes Kneser-Ney special?
queries.answer: Absolute discounting plus continuation counts for the lower-order distribution.

queries.text: What is the Markov assumption here?
queries.answer: The next word depends only on the previous `n − 1` words.

queries.text: Why do transformers need positional encodings?
queries.answer: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant; it cannot otherwise distinguish orderings.

queries.text: Why sines and cosines of geometric frequencies?
queries.answer: Unique, bounded codes for every position, and a shift is a fixed linear map, which makes relative position learnable.

queries.text: How does RoPE encode relative position?
queries.answer: Rotating q and k by position-dependent angles makes their dot product depend only on the position difference.

queries.text: Added vs multiplicative encodings?
queries.answer: Sinusoidal/learned are added to embeddings once; RoPE is applied inside every attention layer to q and k.

queries.text: What happens beyond the training context length?
queries.answer: Learned absolute embeddings have no vector; RoPE sees unfamiliar angles and degrades unless scaled.

queries.text: Why RAG instead of fine-tuning for knowledge?
queries.answer: Up-to-date and private knowledge without retraining, citations, and fewer hallucinations about facts in the corpus.

queries.text: What are the main failure modes?
queries.answer: Retrieval misses, poor chunking, the generator ignoring or misreading context, and context windows overflowing.

queries.text: How do you evaluate a RAG system?
queries.answer: Separately: retrieval (recall@k, MRR) and answer quality (exact match/F1, ROUGE, faithfulness to sources, human or model-based judging).

queries.text: Extractive vs abstractive answering?
queries.answer: Extractive quotes spans (verifiable, limited); abstractive writes new text (fluent, can hallucinate).

queries.text: How would you improve this system?
queries.answer: Better retrieval (hybrid + reranker), smarter chunking, and an abstractive generator conditioned on the retrieved passages.

queries.text: What problem does attention solve in seq2seq?
queries.answer: The fixed-size bottleneck vector: the decoder can look back at all encoder states.

queries.text: Additive (Bahdanau) vs multiplicative (Luong) attention?
queries.answer: Additive scores with a small MLP; multiplicative uses a (scaled) dot product, which is faster and is what transformers use.

queries.text: What is teacher forcing and its downside?
queries.answer: Feeding ground-truth previous tokens during training; mismatch with inference (exposure bias).

queries.text: Why a bidirectional encoder?
queries.answer: Each position's state then summarises both its left and right context.

queries.text: Greedy vs beam search?
queries.answer: Greedy takes the best token each step; beam search keeps the k best partial sequences and usually finds higher-probability outputs.

queries.text: Why subword tokenization?
queries.answer: Bounded vocabulary, no out-of-vocabulary words, and short sequences for common text.

queries.text: How does BPE training work?
queries.answer: Start from characters/bytes and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.

queries.text: BPE vs WordPiece?
queries.answer: BPE merges by raw frequency; WordPiece by a likelihood ratio; WordPiece encodes greedily by longest match and marks continuations with `##`.

queries.text: Why byte-level BPE?
queries.answer: The 256-byte base alphabet can represent any Unicode string, so there is never an unknown token.

queries.text: How does vocabulary size trade off?
queries.answer: Bigger vocab → shorter sequences but a larger embedding matrix and rarer, less-trained tokens.

queries.text: Skip-gram vs CBOW?
queries.answer: Skip-gram predicts context from the center word (better for rare words); CBOW predicts the center from averaged context (faster).

queries.text: Why negative sampling?
queries.answer: It replaces an O(V) softmax with k + 1 binary classifications.

queries.text: Why unigram^0.75 for negatives?
queries.answer: It balances sampling frequent and rare words.

queries.text: Why do vector analogies work?
queries.answer: Consistent relationships correspond to consistent offset directions in the embedding space (a linear structure in log co-occurrence statistics).

queries.text: What does SGNS optimise implicitly?
queries.answer: A factorisation of the PMI matrix shifted by log k.

queries.text: What is the exploration-exploitation trade-off?
queries.answer: Gathering information about uncertain options vs using the best-known option.

queries.text: Why does UCB work?
queries.answer: Optimism: an arm is played either because it is good or because it is uncertain; the bonus shrinks with more pulls, so bad arms are tried only O(log T) times.

queries.text: How does Thompson sampling explore?
queries.answer: Through posterior uncertainty: each arm is chosen with the probability that it is optimal.

queries.text: Regret of ε-greedy with fixed ε?
queries.answer: Linear in T, because it keeps exploring at a constant rate.

queries.text: Bandits vs A/B tests?
queries.answer: A/B tests split traffic evenly and pay full regret during the test; bandits shift traffic toward the winner as evidence accumulates.

queries.text: Value iteration vs policy iteration?
queries.answer: VI does one Bellman optimality backup per sweep (many cheap sweeps); PI fully evaluates then improves (few expensive iterations). Both converge to the optimum.

queries.text: Why does value iteration converge?
queries.answer: The Bellman optimality operator is a γ-contraction in the max norm, so it has a unique fixed point reached geometrically.

queries.text: What does γ do?
queries.answer: Weighs future rewards; smaller γ = more short-sighted, and faster convergence.

queries.text: What is the difference between V and Q?
queries.answer: V(s) is the value of a state; Q(s, a) the value of taking a in s then acting optimally; `V(s) = max_a Q(s, a)`.

queries.text: Why does slipping change the optimal path here?
queries.answer: The expected cost of a −100 fall outweighs the few extra −1 steps of a safer route.

queries.text: On-policy vs off-policy?
queries.answer: On-policy (SARSA) evaluates the policy it follows; off-policy (Q-learning) learns about a different (greedy) policy from exploratory data.

queries.text: Why does SARSA take the safer cliff path?
queries.answer: Its targets include exploratory actions, so states near the cliff look dangerous under the ε-greedy policy it actually runs.

queries.text: What is bootstrapping?
queries.answer: Updating an estimate from other current estimates (`Q(s')`) rather than waiting for the full return.

queries.text: TD vs Monte Carlo?
queries.answer: TD updates every step with lower variance but some bias; Monte Carlo waits for the episode's actual return (unbiased, higher variance).

queries.text: What makes DQN stable where naive deep Q-learning is not?
queries.answer: Experience replay (decorrelates samples) and a slowly updated target network (stabilises the bootstrap target).
